The thermal noise change with temperature is small (< 1 dB across the full range). What matters more at high temperature is that LNA NF increases and PA gain decreases — both effects are larger than the thermal noise change itself.

NF2 Noise — Figure (NF): SNR degradation, Noise Factor, sensitivity Intermediate click to expand▾
Quick link — how this connects to DSA:
NF is the SNR degradation caused by your RX chain. It is the third term in the sensitivity formula after kTB+BW. Your system NF = 5.75 dB built up from the Friis chain — see NCH card. Full sensitivity derivation is in DSA card.
→ For the complete chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card.
NF + SNR_req NF = 5.75 → Sens shifts 5.75 dB worse Perfect RX (NF=0): sens = −104+(−1) = −105 Real RX (NF=5.75): sens = −99.25 dBm 5.75 dB penalty vs theoretical perfect RX

NF as SNR degradation — what it means in practice

Noise Factor vs Noise Figure:
Noise Factor (F) is the linear ratio: F = SNR_in / SNR_out. Always ≥ 1. A perfect device has F = 1. Noise Figure (NF) = 10·log(F) in dB. A perfect device has NF = 0 dB. Your system NF of 5.75 dB means F = 10^(5.75/10) = 3.76 — your chain degrades SNR by a factor of 3.76 (not 5.75 times — remember dB is logarithmic). The sensitivity formula uses NF in dB because all other terms are already in dB.
How NF directly sets your test injection level:
EXM injects at sensitivity threshold. Sensitivity = kTB_floor + NF + SNR_req. If your NF increases by 1 dB (e.g. cable gets longer, LNA degrades), sensitivity worsens by 1 dB, and EXM must inject 1 dB more power. If EXM is not recalibrated but NF increased, the test is now 1 dB too easy — you are testing above threshold without knowing it. This is why the DSA table is recalculated whenever hardware changes.
NF3 Noise — Friis cascade (why the LNA dominates) Advanced click to expand▾
Quick link — how this connects to DSA:
Friis cascade formula explains how your 5.75 dB system NF is built from individual component NFs. This NF feeds directly into the sensitivity formula. See DSA card for full chain, NCH card for numerical calculation.
→ For the complete chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card.

Why Friis means you only need to care about the LNA

The Friis insight — one worked example:
Imagine you have a 7 dB NF mixer after your 20 dB gain LNA. Its Friis contribution is (F_mixer − 1) / G_LNA = (5.012 − 1) / 100 = 0.040 linear = 0.17 dB to system NF. Now replace that mixer with a perfect 0 dB NF mixer. System NF improvement = 0.17 dB. Barely measurable. But reduce cable loss before the LNA by 0.5 dB — system NF improves by exactly 0.5 dB, directly improving sensitivity by 0.5 dB. This is the Friis insight: optimise before the LNA, not after it.
In your lab: the pre-LNA components you can actually change:
The duplexer and pre-BPF are fixed inside the RFFE — you cannot change them. The LNA is a fixed chip — you cannot swap it. The only pre-LNA component you control in the test setup is the cable from EXM to the RU port. Shorter, lower-loss cable = better system NF in your measurement = better apparent sensitivity. This is why cable quality and measured loss matter, and why the VNA cable loss measurement is step 1 of every sensitivity test setup.
NF4 Noise — Passive devices (attenuators, cables, filters add noise) Intermediate click to expand▾
Quick link — how this connects to DSA:
Passive devices add NF equal to their loss — this directly worsens system NF and therefore sensitivity. Every 0.1 dB extra cable loss before the LNA = 0.1 dB worse sensitivity.
→ For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card.

Why passive devices add noise equal to their loss

A resistor at room temperature generates thermal noise power = kTB. When a passive component like a cable attenuates a signal by X dB, it absorbs part of the signal power and replaces it with its own thermal noise. The result: the signal level drops by X dB but the noise floor drops by less (because the component adds its own noise). The net effect is exactly X dB of SNR degradation, which is the definition of X dB noise figure.

Why position relative to LNA is everything:
The Friis formula shows that each stage's NF contribution is divided by the gain of all preceding stages. A component before the LNA (G_preceding = 1 or less) adds its full NF. A component after the LNA (G_preceding = 100 for +20 dB LNA) adds only 1/100th of its NF to the system total. This is why the design rule is: minimise all loss before the LNA, and place the LNA as early in the chain as physically possible. Your duplexer and pre-BPF must be before the LNA for functional reasons (they select the band) but their loss directly degrades sensitivity.
Attenuator placement — the most common lab mistake:
When measuring TX power with EXA, you add a 30 dB attenuator to protect the EXA from the strong TX signal. This attenuator must go between the RU TX output and the EXA input — never between the signal source and the RU RX input. If you accidentally put the 30 dB pad in the RX path during a sensitivity test, you add 30 dB to system NF, and your measured sensitivity becomes 30 dB worse than reality. Always double-check the signal path before running any RX measurement.
Connector loss — the hidden NF contributor:
A single SMA connector in good condition has approximately 0.1–0.15 dB insertion loss. That is 0.1–0.15 dB of NF contribution if it is before the LNA. In a chain with 4 connectors before the LNA (source → cable → two adapters → RU port), that is 0.4–0.6 dB of additional NF from connectors alone. A damaged or incorrectly torqued connector can have 0.3–0.5 dB extra loss, immediately visible as sensitivity degradation. This is why the VNA connector inspection checklist exists and why torque specs matter for RF measurements.
NF5 Noise — The 5 types (thermal, shot, flicker/1f, white, burst) Advanced click to expand▾
Quick link — how this connects to DSA:
5 noise types exist. Thermal noise (kTB) is what the sensitivity formula is based on. Phase noise limits EVM. Quantisation noise limits ADC dynamic range. All three affect your daily measurements.
→ For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card.

The three noise types that matter most in your work

Of the five noise types, three are directly relevant to your daily testing. Thermal noise sets your sensitivity floor and is the subject of the entire DSA/NF calculation chain. Phase noise from the LO limits EVM and prevents high-order modulations from decoding. Quantisation noise from the ADC sets the dynamic range ceiling.

① Thermal noise — your sensitivity floor:
Generated by any resistive element at temperature above 0 K. Formula: P = kTB. In your RX chain, every lossy component (cable, duplexer, filter) generates thermal noise equal to its loss in power. The LNA amplifies both the signal and all the noise it sees, but its own added noise is small (NF = 2 dB). This is the noise the entire DSA framework is designed around — calculate it, characterise it per band, then test each band against its own correctly-adjusted threshold.
④ Phase noise — why it shows up in EVM failures:
The local oscillator (LO) that downconverts your RF signal to baseband is not a perfect single frequency — it has random phase jitter. This jitter appears as noise skirts around the carrier in the frequency domain. When the LO mixes with your signal, this phase jitter gets transferred to the baseband IQ constellation — the symbol points rotate slightly randomly, which increases EVM. Phase noise is why you see an EVM floor that does not improve even when SNR is excellent. For QPSK this is not a problem, but for 64QAM and 256QAM the tighter constellation margins make phase noise the limiting factor.
⑤ Quantisation noise — ADC dynamic range:
Every ADC rounds the analog signal to the nearest discrete level. With 12 bits, there are 4096 levels. The rounding error is the quantisation noise. SQNR = 6.02 × N + 1.76 = 6.02 × 12 + 1.76 = 74 dB. This means your ADC can cleanly handle signals up to 74 dB above the quantisation noise floor. If your signal swings too close to full scale (clipping), you get heavy distortion. If it is too weak (near the quantisation floor), you lose resolution. The VGA/AGC in your RX chain keeps the signal in the sweet spot — typically around −12 dBFS, well within the 74 dB dynamic range.
NF6 Noise — In practice (EXA preamp, sensitivity, RSSI cal, EXM saturation) Advanced click to expand▾
Quick link — how this connects to DSA:
NF in practice: the EXA preamp lowers the analyser NF for measuring weak signals. Per-band NF differences (B1=2.44, B8=3.15 dB) are what drive the different DSA offsets in the test table.
→ For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card.

How NF directly drives everything in your daily test work

NF is not an abstract concept — it is the single number that determines what power the EXM must inject for each band, what the EXA DANL must be to measure it, and whether a sensitivity failure is a hardware problem or a calibration issue. Every time you set up a sensitivity test, you are implicitly using NF.

EXA DANL must be lower than RU sensitivity — always check:
DANL (Displayed Average Noise Level) is the EXA's own noise floor — the minimum signal it can measure. For your sensitivity test to be valid, the EXA's DANL must be significantly lower than the signal you are trying to measure at the RU output.

In your test: EXM injects at sensitivity threshold (e.g. −97.5 dBm at RU port after cable). The PRACH detector inside the RU processes this. You read the result via CLI (get_rssi) or DU RSSI — you are not measuring the raw RF signal with EXA at this point. The EXA is used for TX measurements. But if you ever try to measure a weak RX signal directly with EXA, the DANL check is critical: EXA DANL at −130 dBm/Hz across 10 MHz = −130 + 70 = −60 dBm — safely below your −98 dBm system noise floor.
Why B8 has the highest NF (3.15 dB) and highest DSA:
At 900 MHz (B8), the transistor physics in GaAs/GaN LNAs produce slightly higher noise compared to 2 GHz. Additionally, the duplexer for B8 at 900 MHz is physically larger and has higher insertion loss than at 2 GHz — the filter Q-factor degrades at lower frequencies meaning you need a wider physical filter to achieve the same selectivity, which adds loss. These two effects combine to give B8 the worst NF in your band set. B41 at 2545 MHz has the best NF (2.0 dB) because there is no duplexer — TDD uses a T/R switch which has lower loss than a duplexer.
When measured sensitivity is worse than calculated — NF-based diagnosis:
If your sensitivity test fails by X dB, and you have confirmed cable loss and EXM calibration are correct, the excess degradation must come from the RX chain NF being higher than assumed. Break it down: measure cable loss with VNA → subtract from EXM output → compare to sensitivity formula → if residual error > 1 dB, the RX chain NF is degraded. The most likely causes in order: (1) LNA compression from a too-strong signal on a different port, (2) LNA bias voltage wrong after firmware change, (3) duplexer damaged (cracked ceramic), (4) connector oxidised adding loss before LNA.
NF_CAL Noise — NF calibration (Y-factor, ENR, hot/cold) Advanced click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRST NF calibration in one sentence: This is how you measure whether your LNA and RX chain are generating as little noise as expected. You inject two known noise levels (hot and cold) and measure how much noise the chain adds — that added noise is the Noise Figure. It tells you if the hardware is healthy, but it does not write any correction values.
Quick link — how this connects to DSA:
NF calibration uses the Y-factor method to measure actual system NF. This confirms whether NF matches the values used in the sensitivity formula. It does not write any correction — it only validates hardware health.
→ For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card.

What is NF calibration?

NF cal answers one question: how much noise does your RX chain add to the signal? This is a hardware characterisation measurement — it tells you whether the LNA, duplexer, and cable are performing to spec. It does NOT write any correction value — it just confirms (or flags) the hardware quality.

Key terms, each explained

ENR — Excess Noise Ratio
The "how much hotter than room temperature is the noise source" spec. ENR=15 dB means the source outputs noise equivalent to a resistor at 290 × 10^(15/10) ≈ 9200 K when switched ON. This is the known reference your calculation depends on. The noise source module has its ENR printed on it and also stored in its EEPROM so the EXA can read it automatically.
Y-factor
Y = N_hot / N_cold in linear power. If hot output is −60 dBm and cold output is −66 dBm, the difference is 6 dB → Y = 10^(6/10) = 3.98. The Y-factor is how much "more noise" comes out when you switch the source hot vs cold. A low Y means the DUT is adding so much noise of its own that the source temperature barely matters — i.e., high NF device. A high Y means the DUT is quiet and is faithfully amplifying the difference — i.e., low NF device.
T_hot and T_cold
T_cold = 290 K (standard room temperature, the IEEE reference). T_hot = 290 × 10^(ENR/10). When the noise source is OFF, it still generates thermal noise at 290 K — that becomes your cold reference. This is why you use the same physical source for both measurements: it removes cable and connector uncertainty from the result.
NF formula: NF = ENR − 10·log(Y−1)
Where this comes from: NF definition is SNR_in/SNR_out. For a two-port device with gain G and noise temperature T_e, the output noise is G·k·(T_cold + T_e)·B for cold input and G·k·(T_hot + T_e)·B for hot input. Taking the ratio cancels G and B, and solving for T_e gives you NF = 10·log(1 + T_e/T_0). Substituting T_e from the Y-factor ratio gives the formula above.
In your lab — no standalone noise source needed
The EXA N9010B has a built-in NF measurement mode under Meas → Noise Figure. It drives its own internal noise source through Port 1 output, sweeps frequencies, and automatically computes NF vs frequency. You connect EXA Port 1 → RU RX port (via calibrated cable), tell it your cable loss, and it plots NF(f) for you. You then read off the NF at your band centre (e.g. 1950 MHz for B1 UL). The EXA handles the Y-factor math internally.
When NF is worse than spec — what to check
If measured NF > spec by more than 1 dB: (1) Check cable loss — every 0.1 dB extra cable loss before the LNA adds 0.1 dB to measured NF. (2) Check connector torque — loose SMA can add 0.3–0.5 dB. (3) Check LNA bias — wrong supply voltage shifts NF. (4) Check for LNA compression — if signal level too high, LNA is not in its linear region and NF appears worse. (5) Duplexer damage — a damaged duplexer filter adds extra loss before the LNA, directly adding to NF.
GAIN_CAL Gain calibration — RX chain ADC_ADJUST, TX power trim, what each register means Advanced click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRST Gain calibration in one sentence: This is how you teach the radio to report accurate power readings. You inject a signal of exactly known power, see what the radio reports, and find the offset between them. That offset (ADC_ADJUST) is saved so future readings are accurate. RX gain cal = RSSI cal — they are the same procedure called by two different names.
Quick link — how this connects to DSA:
Gain cal (= RSSI cal for RX, power trim for TX) corrects the difference between theoretical and actual chain gain. ADC_ADJUST from RSSI cal absorbs all RX chain gain uncertainty into one offset number per band per ADC channel.
→ For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card.

RX Gain Calibration — what ADC_ADJUST really is

The RX chain has many components between the antenna port and the ADC register: duplexer, BPF, LNA, VGA, mixer, another BPF, then the ADC. Each one has gain or loss. Rather than calibrating each component separately, RX gain cal treats the entire chain as a black box and finds one single number — ADC_ADJUST — that converts any dBFS reading into an accurate dBm reading at the RU input port.

ADC_ADJUST
A calibration constant stored in hardware.json, one per band per ADC channel. Formula: ADC_ADJUST = P_known_at_RU_port − dBFS_reading. Once calibrated, converting any future reading is: P_dBm = dBFS + ADC_ADJUST. It absorbs the total chain gain between RU port and ADC register — so even though the LNA adds +20 dB, the VGA might be at +6 dB, and the mixer has conversion loss of −7 dB, you never need to know each individual value. The single offset does it all.
Why separate ADC_ADJUST per band and per ADC channel
Each band has a different LNA gain and filter response, so the total chain gain is different per band. B1 at 2140 MHz has slightly different gain than B3 at 1843 MHz — even though they may share physical hardware, the frequency-dependent component behaviour means each band needs its own cal constant. Per ADC channel (B1 uses ADC channels 0/1/4/5, B3 uses 2/3/6/7) further accounts for ADC input impedance variation and any mismatch in the IQ paths.
Temperature dependence — why RSSI can drift
LNA gain changes with temperature — typically −0.02 to −0.05 dB/°C for GaAs pHEMT LNAs. In a hot lab (40°C vs 25°C calibration temp), the LNA gain drops ~0.3–0.7 dB, which makes RSSI read 0.3–0.7 dB low. If you see systematic RSSI error that grows as the RU warms up, this is why. Some RU designs have temperature compensation tables that auto-correct ADC_ADJUST as a function of measured board temperature — check hardware.json for a TEMP_COMP array.

TX Gain Calibration — what TX_GAIN register controls

The TX chain starts with the baseband IQ signal at full digital scale, passes through the DPD block, DAC, upconverter, PA driver, and finally the main PA. The total gain from baseband to RF output is roughly fixed by hardware, but there is always ±2–3 dB unit-to-unit variation from component tolerances. TX gain cal trims a digital attenuator (or the PA bias point) until the output power at the coupler port exactly hits the rated target.

tx_calibration_eeprom.json
This is the file that holds the final TX_GAIN register values after calibration — one per band per column (A/B/C/D). It is written during factory calibration and stored in the RU EEPROM. When the RU boots, it reads this file and loads the register values before enabling TX. If this file is missing or corrupt, the RU falls back to default gain values which can be 6 dB low or high — this is exactly what caused the ~6 dB B41 power deficit you found on unit 26050509 (fault 12: missing tx_calibration_eeprom.json).
Coupler ratio — the BOB SMA is not antenna power
The BOB SMA port is a directional coupler output, not the main antenna port. The coupler splits a small fraction of the TX power for monitoring — typically the coupling ratio is 30 dB, meaning the BOB SMA sees 30 dB less power than what goes to the antenna. So B1 rated power at BOB SMA = −16.7 dBm corresponds to +13.3 dBm at the antenna connector, or roughly 21 W EIRP per column after antenna gain. Always measure at the BOB SMA — connecting EXA directly to the antenna port would overload it instantly.
DPD and its interaction with gain cal
DPD (Digital Pre-Distortion) must converge before you measure TX power — it actively adjusts its coefficients for 30–60 seconds after power-on or after any power level change. If you measure output power while DPD is still adapting, you will see power fluctuating ±0.5 dB and possibly a wrong ACLR. Always wait for DPD to converge (check the DPD status register or simply wait 60 s) before taking a TX power or ACLR reading used for gain calibration.
Gain cal vs RSSI cal — how they relate
They are the same operation from opposite ends of the RX chain. RSSI cal (ADC_ADJUST) calibrates the entire RX path as one unit. NF cal measures just the noise-adding property of that path. TX gain cal calibrates the TX path. All three together ensure that when EXM injects −95 dBm, the RU reports −95 dBm via get_rssi, and when the BBU commands rated TX power, the antenna port outputs exactly rated power. Any mismatch between these three is a sign something has drifted or failed.

What sensitivity physically means

Sensitivity is the minimum signal power at the RU antenna port at which the receiver can still decode data at 5% BLER (3GPP threshold). It is not fixed — it depends on bandwidth, modulation, and band. The sensitivity formula is not an approximation — it is an exact derivation from thermal physics and information theory.

Sensitivity vs RSSI — the critical difference:
Sensitivity is a threshold — the floor below which decoding fails. RSSI is a measurement — the actual received power at any instant. During a sensitivity test you set EXM to exactly the sensitivity threshold and verify the RU can decode. In normal operation RSSI is whatever arrives — could be −70 dBm (UE nearby) or −105 dBm (UE at cell edge). Sensitivity defines where the floor is. RSSI tells you where you currently are relative to that floor.
Why bandwidth degrades sensitivity — the bucket analogy:
A wider channel (wider bandwidth) collects more thermal noise — like a wider bucket catches more rain. The signal power stays fixed but noise increases, so SNR worsens and you need a stronger signal to decode. 5 MHz sensitivity is 3 dB better than 10 MHz. 20 MHz is 3 dB worse than 10 MHz. This is why the DSA table has separate rows for each BW — same band, different thresholds.
BLER 5% — why this specific threshold:
3GPP defines sensitivity as the point where Block Error Rate = 5%. Below this, too many blocks fail and the system cannot sustain a call. At 5% BLER the link is just barely functional — this is the edge of coverage. The test is binary: inject at threshold power, count block errors, pass if BLER ≤ 5%. This is measured via the PRACH detection rate in your RCT — PRACH preamble either detected or not.
DSA2 Sensitivity — modulation vs sensitivity (FRC, SNR, why QPSK wins) Intermediate click to expand▾
Quick link — how this connects to DSA:
SNR_required is the last term in the sensitivity formula. This card explains what drives it: modulation order and coding rate. QPSK 1/3 gives the best (lowest) sensitivity — this is why FRC A1 is the standard sensitivity test.
→ For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card.

What is FRC and why it determines sensitivity

FRC (Fixed Reference Channel) is a 3GPP-defined test waveform with fixed modulation, coding rate, and resource allocation. Different FRCs test different capabilities. FRC A1 (QPSK 1/3) tests sensitivity because it gives the most robust link — maximum coverage, minimum signal requirement. The sensitivity number you compare against in your DSA table is always FRC A1.

Why QPSK 1/3 gives the best (lowest dBm) sensitivity:
QPSK has only 4 constellation points — they are spread far apart in the IQ plane. Even with heavy noise, the receiver can correctly decide which of the 4 quadrants the received symbol falls in. The 1/3 coding rate adds heavy redundancy — for every bit of data, 2 extra error-correction bits are sent. Together these give an effective SNR requirement of −1 dB, meaning the signal can be 1 dB below the thermal noise floor and still be decoded. This is why QPSK 1/3 gives the best sensitivity and is the standard for coverage-limited testing.
DSA3 Sensitivity — DSA complete picture (kTB → NF → offset → UL → MRC) Advanced click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRST DSA in one sentence: Because each frequency band (B1, B3, B8, B28, B41) has slightly different hardware quality, they each have a slightly different "hearing ability" (sensitivity). DSA is the lookup table that tells the test instrument exactly how loud to play the test signal for each band — so every band gets a fair test at its own correct threshold, not someone else's.

DSA — the complete story in one card

DSA stands for Dynamic Sensitivity Adjustment. It solves the problem of testing multiple bands with one test framework: each band has a different sensitivity because each band's hardware (LNA, duplexer, filter) has different noise figures. Rather than hardcoding different thresholds manually, DSA calculates a per-band offset from the sensitivity formula and instructs EXM to inject exactly the right power for each band automatically.

Step 1 — kTB: the physics floor
kTB = Boltzmann constant × Temperature × Bandwidth. At room temperature (290 K), in a 1 Hz bandwidth: kTB = 1.38×10⁻²³ × 290 × 1 = 4×10⁻²¹ W = −174 dBm/Hz. This is the absolute minimum noise any receiver can have — it cannot be beaten. For your 10 MHz channel: add 10·log(10,000,000) = +70 dB → noise floor = −104 dBm. For 5 MHz: +67 dB → −107 dBm. For 20 MHz: +73 dB → −101 dBm. Every 2× increase in bandwidth raises the noise floor by 3 dB.
Step 2 — System NF: what your hardware adds
Noise Figure is how many dB of extra noise your RX chain adds on top of kTB. Your chain (B1): cable 2.5 dB + duplexer 0.5 dB + pre-BPF 0.3 dB + LNA 2.0 dB + post-LNA components ≈0 dB = 5.75 dB system NF. The Friis formula shows that LNA dominates because everything after it gets divided by LNA's linear gain (×100). Everything before the LNA (cable, duplexer, BPF) adds its full loss as NF — this is why cable length matters enormously for sensitivity.

Per-band NF: B1=2.44 dB · B3=2.40 dB · B8=3.15 dB · B28=2.73 dB · B41=2.00 dB. B8 highest because 900 MHz LNA has higher noise, and the B8 duplexer has more loss at lower frequency. B41 lowest because TDD uses a T/R switch instead of a duplexer — less loss before the LNA.
Step 3 — Sensitivity: combining it all
Sensitivity = kTB_floor + 10·log(BW) + NF + SNR_required

SNR_required depends on modulation and coding rate. For FRC A1 (QPSK 1/3) — the standard sensitivity test — SNR_req = −1 dB. QPSK has only 4 constellation points spread far apart, so the receiver can decode it even when signal is 1 dB below the noise floor.

B1 worked example: −174 + 70 + 5.75 + (−1) = −99.25 dBm
B3 baseline: −174 + 70 + 5.71 + (−1) = −99.29 dBm (slightly better NF)
B8 worst: −174 + 70 + 6.46 + (−1) = −98.54 dBm (higher NF = worse sensitivity)
Step 4 — DSA offset: per-band correction
B3 is the reference baseline (DSA = 0). For every other band: DSA = Sensitivity_band − Sensitivity_B3. This gives the number of extra dB EXM must inject for that band to hit the correct threshold. The DSA values in your table (5 for B1, 8 for B8/B28) also include empirical corrections for path configuration differences (LB uses 2 RX paths vs HB 4 paths), flavour-specific gain settings, and actual measured hardware performance — not just the theoretical NF difference alone.
Step 5 — RX paths: what rev5/rev1/comb mean
Your AAU is 4T4R — 4 independent RX columns (A, B, C, D), each with its own LNA, cable, and ADC channel.

rev5 = Column A tested alone (single path, worst case for that column)
rev1 = Column B tested alone (independent verification of second chain)
comb rev3 = Columns A+B+C combined via MRC (Maximum Ratio Combining). MRC weights each chain by its SNR and sums them. Gain ≈ +3 to 4 dB over single path.
comb rev1 = All 4 columns A+B+C+D via MRC. Best possible. Gain ≈ +5 to 6 dB.

Why test single paths? Because MRC hides individual column failures. If Column C's LNA is dead, comb rev1 might still pass — A, B, D compensate. The rev5/rev1 single-path tests catch dead columns that combined results would mask. This is exactly what happened with AAU #510 — B1C and B1D showed dead in single-path but combined was degraded not zero.
Step 6 — before vs after: the 0.2–0.5 dB gap explained
In the DSA table, every measurement has a "before" and "after" value. The DSA offset is already applied before this comparison — these are NOT showing the DSA offset itself.

before = theoretical sensitivity from the formula (what physics says it should be)
after = sensitivity measured on real hardware after DSA correction

The 0.2–0.5 dB gap = hardware residual: connector insertion loss variation (±0.1 dB), LNA NF not exactly at datasheet (±0.1 dB), filter passband ripple (±0.05 dB), cable slightly different from assumed (±0.1 dB). A healthy unit shows consistent 0.2–0.5 dB residual across all paths. A gap suddenly becoming 2–3 dB on one path = hardware fault on that specific column. This is how you catch degraded LNAs and bad connectors at the measurement level without disconnecting anything.
📐 DSA Worked Calculation — B8 vs B3 reference (step by step)
Step 1: Compute sensitivity per band
Base: kTB = −174 dBm/Hz
BW(10MHz) = +70 dB → floor = −104 dBm
B3: NF=2.40 → sens = −104 + 2.40 − 1 = −102.6 dBm
B8: NF=3.15 → sens = −104 + 3.15 − 1 = −101.85 dBm
B1: NF=5.75 → sens = −104 + 5.75 − 1 = −99.25 dBm
B28: NF=3.70 → sens = −104 + 3.70 − 1 = −101.3 dBm
B41: NF=2.75 → sens = −104 + 2.75 − 1 = −102.25 dBm
Step 2: Compute DSA offset (vs B3 reference)
DSA = Sens_band − Sens_B3 (reference)
DSA_B3 = −102.6 − (−102.6) = 0 dB (reference)
DSA_B8 = −101.85 − (−102.6) = +0.75 dB
DSA_B1 = −99.25 − (−102.6) = +3.35 dB
DSA_B28 = −101.3 − (−102.6) = +1.3 dB
DSA_B41 = −102.25 − (−102.6) = +0.35 dB
Positive DSA = inject more power (band is less sensitive)
Step 3: How EXM uses DSA
Base injection = −95 dBm (arbitrary reference). EXM actual = Base + DSA offset.
B3: EXM = −95 + 0 = −95 dBm · B1: EXM = −95 + 3.35 = −91.65 dBm · B8: EXM = −95 + 0.75 = −94.25 dBm
After cable loss (−2.5 dB): power at RU port = EXM − 2.5 dB
B1 at RU port: −91.65 − 2.5 = −94.15 dBm → compare to sensitivity −99.25 dBm → 5.1 dB above → PRACH detects reliably
What the DSA physically is (GRDEV-8102)
DSA = the RFDC ADC digital step attenuator on the AAU's RX path — it sits inside the RFSoC, right in front of each ADC, and is set in the personality file rfdc.txt as an opcode-2 entry per tile/block (per ADC channel). Before GRDEV-8102 every band ran DSA = 0 dB.
Why it exists: the problem is ADC over-range at the top of the RX range, not sensitivity at the bottom. At DSA=0 the ADC clipped under strong uplink and raised fault id 20 ("RX out of order" / Alarm 20); the DSA backs the signal off ADC full-scale so it stops clipping. It's almost free because the noise floor is set by the LNA at the front (Friis — first stage dominates), not by the attenuator later in the chain — so headroom at the top costs ≤ ~1 dB at the bottom. (Register-level detail + the RSSI trap are in DSA4.)

What every column in the DSA table means

Flavour / Band:
"Flavour" = which band combination config the RU is running (b1b3 = B1+B3 active, b1b3b41 = B1+B3+B41 active, etc.). Different flavours can have slightly different gain settings even for the same band because the RF front-end is shared between bands. This is why B1 DSA might differ between b1b3 and b1b3b41 flavours even though B1 NF itself does not change — the shared hardware context changes.
DSA (dB) — the offset column:
This is how many dB above the B3 baseline this band's sensitivity sits. DSA = 0 for B3 (it is the reference). DSA = 5 for B1 means B1 is 5 dB less sensitive than B3 in this flavour/BW combination — EXM injects 5 dB more power for B1 tests than it does for B3 tests. DSA = 8 for B28 means EXM injects 8 dB more. This correction ensures every band is tested at exactly its own correct threshold, not B3's easier threshold.
RX paths — why B28 has 2 instead of 4:
High-band (B1/B3/B41) uses 4 RX paths — all 4 columns (A/B/C/D) active. Low-band (B8/B28) uses only 2 RX paths — columns A and B only. This is a hardware design choice: the low-band RFFE only connects to 2 of the 4 columns to save cost and board space, since low-band coverage is wide enough that 2-path MRC is sufficient. This also means low-band combined sensitivity gain is only +3 dB (2 paths) vs +5-6 dB for high-band (4 paths).
before vs after — the 0.2–0.5 dB gap:
The DSA offset is already applied before the before/after comparison. These two numbers show:
before = sensitivity calculated purely from formula (theoretical, perfect components assumed)
after = sensitivity measured on your actual hardware after DSA correction

The gap is the sum of all real-world imperfections the formula cannot predict: connector loss variation (±0.1 dB), LNA NF tolerance (±0.1 dB), filter ripple (±0.05 dB), cable slightly different (±0.1 dB). All these add up to 0.2–0.5 dB on a healthy unit. When this gap suddenly becomes 2–3 dB on one specific path — that path has a hardware problem. This is how you pinpoint a bad LNA or connector without disassembling anything.
MRC — how the +5 dB combining gain works:
MRC (Maximum Ratio Combining) does not simply add signals — it weights each chain by its own SNR quality before summing. A chain with strong, clean signal gets high weight. A chain with a degraded LNA gets low weight automatically. The combined SNR in linear scale = sum of all individual SNRs. For 4 equal chains each at SNR = S: combined = 4S = 10·log(4) = +6 dB. In practice chains are slightly unequal so you get +5 to 5.5 dB. For 2 paths (LB): +3 dB. For 3 paths: +4.8 dB.

Key takeaway — what you should remember
Sensitivity = minimum power (at RU port, cable-loss corrected) for successful decode. Set by physics (kTB) + your hardware (NF) + your modulation (required SNR).
NF dominates = LNA is first in chain → Friis formula → LNA NF is system NF. Every other stage is negligible.
Cable loss = NF penalty = your 2 dB test cable before the LNA makes the system 2 dB worse. This is why you always subtract cable loss when reporting sensitivity — you are removing the noise penalty your test setup added.
DSA = the measured per-band sensitivity offset from a common reference. Derived experimentally. Stored in config. Used so the PRACH test threshold matches real hardware capability per band.
Modulation changes sensitivity by 17+ dB = QPSK 1/3 (A1, −102 dBm) vs 64QAM 3/4 (A5, −85 dBm). Same radio, same hardware, completely different sensitivity number. This is why your ul-rct-test results show different sensitivity per FRC scenario.

The adc_dbfs_adj coupling — the trap

PLAIN ENGLISH FIRST Noise chain in one sentence: Every component between the antenna and the ADC adds a tiny amount of its own noise. This card shows exactly how much each component contributes, why the LNA dominates, and why a longer cable on the bench will directly worsen your sensitivity measurement.

Friis formula — why LNA position is everything

Friis numerical calculation (all values in linear):
Convert each component: NF_linear = 10^(NF_dB/10)
Cable: 1.778, G=0.562 · Dup: 1.122, G=0.891 · BPF: 1.071, G=0.933 · LNA: 1.585, G=100 · PostBPF: 1.259 · Mixer: 5.012

NF_total = 1.778 + (1.122−1)/0.562 + (1.071−1)/0.501 + (1.585−1)/0.447 + (1.259−1)/44.7 + (5.012−1)/4470
= 1.778 + 0.217 + 0.142 + 1.309 + 0.006 + 0.001 = 3.45 linear = 5.38 dB
(Slight variation from 5.75 dB due to component tolerances and cable length — 5.75 is measured value)
The cable before LNA — your biggest variable in lab tests:
The 2.5 dB cable loss adds its full value to system NF because it comes before the LNA (no gain divides it). When you change cables, swap adapters, or use a different length cable between EXM and RU port, the system NF changes. Every 0.1 dB extra cable loss = 0.1 dB worse sensitivity = your test threshold moves by 0.1 dB. Always measure cable loss with VNA before any sensitivity test and subtract it from EXM output when calculating the power arriving at the RU port.
Why everything after the LNA is negligible:
LNA gain = +20 dB = ×100 linear. Post-BPF NF = 1.0 dB → linear 1.259. Its Friis contribution = (1.259−1)/100 = 0.0026 linear = 0.011 dB. Mixer NF = 7 dB → linear 5.012. Contribution = (5.012−1)/100 = 0.040 linear = 0.17 dB. These are completely insignificant compared to the 2.5 dB from the cable. This is why once the LNA is working correctly, improving anything after it gives virtually zero sensitivity improvement.
🎯 Analogy: the Friis formula is like a telephone game

Imagine passing a message (your signal) through a line of people. The first person in line can mishear the message and corrupt it — and everyone after will repeat the corrupted version louder. The second person can also mishear, but their error gets divided by how loudly the first person spoke (the LNA gain). By the time you get to the 10th person, their individual errors are completely drowned out by the first person's mistake. This is why the LNA (first active component) dominates the system NF — and why every millimetre of cable before the LNA directly costs you sensitivity.

The single most important rule from all of this
Everything before the LNA costs you sensitivity. Everything after the LNA is free.
→ Your test cable before the LNA: every dB of loss = 1 dB worse sensitivity
→ Your duplexer before the LNA: every dB of insertion loss = 1 dB worse sensitivity
→ Your connector quality before the LNA: loose connector = worse sensitivity
→ Your LNA itself: its NF determines the system. 1 dB better LNA = 1 dB better sensitivity
→ Your mixer NF: irrelevant — divided by LNA gain (×100)
→ Your ADC: irrelevant for sensitivity — quantisation noise is far below thermal noise
→ Your DU / software: irrelevant for NF — only affects required SNR (which depends on modulation)

RSSI RSSI — Sensitivity & Dynamic Range Test (manual + automation) Advanced click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRST RSSI calibration in one sentence: RSSI cal is the same as RX gain calibration — inject known power from EXM, read what the ADC reports in dBFS, compute the difference (ADC_ADJUST), save it. From then on, the radio can convert any ADC reading into an accurate power in dBm. The test passes when all three sources (EXM, CLI, DU) agree within ±2 dB.
Quick link — how this connects to DSA:
RSSI cal and RX gain cal are the same procedure. It finds ADC_ADJUST: inject known power from EXM, read dBFS from ADC, compute offset. Once calibrated, the RU can report accurate dBm for any received signal level.
→ For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card.

What RSSI calibration actually is

RSSI calibration and RX gain calibration are the same procedure with different names. The goal is to find the single offset number — ADC_ADJUST — that converts any raw dBFS reading from the ADC into an accurate dBm power level at the RU antenna port. Once calibrated, P_dBm = dBFS_reading + ADC_ADJUST for any signal in that band.

The three numbers that must agree within 2 dB:

EXM output − cable loss = what arrives at the RU port (your reference, measured physically)
CLI get_rssi + ADC_ADJUST = what the RU's ADC chain reports (your calibrated reading)
DU testmac RSSI = what the baseband processing chain reports after FFT (another independent path)

All three must agree within ±2 dB. If EXM says −97.5 dBm, CLI should report −97.5 ± 2 dBm, and DU should also report −97.5 ± 2 dBm. If CLI is accurate but DU is off, the problem is in the FHGW/baseband path. If both CLI and DU are off from EXM, the ADC_ADJUST value is wrong.
Why separate ADC_ADJUST per band and per ADC channel:
B1 UL (1950 MHz) and B3 UL (1747 MHz) use different LNA gain settings, different filter responses, and different ADC input stages. Even if two ADC channels share the same physical ADC chip, the analog input path leading to each channel varies. Unit-to-unit component tolerance means the ADC_ADJUST for B1 on ADC channel 0 of unit 26050509 will differ slightly from the same channel on unit 26050508. This is precisely what RSSI cal measures and corrects — it is a per-unit, per-band, per-channel characterisation.
Common RSSI cal failures and root causes:
CLI reads 3 dB low → ADC_ADJUST was set with a different cable. Cable got swapped. Measure new cable loss with VNA and re-run cal.
CLI accurate but DU off by 2 dB → FHGW BFP decompression issue or testmac RSSI averaging window mismatch. Check FHGW firmware version.
RSSI drifts as unit warms up → LNA gain is temperature-sensitive. Re-run cal at operating temperature (after 30 min warm-up), or check if temperature compensation table (TEMP_COMP in hardware.json) is configured.
All bands off by same amount → EXM output power was wrong during cal. Re-verify EXM output with EXA before running cal.
ADC channel mapping — which channel reads which band/column:
B1 Column A → ADC channel 0  ·  B1 Column B → ADC channel 1
B1 Column C → ADC channel 4  ·  B1 Column D → ADC channel 5
B3 Column A → ADC channel 2  ·  B3 Column B → ADC channel 3
B3 Column C → ADC channel 6  ·  B3 Column D → ADC channel 7
B8/B28 use 2 RX paths (columns A and B only) → channels 0 and 1 with band-specific ADC_ADJUST values

So get_rssi 0 reads B1 Column A. get_rssi 2 reads B3 Column A. This mapping is why if Column C shows a bad RSSI reading (channel 4 for B1), you know exactly which physical LNA and cable path to inspect.
🚨 Common RSSI calibration mistakes (from real lab experience):
Mistake: Measuring cable loss at wrong frequency
Result: ADC_ADJUST off by 0.3-1 dB, RSSI always wrong by that amount
Fix: Always measure cable loss at band centre (e.g. 1950 MHz for B1 UL)
Mistake: Using wrong ADC channel number
Result: B3 cal written to ADC_ADJUST for B1 channel — completely wrong
Fix: Always verify: B1 Col A = get_rssi 0, B3 Col A = get_rssi 2
Mistake: Not verifying EXM output before injection
Result: EXM was off by 1.2 dB → ADC_ADJUST stored with 1.2 dB error
Fix: Always verify EXM output with EXA (±0.5 dB) before any cal
Mistake: Cal at room temp, field unit gets hot
Result: RSSI drifts 1-2 dB in summer — TEMP_COMP table empty
Fix: Run cal at 25°C and 55°C, populate TEMP_COMP table
B41T B41 TDD Trigger Timing — the exact 9.9765 ms delay: what it is and what breaks if wrong ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRST — real lab finding B41 TDD shares one frequency for DL and UL — separated only in time. The EXM must inject its UL signal only during SF2 and SF7 (the only full UL subframes in Config 2). The 9.9765 ms delay aligns the ARB waveform so it lands there. If the delay toggle is OFF, injection is uncontrolled — it lands in DL subframes and the RU cannot receive it. This was the first thing to check for the B41 ~5 dB sensitivity gap on units 26050508/26050509.

Correct frame structure and what the 9.9765 ms actually does

Corrected TDD Config 2 frame — D S U D D D S U D D:
Only SF2 and SF7 are full UL subframes. SF3, SF4, SF5 and SF8, SF9 are Downlink — not UL as previously shown incorrectly.

SF Type Time UL receive window
0D0–1 ms—
1S1–2 msDwPTS 1.000–1.643 ms · GP 1.643–1.857 ms · UpPTS 1.857–2.000 ms
2U2–3 ms← FULL UL burst (PRACH / PUSCH)
3D3–4 ms—
4D4–5 ms—
5D5–6 ms—
6S6–7 msDwPTS 6.000–6.643 ms · GP 6.643–6.857 ms · UpPTS 6.857–7.000 ms
7U7–8 ms← FULL UL burst (PRACH / PUSCH)
8D8–9 ms—
9D9–10 ms—
Special Subframe Config 6 (normal CP) decoded:
Total = 14 OFDM symbols per 1 ms subframe.
DwPTS = 9 symbols = 9 × 71.35 µs = 642.9 µs (DL pilot — RU transmits)
GP = 3 symbols = 3 × 71.35 µs = 214.1 µs (guard — silence for switching + propagation)
UpPTS = 2 symbols = 2 × 71.35 µs = 142.7 µs (UL pilot — narrow window)

The GP is only 214 µs. If the EXM injection is even 0.3 ms off, the UL burst clips into the guard period and the RU ignores it. For PRACH specifically — UpPTS is only 142.7 µs — a near-zero tolerance on timing alignment.
Why 9.9765 ms — the physics drops out exactly:
10.0000 ms   one LTE TDD frame (External 2 trigger period)
− 0.0203 ms   N_TA offset = 624 × Ts = 624 / 30,720,000 = 20.3 µs (3GPP TS 36.213 — mandatory UL timing advance for TDD)
− ~0.003 ms   cable length + Tx/Rx processing latency (~3 µs empirical)
──────────
= 9.9767 ms ≈ 9.9765 ms ✓   exactly matches your EXM screen
The 23.5 µs shortfall is not arbitrary. The N_TA advance ensures the UL burst's OFDM symbols (with cyclic prefix) land cleanly inside the RU's FFT capture window — arriving slightly early so the CP absorbs propagation uncertainty rather than clipping the GP→UpPTS boundary.
Two scenarios for the B41 sensitivity gap:

Scenario A — Delay toggle OFF (what the screenshot shows):
9.9765 ms value is configured but the toggle is OFF → delay not applied → injection is uncontrolled → most UL bursts land in DL subframes (SF3/SF4/SF5) → RU cannot receive them → BLER high → sensitivity appears ~5 dB worse than real. This is the cheap fix — just turn the toggle ON.

Scenario B — Delay ON but cable offset stale:
If your cable run differs from the ~3 µs assumed when the delay was calibrated, the fine offset is slightly wrong. Even a 0.2 ms error at the GP boundary causes partial burst loss. Test: with delay ON and fixed inject power (e.g. −97 dBm), sweep delay ±200 µs around 9.9765 ms in 20 µs steps — watch UL BLER. If BLER bottoms out at exactly 9.9765 ms: alignment is correct, the 5 dB is a real RX path issue. If BLER bottoms out at a different value: recalibrate the delay for your specific cable.
✅ B41 test setup checklist
□ ARB Trigger Source → External 2
□ Ext Trig Polarity → Pos
□ Ext Trig Delay value → 9.9765 ms (9.976500 ms)
□ Ext Trig Delay toggle → ON ← confirm this — was OFF on your screenshot
□ Mode Setup → TDD Config 2, Special SF Config 6 — must match DU exactly
□ ARB bin file → correct TDD waveform (e.g. A1-3_BW10_TDD_RNTI_0.bin)
□ GPS/PTP → LOCKED (B41 TDD requires ±1.5 µs timing accuracy)
□ If B41 still 5 dB off after delay ON → sweep delay ±200 µs to confirm alignment or identify RX path issue
□ Check UL BLER at fixed power to separate "timing artifact" from "real 5 dB RX path loss"
REF RF & RCT Glossary — quick definitions of every term Reference click to expand▾

Complete term reference — every RF and RCT acronym

RF measurement terms:
DANL: Displayed Average Noise Level — EXA own noise floor (−130 dBm/Hz with preamp ON)
P1dB: 1 dB compression point — input power where PA gain drops 1 dB from linear
IIP3: Input 3rd-order Intercept Point — linearity spec for mixers
PAPR: Peak to Average Power Ratio — OFDM signal crest factor (10–12 dB)
VSWR: Voltage Standing Wave Ratio — impedance mismatch indicator (1.0 = perfect)
NF: Noise Figure — how much SNR the RX chain degrades (dB)
ENR: Excess Noise Ratio — calibrated noise source spec for NF measurement
kTB: Thermal noise power = Boltzmann × Temperature × Bandwidth = −174 dBm/Hz
SQNR: Signal to Quantisation Noise Ratio = 6.02N + 1.76 dB (12-bit → 74 dB)
System and architecture terms:
midBRD: Mid-band Board — digital processing (FPGA, DAC/ADC) for B1/B3/B41
RFFE: Radio Frequency Front End — analog RF board (PA, LNA, duplexer) per column
FHGW: Fronthaul Gateway — Low-PHY processor (IFFT/FFT, BFP, CFR, DPD)
eCPRI: evolved Common Public Radio Interface — IQ data over 10GbE
BFP: Block Floating Point — IQ compression (9+4 bit → saves ~50% bandwidth)
PE44820DS: Digital phase shifter IC per column (beamforming control)
ORX: Observation Receiver — DPD feedback ADC (samples PA output)
JESD204B: High-speed serial interface between FPGA and DAC/ADC
O-RU/O-DU/O-CU: Open RAN Radio Unit / Distributed Unit / Centralised Unit
Test framework terms:
RuAuto: PW automated RF test framework
tc_cadence.json: Test configuration file (bands, BWs, DSA offsets, limits)
rct_results.json: Output file with all measurement results and pass/fail
Group-ID: Test group category (TX_POWER, RSSI_CAL, SENSITIVITY, ACLR)
Test-ID: Specific test case within group (B1_10M_QPSK_A1)
ETM: Embedded Test Mode — partial RCT without full DU connection
FRC A1: QPSK 1/3 — the standard sensitivity test FRC (best sensitivity, FRC A1-A5)
PRACH: Physical Random Access Channel — UE's first transmission (Zadoff-Chu preamble)
TA: Timing Advance — propagation delay correction sent by gNB to UE

PRA01 PRACH Detector Deep-Dive — Ncs/ZCZ/K, Zadoff-Chu, the FlexRAN noise-estimator/peak-multiplier Advanced click to expand ▾
What the detector must do
A UE with no uplink timing sends a random-access preamble; the base station must detect it and reply with a timing advance. Two error rates define the test (RCT clause 8.4): missed detection and false alarm. This is the algorithm behind the FC10 PRACH sensitivity test.
Preamble = CP + Zadoff-Chu + guard — baseband generation
Base sequence build: DFT → IDFT + frequency shift + CP addition → power scaling (ramp-up) → half-bin shift → configurable frequency shift (from SIB2, in units of 15 kHz subcarriers, with a resampling factor K). Bin distance is 1.25 kHz for formats 0–3.
Zadoff-Chu, roots & cyclic shifts
The signature is a Zadoff-Chu sequence — constant amplitude, one sharp autocorrelation peak, low cross-correlation. The cell broadcasts a root; the 64 signatures (preamble index 0–63) come from choosing a root u and a cyclic shift v. Shift granularity is set by Ncs, which defines the Zero-Correlation Zone (ZCZ).
The Ncs / ZCZ / K / roots trade
SettingK (preambles/root)RootsEffect
ZCZ = 1641small allowable delay, no inter-root noise
ZCZ = 12~6/7~10larger allowable delay, higher inter-root noise
Allowable delay per UE = Ncs × FFT_size / 839. Bigger cells need more allowable delay (more cyclic-shift room) → more roots → more inter-root noise. That is the core PRACH planning trade.
The FlexRAN-style detector
front end
remove CP → FFT → extract PRACH subcarriers
× conjugate of the root ZC (correlation)
IFFT → power-delay profile
decision
Noise_est = mean(noise vector)
detected if peak / Noise_est > peak-multiplier
peak position → timing advance
The peak multiplier is the tunable threshold separating a real preamble peak from noise.
In RuAuto
test_Rx_PRACH plays a PRACH IQ waveform and sweeps the input power down (binary or stepped “sensitivity” search) to find the detection threshold against PRACH_KPI — your PRACH ALGO deck made executable. (See FC10 / FC08T for the trace.)
Interview Q&A
Q: What do the noise estimator and peak multiplier decide, and what does the peak position give you?
A: The noise estimator computes Noise_est = mean of the noise vector from the post-IFFT correlation; the peak multiplier is the threshold — a correlation peak counts as a detected preamble only if peak/Noise_est exceeds it. The position of that peak in the power-delay profile gives the timing advance sent back to the UE.
Q: ZCZ=1 vs ZCZ=12 — which gives more roots and more inter-root noise, and why would you use it?
A: ZCZ=12 gives ~10 roots (K≈6–7 preambles each) and higher inter-root noise, but it also allows a larger allowable delay (Ncs×FFT/839), which bigger cells need so a distant UE’s delayed preamble still lands in its zero-correlation zone. ZCZ=1 packs all 64 preambles on one root with no inter-root noise but only a tiny allowable delay — fine for small cells.
PAE01 PA Efficiency — Dynamic Vdd, gate bias, DAC current & bias sequencing Advanced click to expand ▾
Linearity is half the story — efficiency is the other half
DPD/CFR (FC-series) make the PA clean; this makes it cheap to run. The PA is the biggest slice of a base station’s energy bill. The lever: feed the PA only as much DC power as the current traffic needs. This is the supply-side complement to ET01.
Drain efficiency & back-off
Drain efficiency = RF power out / DC power in. A PA is most efficient near saturation and worst when backed off — but OFDM’s high PAPR forces back-off. So at low traffic the PA sits deep in back-off, burning power for little output.
Dynamic Vdd — step the drain voltage with traffic
Load (RB occupancy)B1 / B3 VddNote
100% (full)40 V (nominal)reference
50% (busy hour)32 V (Vdd_Low1)—
30% (medium)25 V (Vdd_Low2)—
0% (no data RBs)25 Vlow/idle
Other bands carry their own nominal: B8/B28 ~48 V, B41 ~45 V. Lower Vdd at low load moves the efficiency peak to where you are actually operating.
You cannot just drop Vdd — you must re-tune
Lowering Vdd changes PA behaviour, so the plan compensates to keep ACLR/EVM in spec: re-set the CFR working point (pre-CFR gain register 0xb0290000: 0xD7 for occupancy > 50%, 0x128 for ≤ 50%) and re-adjust output power via the DAC current. The DAC-current gain relation: DAC_Current_New = DAC_Current_Old × 10^(X/20), where X is the gain reduction in dB. (This is Modules 6 & 11 joined at the hip.)
Gate bias & the GaN PA
Second lever: gate bias Vgg3_p (tested −6.5 V datasheet, −5.5 V, −4.5 V) trades quiescent current for linearity. The GaN PA (RENESAS F8410 / F84012) has a drain rail (VDD) + gate rails (VGG1/2/3), enabled by an AND of TX_EN and MC_EN. Bias must be sequenced in the defined RENESAS order to avoid damage. Even fully OFF it draws ~108 mA from VDD1 (+~1 mA leakage).
Transition timing & measuring the DC side
Switching Vdd live is delicate: when load drops, lower Vdd only after the lower occupancy is in effect; when load rises, raise Vdd before it — and the spectrum must stay 3GPP-compliant throughout. To prove savings, DC-in is read from the −48 V PSU → PSU#1-3 + 3 DC-DC converters via the Common-Board MCU. Efficiency = RF out (TRP, incl. beamforming gain ~+12 dB for B1/B3/B41, +6 dB for B8/B28) / DC in.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why does a fixed drain voltage waste power at low traffic, and what is the fix?
A: With OFDM the PA must be backed off to handle high PAPR, and at low occupancy it sits deep in back-off where drain efficiency is poor — yet a fixed Vdd keeps burning full drain power. Dynamic Vdd lowers the drain voltage as RB occupancy falls (e.g. B1/B3: 40→32→25 V), moving the efficiency peak to the real operating point.
Q: When traffic drops, do you lower Vdd before or after the occupancy change, and why?
A: After. If you lowered Vdd before the load actually dropped, the still-high signal could be pushed into clipping and violate ACLR/EVM. Conversely, when load rises you raise Vdd first. And after any Vdd change you re-tune the CFR working point and DAC current so the radiated power and spectrum stay in spec.
FHGW01 FHGW Embedded UL RCT — standalone on-target sensitivity test (no DU, no PC) Advanced click to expand ▾
What it is
A self-contained uplink receiver-chain validation that runs entirely on the FHGW — no DU, no external test PC, one CLI command (ul-rct-test). It records IQ, runs the PHY decoder on-box, and sweeps power to find sensitivity.
The 2 GB RAM budget (the tool plans every byte)
AllocationSizePurpose
Hugepages (PHY)768 MB (384×2 MB)pre-reserved for the PHY decoder → zero alloc jitter
Binaries~90 MBthe tool + PHY apps
IQ + OS + apps~1.19 GBeverything else
tmpfs1 GB at bootRAM-backed store for binaries + IQ recordings
A pre-flight RAM check aborts early with a clear message if memory is short; auto-cleanup deletes the oldest IQ recordings first (keeps the 5 newest).
Per-sensitivity-step pipeline (~33 s)
Step 1 IQ recording ............ 8.3 s (25%)
Step 2 LTE downsample .......... 7.9 s (24%)
Step 3 HugePages alloc ......... 0.5 s (1.5%)
Step 4 test_ulsim (PHY decode) . 16.0 s (49%)
PHY init 9.5 s one-time · PHY destroy 2.1 s · DPDK init 525 ms
Validation — embedded vs DU sensitivity (all PASS)
CaseBWDU (dBm)RU (dBm)Δ (dB)
QPSK A1-35–20−111.9−112.10.20 (flat)
64QAM A5-x5 / 10−92.8 / −89.3−92.85 / −89.850.05 / 0.55
64QAM A5-720−83.6−84.851.25 (review)
8/8 cases pass, max delta 1.25 dB. A separate FHGW BOB 4-antenna sweep (B1, DSA=5, cable ~5.7 dB) passed 32/32 (4 BW × 2 mod × 4 ant).
Commands & logs
ul-rct-test -l # list scenarios
ul-rct-test 10 a34 0 # run: BW=10, FRC a34, ant 0
OPERATIONAL log = SNR/RSSI/BLER summary (Python-parseable); DEBUG = full PHY logs + per-stage timing. Raw IQ .dat lands in /mnt/tmp_ulsim/iq_recordings/ for offline post-processing.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why does an embedded, on-target RCT matter versus the normal DU-based test?
A: It removes the DU and the external test PC entirely — you SSH into the RU and run one command, so you can validate the uplink receiver chain in the factory or field with no test rig, and the results track the DU-based sensitivity to within ~1 dB. That makes it fast, portable and automatable (Python-parseable summary).
Q: Why pre-reserve 768 MB of hugepages on a 2 GB box?
A: The PHY decoder needs a large, contiguous, non-swapping memory region; pre-reserving 384×2 MB hugepages guarantees it up front with zero runtime allocation jitter, which keeps the per-step timing deterministic on a memory-constrained (2 GB) FHGW.
PHYT01 3rd-Party PHY Test Matrix — cross-checking RCT UL/DL & PRACH (TDD & FDD) Advanced click to expand ▾
What it is
A cross-check that runs the same UL/DL/PRACH waveforms through a 3rd-party PHY and compares against your RCT results — covering both FDD and TDD. It is how you confirm the RU numbers are the PHY’s, not an artefact of your own decoder.
Waveforms exercised
DirectionWaveforms
DL (ETM)ETM1.1, 1.2, 2, 2a, 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.1a (TM=1 and TM=2)
UL (FRC)A1-3, A2-3 (QPSK sensitivity); A5-4 … A5-7 (64QAM)
PRACHPID32, FreqOffset {14,32,35,59,83}, ZCZ8 / ZCZ12, 1 UE
Commands & structure
FDD: rctul / rctdl. TDD: rctul-tdd / rctdl-tdd. Common params: RNTI 0, rb_offset 2/6, per-BW .bin waveforms for 5/10/15/20 MHz (e.g. A1-3_BW10_FDD_RNTI_0.bin, PRACH_Bw20_PID32_FreqOffset83_ZCZ8_1UEs.bin).
Sensitivity references from the matrix (FDD)
FRC5 MHz10 MHz15 MHz20 MHz
A1-3 (QPSK)−103.5−104.5−105.0−104.5
A5-x (64QAM)−82.0−80.5−80.0−79.0
QPSK sits ~24 dB more sensitive than 64QAM — the FRC/modulation-vs-sensitivity relationship (see DSA2).
Interview Q&A
Q: Why cross-check the RU against a 3rd-party PHY?
A: To prove the sensitivity/BLER numbers come from the actual received signal and standard PHY processing, not a quirk of your own decoder or test harness. Feeding identical FRC/ETM/PRACH waveforms through an independent PHY and matching the results validates both the RU hardware and your RCT chain.
Q: Why is the QPSK (A1-3) sensitivity so much better than 64QAM (A5-x)?
A: QPSK carries 2 bits/symbol and tolerates a low SINR, so it decodes at a much lower received power (~−104 dBm); 64QAM carries 6 bits/symbol and needs a far higher SINR, so its sensitivity floor is ~−80 dBm. The ~24 dB gap is the modulation-order vs required-SNR trade.
SPEC01 Conformance — LTE TS 36.141 (TX cl.6 / RX cl.7 → RCT tests) Reference click to expand ▾
What this is
TS 36.141 is the LTE base-station conformance spec. Clause 6 = transmitter characteristics, clause 7 = receiver characteristics. Every clause maps to a test_Tx_* / test_Rx_* function in your RCT — this card is that index.
Clause 6 — Transmitter characteristics
ClauseFeatureYour test
6.1General — E-UTRA Test Models (E-TM 1.1/1.2/2/2a/2b/3.1/3.1a/3.1b/3.2/3.3) + NB-IoT TMthe ETM config key
6.2Base station output power (+6.2.6/7/8 Home-BS: adjacent UTRA / adjacent E-UTRA / co-channel protection)test_Tx_BS_Output_Power
6.3Output power dynamics — 6.3.1 RE power control range · 6.3.2 total power range · 6.3.3 NB-IoT RBtest_Tx_dynamic_range
6.4Transmit ON/OFF power — 6.4.1 OFF power · 6.4.2 transient periodTX Off Power
6.5Signal quality — 6.5.1 frequency error · 6.5.2 EVM · 6.5.3 time alignment error · 6.5.4 DL RS powertest_Tx_FrequencyError / EVM / TimeAlignment / DLRS
6.6Unwanted emissions — 6.6.1 OBW · 6.6.2 ACLR · 6.6.3 operating-band unwanted emissions (SEM) · 6.6.4 spurioustest_Tx_Occupied_Bandwidth / ACLR / test_lte_Tx_Mask / test_lte_Tx_Spurious
6.7Transmitter intermodulation (+6.7.2A / 6.7.6 additional for Band 41)— (not yet automated)
Clause 7 — Receiver characteristics (only 7 RX clauses — the complete RF list)
ClauseFeatureYour test
7.2Reference sensitivity levelsensitivity / DSA work
7.3Dynamic rangeRX Dynamic Range
7.4In-channel selectivity—
7.5Adjacent Channel Selectivity (ACS) & narrow-band blocking—
7.6BlockingRX Blocking
7.7Receiver spurious emissions—
7.8Receiver intermodulationRX IMD
PRACH is NOT in clause 7 — it lives in clause 8
Clause 7 is RF receiver characteristics. PRACH is a performance / demodulation requirement in clause 8 (8.2 PUSCH · 8.3 PUCCH · 8.4 PRACH · 8.5 NB-IoT · 8.6 subslot-PUSCH · 8.7 SPUCCH). Your guide correctly cites §8.4.1 for test_Rx_PRACH — a different category from everything above. (See FC10 / PRA01.)
Interview Q&A
Q: Which clause defines EVM, and which defines reference sensitivity, in LTE 36.141?
A: EVM is clause 6.5.2 (transmitted signal quality, TX side); reference sensitivity is clause 7.2 (receiver characteristics, RX side). They live in different top-level clauses because 6 is transmitter and 7 is receiver.
Q: Why is PRACH not in clause 7 with the other receiver tests?
A: Because clause 7 covers RF receiver characteristics (sensitivity, blocking, selectivity, intermod), whereas PRACH detection is a demodulation/performance requirement — it is in clause 8 (8.4). It tests whether the PHY can detect a preamble at a given SNR/level, not a raw RF receiver property.
SPEC02 Conformance — NR TS 38.141-1 (conducted, BS type 1-C / 1-H) Reference click to expand ▾
What this is
TS 38.141-1 is the NR base-station conformance spec for the conducted case — measured at an antenna/TAB connector. BS type 1-C = conducted at the connector; 1-H = hybrid (conducted per-TAB-connector plus some OTA requirements). Same clause structure as LTE, with a few renames.

ClauseFeature

ClauseFeature
7.2Reference sensitivity level
7.3Dynamic range
7.4In-band selectivity and blocking (7.4.1 ACS · 7.4.2 in-band blocking)
7.5Out-of-band blocking
7.6Receiver spurious emissions
7.7Receiver intermodulation
7.8In-channel selectivity
Note the RX regrouping vs LTE
NR merges what LTE split across 7.4/7.5/7.6 into 7.4 in-band selectivity & blocking + 7.5 out-of-band blocking, and moves in-channel selectivity to the end (7.8). And LTE’s “EVM” (6.5.2) is called “modulation quality” (6.5.3) in NR — same concept, renamed. Full comparison in SPEC03.
Interview Q&A
Q: What is the difference between BS type 1-C and 1-H in 38.141-1?
A: 1-C is a purely conducted radio tested at its antenna connector. 1-H (hybrid) has an array of transceiver-array-boundary (TAB) connectors: some requirements are verified conducted per TAB connector, while others (e.g. certain emissions/steering) are verified OTA. Fully integrated AAS with no connector are type 1-O and tested under 38.141-2.
SPEC03 Conformance — NR TS 38.141-2 (OTA / radiated) + differences Reference click to expand ▾
What this is
TS 38.141-2 is the NR conformance spec for the radiated / OTA case (BS type 1-O) — an integrated AAS/AAU with no antenna connector, so every requirement is measured over the air. This is what your NR OTA (n41) section uses.
Clause 6 — Transmitter (OTA)
ClauseFeature
6.2Radiated transmit power (OTA-only — no conducted equivalent)
6.3OTA BS output power
6.4OTA output power dynamics
6.5OTA transmit ON/OFF power
6.6OTA transmitted signal quality
6.7OTA unwanted emissions
6.8OTA transmitter intermodulation
6.9OTA spatial emission (OTA-only — no conducted equivalent)
Clause 7 — Receiver (OTA)
ClauseFeature
7.2OTA sensitivity
7.3OTA reference sensitivity level
7.4OTA dynamic range
7.5OTA in-band selectivity and blocking
7.6OTA out-of-band blocking
7.7OTA receiver spurious emissions
7.8OTA receiver intermodulation
7.9OTA in-channel selectivity
Four differences worth memorising
#Difference
1LTE 6.5.2 “Error Vector Magnitude” → NR 6.5.3 “Modulation quality”. Renamed, same concept.
2RX selectivity regrouped: LTE = 7.4 in-channel / 7.5 ACS+narrowband / 7.6 blocking → NR = 7.4 in-band selectivity & blocking / 7.5 out-of-band blocking, with in-channel selectivity moved to the end (7.8 conducted, 7.9 OTA).
3OTA adds two clauses with no conducted equivalent: 6.2 Radiated transmit power & 6.9 OTA spatial emission — only meaningful with no antenna connector.
4OTA has both 7.2 “OTA sensitivity” and 7.3 “OTA reference sensitivity level” — two distinct tests. Conducted has only reference sensitivity. Easy to conflate.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why does an AAU use 38.141-2 (OTA) instead of 38.141-1 (conducted)?
A: A fully integrated active antenna system has no accessible antenna connector — the array and radio are one unit — so power, emissions and sensitivity can only be defined and measured over the air (radiated), in a test range/anechoic chamber. That is the type 1-O / 38.141-2 regime, which also adds beam-direction-dependent requirements (radiated transmit power, spatial emission) that have no conducted meaning.
Q: OTA defines both 7.2 OTA sensitivity and 7.3 OTA reference sensitivity level — what is the distinction?
A: OTA sensitivity (7.2) is the declared best-case sensitivity in the most sensitive direction/beam (OSDD-based), while OTA reference sensitivity level (7.3) is the minimum-level conformance figure analogous to the conducted reference sensitivity. Conducted specs only have the reference-sensitivity notion; OTA splits the “how good can it be” from the “minimum it must meet.”

Reading the suite
sanity = a quick smoke run; road_trip = the full sequential run of every test in the file (what CI executes). OTA variants are the radiated versions (38.141-2 / SPEC03) for your n41. RSSI / RSSI_Accuracy are the GRDEV-9075 items on your branch (see FC15 / RSSI). PRACH is not here — it is a clause-8 performance test (see RCT02 NR TDD + FC10).
Interview Q&A
Q: What is the difference between a "sanity" and a "road_trip" test in the suite?
A: sanity is a fast smoke test that confirms the setup and a couple of key measurements work before you commit to a long run; road_trip is the full sequential execution of every conformance test in that file — the complete conformance pass that CI runs end-to-end.
Q: Why does test_Tx_modulation_analysis map to several clauses at once?
A: It is a composite measurement: from one captured waveform the analyzer derives BS output power (6.2), frequency error (6.5.1), EVM (6.5.2) and DL RS power (6.5.4) plus the time offset — so one test efficiently covers what would otherwise be four separate captures.

Interview Q&A
Q: What is the difference between the conformance and non-conformance suites?
A: Conformance suites verify the 3GPP TS 36.141/38.141 pass/fail requirements exactly. Non-conformance suites are PW-internal engineering tests that go beyond (or aside from) the spec — e.g. PA/PB power-sharing, PHY profiling, gain characterization, PUCCH and timing-advance test cases, and counter checks — used for debug and characterization, not certification.
Q: What does the _2CC set in conformance_nr_tdd_tx.py verify?
A: The 2-component-carrier (carrier-aggregation) variants: it repeats modulation analysis, dynamic range, TAE, OBW, ACLR and reference sensitivity with two carriers active, to confirm the radio still meets spec when aggregating — the inter-carrier effects (e.g. cross-modulation into the adjacent channel) that a single-carrier run cannot catch.
