Interview Q&A
Q: Where does PA Protection live and why is it not a test of its own?
A: It is a helper module, pa_protection.py, not a test_ function — it is invoked from test_main_procedure. PA protection (~3 dB back-off on carrier activation, adjusting DAC current via rfdc-app) is a safety behaviour applied during bring-up of every run, so it is shared infrastructure rather than a standalone conformance test.
Q: The e2e location-update flow mentions auth + ciphering — where is that defined?
A: That ties to the security stack (SEC01): the location-update procedure runs AKA authentication and then NAS/AS ciphering + integrity before the UE is served. The e2e test exercises that whole call flow end to end, including the MME overload-reject path.
NBIOT01 NB-IoT + LTE Combined TX — guard-band / standalone / LTE-only (GRDEV-6813) Advanced click to expand ▾
What it is
NB-IoT is an LPWA carrier — a single 200 kHz tone that rides in-band, in an LTE guard-band, or fully standalone. This suite validates NB-IoT TX conformance alongside LTE on the same radio. Entry file: conformance_unified_nbiot_lte_tx.py.
Three deployment modes = three entry points
Entry / PHY modeWhat runs
test_lte_only_Tx_sanity (mode 0)LTE single-CC only
test_nbiot_Tx_sanity (mode 1+2, GBAN)NB-IoT + LTE in guard-band, both on the same CEVM
test_nbiot_standalone_sanity (mode 3, SAL)NB-IoT only (CC1)
test_combined_Tx_dl_antenna_mappingNB-IoT + LTE TM2 tx-diversity (2 antenna ports) → per-antenna EVM
The per-setup nbiot_test_mode field gates which entry is allowed; the others pytest.skip.
JSON-driven matrix — tc_cadence_nbiot.json
Test-IDs = the test defs (EVM, freq error, freq raster, OBW, ACLR, power boost, TAE, NRS power, plus LTE reference tests and NB-IoT standalone tests). Group-IDs = axis sets (bands, bandwidths, frequencies, guard_bands, modes, etms, antennas). Cadence-IDs = named presets selectable via --cadence=<name> — e.g. P0 full (~72 iters, nightly target), P1 smoke (6), P_MultiBW, P_AntSweepAll. Adding a scalar test is a single JSON entry — the generic runner applies the op (≤, ≥, abs_ppm, abs_dB…) to the named field.
Measured on the EXM (E6640A) — pure-SCPI CEVM dual-CC
LTE-AFDD mode → CEVM measurement → 2 carriers: LTE (CC0) + NB-IoT 200 kHz (CC1) at a frequency offset → op mode GBAN / SAL / NONE. NB-IoT-standalone extras: OBW_SAL < 200 kHz (TS 36.141 Table 5.6-3) and ACLR_SAL at ±300 kHz (limit 40 dB) & ±500 kHz (limit 50 dB) with a 180 kHz integration filter (TS 36.141 Table 6.6.2.1-2b).
Interview Q&A
Q: What are the three NB-IoT deployment modes and how does the suite pick one?
A: In-band (NB-IoT inside an LTE PRB), guard-band (in the LTE channel guard-band — GBAN), and standalone (its own spectrum — SAL). The suite has one entry point per mode (lte_only / nbiot combined-GBAN / standalone-SAL); the setup's nbiot_test_mode field enables the matching entry and skips the others.
Q: Why is NB-IoT ACLR specified at ±300/±500 kHz with a 180 kHz filter instead of the LTE offsets?
A: Because NB-IoT is a 200 kHz carrier, not a 1.4–20 MHz LTE channel, so its adjacent-channel offsets and integration bandwidth are scaled to its own carrier (per TS 36.141 Table 6.6.2.1-2b): ±300 kHz at 40 dB and ±500 kHz at 50 dB, integrated over 180 kHz.
SPLANE01 5G S-Plane / PTP Sync Verification — LOCKED, HOLDOVER & recovery (splane_verification_nr.py) Advanced click to expand ▾
What it verifies
The S-plane (synchronization plane) carries timing. This suite verifies the RU's timing & frequency sync under a stable PTP lock and in holdover. Driven by splane_verification_nr.py + tc_cadence.json, in two phases: pre-tests (reach a known state) then measurements.
Pre-tests (get the DUT to a clean, known state)
Pre-testWhat it does
delete logsclear old synctiming / tcpdump logs for a clean capture
start tcpdumpbackground PTP packet capture on FHGW → PCAP for Wireshark
temperature_monitoringpoll temp until it stabilizes (crystal oscillators drift while temp changes)
ptp_restartLOCKED → disable GM → confirm HOLDOVER → re-enable → confirm re-LOCK (recovery test)
ru_reboot_and_syncreboot the RU and confirm it re-acquires sync
Sync states — the heart of it
LOCKED: RU is tracking the PTP grandmaster (all good). HOLDOVER: grandmaster lost → RU coasts on its own internal clock (must stay in spec for a while). Freerun: no valid timing. The test deliberately forces holdover to prove the RU coasts within limits and then recovers lock. (This is exactly the FH LED green-fast-blink = holdover state in LED01.)
Measurements & why temperature matters
A spectrum analyzer measures frequency error & time offset vs the reference; an oscilloscope analyses the 1 PPS and 10 MHz pulses (time-alignment / jitter). Testing is done at stable temperature because a crystal oscillator's frequency drifts while temperature is changing — measuring mid-drift gives non-repeatable results. Ties to TAE (§6.5.3) and your FH/PTP LED (LED01).
Interview Q&A
Q: What is the difference between LOCKED and HOLDOVER, and why does the test force holdover?
A: LOCKED means the RU is actively synchronised to the PTP grandmaster; HOLDOVER means it has lost the grandmaster and is coasting on its own oscillator, which must stay within a timing/frequency mask for a specified period. The test disables the grandmaster on purpose to confirm the RU enters holdover, holds accuracy, and then re-locks when PTP returns — i.e. it survives a real grandmaster outage.
Q: Why capture PTP traffic with tcpdump during the test?
A: To record the actual PTP protocol exchange (Sync/Follow-Up/Delay-Req etc.) into a PCAP so timing anomalies can be analysed offline in Wireshark — correlating a sync failure or holdover entry with what happened on the wire, rather than only seeing the RU's reported state.
PRACHDM01 PRACH Sensitivity — dual-mode search: binary vs 3-resolution sensitivity loop Advanced click to expand ▾
Two ways to find the PRACH sensitivity level
test_Rx_PRACH supports two search modes to converge on the power where miss-detection hits the 1% target. Set via search_mode.
Binary vs sensitivity loop
BinarySensitivity loop (recommended)
Howhalve the power range [KPI+low, KPI+high] on miss≤1% until range < res3 phases: coarse 2 dB → fine 0.5 dB → finest 0.1 dB, reversing direction to change phase
Iterations~5–7 per delay~15–25 per delay
Precision±0.5 dB±0.1 dB
Usequick / CI runsconformance / certification
Config & verdict
Common params (this setup): PRACH format B4, idx158, 30 kHz SCS, n_rb 12, NF 24, PRACH_KPI −70, tolerance 1, a delay sweep 0–800 ns, and fault_power −34 (safety ceiling). Verdict: Pass (RU input ≤ KPI), Pass (Tolerance) (KPI < p ≤ KPI+tol), Fail (p > KPI+tol).
Output columns (Excel — identical for both modes)
SG output power · setup loss · RU input power · SNR · ext_delay · TA / TA_avg / TA_std · PAPR · miss detection % · false alarm % · Verdict. (Detector internals — Ncs/ZCZ/K, correlate→IFFT→noise-est→peak-multiplier — are in PRA01; RF context in FC10.)
Interview Q&A
Q: When would you use binary search vs the sensitivity loop for PRACH?
A: Binary search is fast (~5–7 iterations, ±0.5 dB) — good for CI smoke and quick validation. The 3-resolution sensitivity loop (coarse 2 dB → fine 0.5 → finest 0.1) is slower (~15–25 iterations) but hits ±0.1 dB precision and mirrors the other uplink sensitivity tests, so it is used for final conformance/certification.
Q: What is the difference between miss detection and false alarm in the PRACH result?
A: Miss detection is the percentage of transmitted preambles the receiver failed to detect (the sensitivity metric — must stay ≤1% at the KPI power). False alarm is the probability the detector reports a preamble when none was sent — measured with no signal present. A good PRACH detector keeps both low; the sensitivity search targets 1% miss detection.
G2SENS01 2G Static Reference Sensitivity — GSM TS 51.021 §7.3 (SISO/MRC/IRC) Advanced click to expand ▾
What it is
The 2G/GSM receiver sensitivity test (TS 51.021 §7.3): the minimum RX input level at which the decoded data meets the error-rate limits (FER / RBER / BER) for each logical channel, under static conditions (no fading, no frequency offset). Automated in conformance_unified_2G_rx.py.
The test rules (§7.3.2)
RuleImplementation
All TRX ON, full DL power, all timeslots4-carrier / 32-TS cell config
Wanted signal per Table 7.3-1 (CS) / 7.3-2 (PS)injected via the EXM (E6640A) into the UL port
Adjacent timeslotstwo adjacent TS at 50 dB above ref sensitivity (valid GMSK), rest empty → BTS must keep RXQUAL ≤ 6
Test at B / M / T ARFCNBand 8 (P-GSM 900): 975 (B) · 38 (M) · 124 (T)
SFH supported → repeat with hoppingcentre the hop range on M
Reference levels & the antenna-mode matrix
Reference sensitivity ≈ −104 dBm for TCH/FS/HS/EFS/AFS on a wide-area multi-carrier BTS (Table 7.3-5 correction = 0 dB). Three UL antenna modes multiply the runs: SISO (1 RX ant → 4 iters), MRC (2 ants combined → 6), IRC (2 ants → 6) = 16 per frequency × channel type. KPIs are read from the BTS L2 RCT statistics.
How 2G sensitivity differs from 4G/5G
GSM uses FER/RBER/BER on GMSK logical channels (not BLER/throughput like LTE/NR), the floor is ~−104 dBm, and the pass check reads L2 error stats from the BTS rather than a PHY BLER counter. It is the 2G analogue of LTE §7.2 / NR §7.2 (see SPEC01) — same idea, different error metric and framing.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why must all four TRX transmit at full power during the 2G sensitivity test?
A: TS 51.021 §7.3.2 requires the BTS to be in its worst-case realistic operating state — all carriers active at full downlink power in every timeslot — so the receiver is tested with the maximum self-generated interference/desense present, not in an artificially quiet configuration.
Q: What does "static" reference sensitivity mean?
A: It is measured under static propagation — no multipath fading and no frequency offset applied to the wanted signal — so it isolates the raw receiver sensitivity floor. Multipath/fading and TU/RA channel conditions are covered by the separate reference-performance (fading) tests, not §7.3.
RFFE01 RFFE Control — per-RFFE / per-polarisation TX isolation on the AAU Advanced click to expand ▾
What it adds
The normal conformance road-trip iterates band → BW → power → freq → ETM → antenna, where “antenna” is a test-equipment port, not an RU front-end. RFFE Control adds the ability to isolate each RFFE of the radio — down to each polarisation — and measure its TX-downlink performance (ACLR, EVM, power, freq error, DLRS, TAE, mask, spurious), plus a combined all-RFFEs pass. TX only, no RX. Code: RffeMixin in source/products/rrh/mixins/rffe.py.
Topology — verified on the B1B3B8B28n41 unit
PropertyVerified value
BandsB1/B3/B41 = all-RFFE-per-pol-pair · B8/B28 = split-RFFE-per-pol-pair
RFFEs (band 41)4 (reported RFFE1..RFFE4, 1-indexed)
Polarisations per RFFE4 — A, B, C, D (not 2)
Logical TX paths (B41)4 RFFE × 4 pol = 16
Columns (“midboard”)only column 0 populated
CLI band ids & the isolation lever
Control band ids: B1=1, B3=3, B8=8, B28=9928 (sentinel!), B41=41. The lever is mb-modify-rffe (enable/disable a specific RFFE+pol's PA). Health reads: mb-get-pa/-lna, mb-get-rffe-temperature/-current/-alarms. A unique RF path = (RFFE 1–4, pol A/B/C/D) — column is fixed at 0 on this HW.
Gotchas discovered on live hardware (do not skip these)
• mb-modify-pa is NOT per-RFFE — it broadcasts to all 4 RFFEs → use mb-modify-rffe for isolation.
• set-rffe-switch-state does not work here → rely on PA/LNA enable, not switch-state.
• Band 7 is rejected (Tx7/41 labels are shared-HW naming) → control band for B41 is 41.
• CLI indexing is inconsistent: mb-modify-rffe uses RFFE 1–4, switch-state uses 0–3.
• help -a text is stale (omits band 41). B28 must use the 9928 sentinel (28/20 rejected).
Feature gating
Gated by the existing per-RRH RFFE boolean in rrh_setup.json — already true on the AAU/MiniMetro units this targets, false/absent on FHGW rigs. If not true, the per-RFFE orchestration is inert and the legacy single-path road-trip runs unchanged. Structured settings live under a separate rffe_control key. Gate is OFF by default.
Interview Q&A
Q: To isolate one RFFE for a per-front-end ACLR measurement, which CLI command do you use and which must you avoid?
A: Use mb-modify-rffe, which disables a specific (RFFE, polarisation) PA so only the target front end transmits. Avoid mb-modify-pa — on this hardware it is a per-polarisation broadcast that disables that pol on all four RFFEs at once, so it cannot isolate a single RFFE. set-rffe-switch-state is also non-functional here.
Q: Why is B28 addressed as 9928 in the RFFE CLI?
A: 9928 is a sentinel control-band id the firmware accepts for B28 — the natural ids 28 and 20 are both rejected. Using 9928 returns real per-RFFE data with the same split-RFFE-per-pol-pair layout as band 8.
CLI01 RCT CLI Reference — run_pytest.py options (conftest.py) Advanced click to expand ▾
53 custom CLI options
The framework defines 53 custom options in conftest.py (pytest_addoption) that control execution, configuration, technology and integration. You pass them to run_pytest.py along with the test path.
The options that matter day-to-day
GroupKey options
Core config--conf-file-path · --test-input-prm (section#json) · --setup-name · --res-mgr
Execution--test-mode conformance|non_conformance · --cadence P0/P1/… · --repeat · --test-log-level
Technology--technology 2g/3g/4g/5g · --multirat · --4g_multirat
Band--dual-band · --dual-band-sequencing · --fhgw-band (e.g. b0307) · --dualband-step first_run
CI / upload--jenkins-run · --rct-elastic · --rct-container · --full-rct
Install--phy_install_tgz · --fhgw_install_tgz · --cws-install · --phy-version
Hardware--rrh-upgrade · --rrh-index (multi-RRH) · --third-party-run · --pw-phy
2G / drive--direction2g Tx|Rx · --drive-test-type greenran|5g-mimo · --gps-receiver-port
TestRail--testrail-result-id · --testrail-username · --testrail-password
Example runs
basic 4G FDD conformance
python run_pytest.py --conf-file-path .../setup.json \
--test-mode conformance source/features/tech_4g/fdd/
CI: cadence P0 + elastic upload
python run_pytest.py --jenkins-run true --rct-elastic True \
--cadence P0 --test-input-prm "tx#.../tx_tests.json" \
source/features/tech_4g/fdd/Tx/
5G container
python run_pytest.py source/features/tech_4g/tdd/Tx/conformance_nr_tdd_speed.py \
--rct-container True --cadence P0 --phy_install_tgz PhyDownload/*-phy*.tgz \
--conf-file-path .../5G_setup/setup_conf.ini
Adding a new CLI parameter = edit 3 files
1) conftest.py → pytest_addoption() (use --kebab-case, set type + default + help). 2) conftest.py → test_args fixture (map to a snake_case key; check is not None for numeric params so 0 stays valid). 3) test_config.py → the load_configurations() arg loop. Miss any one and the value never reaches the test.
Interview Q&A
Q: What is the difference between --test-mode conformance and non_conformance?
A: conformance runs the 3GPP TS 36.141/38.141 pass/fail suites; non_conformance runs the PW-internal engineering tests (PA/PB, PHY profiling, gain, PUCCH/TA, counters) that go beyond the spec — see RCT02. The flag selects which suite the same runner executes.
Q: What does --cadence control?
A: It selects a named preset from the test-config JSON (P0 full/nightly, P1 smoke, and feature-specific ones) that decides which tests and which band/BW/freq/ETM iterations run — so you scale the same suite from a quick smoke to a full conformance pass without editing code.
KPI01 KPI Threshold Structure — the real pass/fail overrides (kpi_thresholds_4g_dl.json) Advanced click to expand ▾
One source of truth
kpi_thresholds_4g_dl.json centralises pass/fail limits + tolerances for every 4G DL test, each mapped to its TS 36.141 clause, and can be overridden by tc_cadence.json RRH thresholds. This is the machinery behind the numbers in FC16.
Five kinds of threshold
FlavourApplies to
Frequency-dependent (band_0_3000 / band_3000_4200)BS output power, frequency error, DL RS power
Band-specific min override (band_min_limit)ACLR
Bandwidth-dependentdynamic range, OBW, TX-OFF power, DL RS
ETM-dependent (etm_limits)EVM, TX diversity
Dynamic table-basedfrequency-table tests
Real numbers to know
TestLimit
EVM by ETM (3GPP %)1.1 = 17.5 · 2.0/3.1 = 8.0 · 3.2 = 12.5 · 3.3 = 17.5 (PW is far stricter — see FC16)
Dynamic range by BW (dB)5 MHz = 13.9 · 10 = 16.9 · 15 = 18.7 · 20 = 20.0
ACLRmin 55 dBc; band_min_limit 52 for b0407 / b0307_second_run / b082028_second_run / b41_first_run
Overrides & the intermod test
The ACLR 52 dBc overrides fire in dual-band runs (inter-band cross-modulation is a known HW effect, not a DPD fail); the lookup key is {fhgw_band}_{dualband_step}. FHGW_Box_kpi_thresholds.json now includes n78 (5G TDD, integrity Integrity-MM-0-B4B7n78-00-1). test_Tx_Intermodulation (6.7) re-runs ACLR/Mask/Spurious with a 5 MHz E-UTRA interferer at TS 36.141 Table 6.7.1-1 offsets (default backoff 30 dB, waveform ETM1_1_BW5), excluding the interferer-occupied bins per clause 6.7.5.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why is the ACLR limit relaxed from 55 to 52 dBc on a dual-band run?
A: When two bands transmit together, inter-band cross-modulation products land in each other's adjacent channel — a physical hardware effect, not a DPD/linearity failure. The band_min_limit override (52 dBc for the second-run/dual-band keys) accounts for it so a healthy radio is not failed for a known coupling effect.
Q: What is the precedence when resolving a KPI threshold?
A: tc_cadence.json RRH-Thresholds override → the KPI JSON (with its frequency/band/BW/ETM-specific entry, e.g. band_min_limit keyed by {fhgw_band}_{dualband_step}) → the hard-coded fallback. The most specific matching entry wins.
The ACLR pass-criterion trap: 55 dBc configured vs 44.2 dB 3GPP
What the config says: Metro_kpi_thresholds.json sets test_Tx_ACLR min_limit = 55 dBc, with a comment calling it the "3GPP minimum". What 3GPP says: TS 36.141 §6.6.2.5 (Table 6.6.2-1) gives 44.2 dB for paired spectrum at 1.4–20 MHz. The configured limit is ≈10.8 dB tighter than the requirement it claims to implement.
Where 44.2 comes from: TS 36.104 sets the core requirement at 45 dB, and TS 36.141 relaxes it by the 0.8 dB ACLR test tolerance to give the test requirement of 44.2 dB. ACLREVM01 explains the absolute-limit alternative (−13 dBm/MHz for Category A), which can make the effective limit even looser for wide carriers.
What it did in practice: automated TX runs on B1, B3 and B28 recorded ACLR Fail on adjacent-channel offsets, while the customer workbook (graded against 3GPP) showed the same points Pass. Both are arithmetically correct: they grade the same measurement against different limits. Every measured ACLR value was between 50.5 and 63.2 dBc, so every point cleared 44.2 dB by at least 6 dB. Only the automatic verdict was wrong, and only in the conservative direction.
LimitValueMeasured 50.5–63.2 dBc gives
Automation config (Metro)55 dBcsome points "Fail"
3GPP TS 36.141 test requirement44.2 dBall Pass, ≥ 6.3 dB margin
Dual-band / second-run override (above)52 dBcinternal relaxation for inter-band cross-modulation
Rules to take away:
• The customer workbook (graded against the standard) is the record of truth. Automation sheets are intermediate.
• A limit is either an internal target or the standard, never both. If 55 dBc is a deliberate internal or customer margin, fix the comment and report "internal-target fail, 3GPP pass". If it was meant to be 3GPP, change it to 44.2 and regrade the affected verdicts.
• When a "fail" appears, first ask which limit graded it, then look at the measured value and its margin to the standard.
• Tight internal targets are useful as early warnings, but only when they are labelled as such in the config, the report and the Jira comment.
RSSI02 RSSI Calibration Method — Z = X + Y (gain budget → expected ADC value) Advanced click to expand ▾

RSSI accuracy work (GRDEV-9075) · RX chain calibration · source: RSSI design walkthrough with the RF engineering lead

The problem — the ADC-read RSSI is not the true power
get_rssi reads the received power at the ADC and returns it in dBm and dBFS — but that raw value is not correct. The only value you can trust is the power at the antenna port, because the cable and port are already calibrated. So the whole job is: calibrate the dBm the ADC reports so it matches the true port power.
The RX path (where RSSI is read)
RX antenna → the 4 RFFEs are summed (A1+A2+A3+A4 for B1/B3/B41) → LNA → filters → ADC (index 0–7, which one depends on the antenna/band) → FHGW → FFT → DU. get_rssi reads at the ADC; the DU also reports an RSSI after the FFT. (See M09b / AAUBD1 for the chain, RS01 for the path context.)
The calibration equation: Z = X + Y
The expected ADC/RSSI value is the port power plus the RX-chain gain:
Z = X + Y
Z = expected value at the ADC (dBm) = what get_rssi should read
Y = input power at the PORT (dBm) = the trusted truth; automation sweeps it min->max
X = total RX-chain gain to the ADC (dB) = from the GAIN BUDGET, band-dependent, PWK-calibrated
dBFS uses a separate log-based formula that also depends on the ADC full-scale. X depends on the band and comes straight from the gain budget (GAIN01).
Worked example (B1) — straight from the gain budget
For the B1 RX path, the gain-budget total gain to the ADC inside the FHGW is 32.75 dB (PWK-calibrated). So:
port power (Y) = -30 dBm, chain gain (X) = +32.75 dB
Z = -30 + 32.75 = +2.75 dBm <- get_rssi should read this
If get_rssi instead reads, say, −25 when the port is −30, the gap (here 5 dB) is the per-ADC error to correct.
How the gap is closed (ties to FC15)
Inject a known power at the port at several levels, read the ADC RSSI at each, and the difference from the expected Z is the per-ADC offset. That offset is written per ADC (the ADC_ADJUST vector in hardware.json — see FC15). Your automation sweeping the port power min → max both maps the offset and characterises the dynamic range of the chain (the upper end is bounded by the EXM output power).
Interview Q&A
Q: Why is the port power the reference and not the ADC value?
A: The port power is trustworthy because the cable loss and port are already calibrated, so you know it exactly. The ADC value has passed through the whole RX chain (RFFE summing, LNA, filters, ADC conversion) whose gain/offset isn't precisely known per unit — that is exactly what RSSI calibration is measuring and correcting.
Q: In Z = X + Y, what is X and where does it come from?
A: X is the total RX-chain gain from the antenna port up to the ADC (band-dependent) — it is read from the gain budget (e.g. 32.75 dB for B1). Y is the swept port input power; their sum Z is the value the ADC/RSSI should report, which is compared against the actual reading to derive the per-ADC offset.
Q: Open design question from the walkthrough?
A: Whether to calibrate the real ADC chain (so the raw ADC value is true) or to make the CLI RSSI match the DU-reported RSSI (measured after the FFT) — to be confirmed. This is the CLI-get_rssi vs DU comparison in Module 14.
RSSI03 RSSI — Offset characterisation & the rssi_model_offsets table (GRDEV-7441) Advanced click to expand ▾

GRDEV-7441 · RSSI accuracy characterisation · offset = −error, stored per model/band/antenna

What the RSSI offset is
The calibration correction stored so the RU's reported RSSI matches what is actually at its antenna port. It is a per-model → flavour → band → antenna bias applied to the final readout. Note — this is a different offset from FC15's per-ADC ADC_ADJUST (in hardware.json): this one is a model-level RSSI bias in the setup config, applied on top of the readout. RSSI02 explains the Z = X + Y expected value; this card is how the residual bias is measured and stored (GRDEV-7441).
How it is derived — offset = −error
Each sweep step gives two knowns:
• EIRP = what you genuinely inject at the port = generator power + measured cable loss (the truth).
• CLI_dBm = what the RU says it received, from get-rssi.
error = CLI_dBm - EIRP
offset = -error (what you ADD to the reading to make it truthful)
example (run 1974): SG -35 EIRP -75.8 CLI -78.46
error = -78.46 - (-75.8) = -2.66 dB -> offset = +2.66 dB
i.e. we put −75.8 dBm in and the radio reported −78.46 — it under-reports by 2.66 dB, so store +2.66.
Where it lives & how it is applied
In rssi_model_offsets in the setup config, keyed model → flavour → band → antenna; the test adds it straight to the readout:
offset = cws.get('rssi_model_offsets',{})
.get(model,{}).get(fhgw_band,{}).get(str(band),{}).get(ant_name, 0.0)
c_dbm, c_dbfs = float(c_dbm) + offset, float(c_dbfs) + offset
In the characterisation runs it is 0 on purpose — rssi_model_offsets is unset, so you measure the raw, uncorrected error. (You can't derive the correction if the correction is already applied.)
Why a single constant works — it's a pure bias, not a slope
The error is flat across level, so one number removes it cleanly:
RunSG −3..−25SG −26..−45
1974−2.67 dB−2.66 dB
1969−2.34 dB−2.23 dB
Flat to within 0.01–0.11 dB across 40 dB — a pure bias, not a slope or non-linearity.
Measured offsets to store (GRDEV-7441 pass criterion)
BandMeasured errorOffset to store
B3 PNG+0.04 dB~0 (DSA already fixed it)
B1 (run 1969)−2.34 dB+2.3
B1 (run 1974)−2.67 dB+2.7
B8+1.09 dB−1.1
The pass criterion of GRDEV-7441 is literally “per-model offset table documented and stored in the source-of-truth file”.
The caveat — one antenna per band, and branch spread is real
Why the RSSI matters: the network uses it for power control and coverage decisions — if it reads 2.7 dB low, everything downstream inherits that error. But: we measured one antenna per band, and David's B41 showed 2.55 dB of spread between branches (his ant1 needed +12.77 dB, which he flagged as suspicious rather than storing blindly). So populate the measured antenna honestly and leave the other three at 0 rather than assume they match.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why is rssi_model_offsets 0 during a characterisation run?
A: Because you are measuring the raw error to derive the correction. If the offset were already applied, get-rssi would read corrected values and error = CLI − EIRP would come out ~0 — you'd be measuring your own correction, not the hardware bias. So you characterise with offset = 0, compute offset = −error, then store it.
Q: How is this different from the FC15 ADC_ADJUST offset?
A: ADC_ADJUST is a per-ADC hardware calibration in hardware.json that corrects the dBFS→dBm conversion at the converter. rssi_model_offsets is a higher-level per-model/band/antenna bias in the setup config, added to the final reported RSSI. This characterisation isolates whatever residual bias remains after the DSA/ADC calibration (note B3 already read ~0 because the DSA fixed it).
USLEEP01 Micro-Sleep (uSleep) — symbol-rate PA gating for energy saving RU / Platform click to expand ▾
What it is & the problem it solves
The PA is the dominant power consumer and it draws bias current whenever it is enabled — even on empty symbols. An LTE/NR downlink is bursty at the symbol level: whole OFDM symbols carry nothing (only the always-on CRS and PSS/SSS/PBCH are guaranteed). uSleep is an FPGA feature that watches the DL sample stream, detects all-zero OFDM symbols, and de-asserts the PA-enable GPIO for their duration — re-asserting tx_en_advance ahead of the next occupied symbol so the PA is settled before real signal arrives.
Where the detector taps (this explains everything)
The detector reads the frequency-domain, post-decompression CC stream (usleep_detect all-zero test on dl_chain_din) — far upstream of the IFFT, DFE, DAC and PA. Control path: usleep_top → usleep_fsm (SLEEP/AWAKE per PA) → rf_gpio_logic (priority: uSleep > TDD > AGC > register) → PA-enable GPIO. Consequence: IQ playback substitutes its samples at the WOLA output — downstream of the tap — so the detector never sees played-back content, and IQ-playback cannot validate uSleep.
Per-array-carrier control (GRDEV-9323) — PROVEN
A uSleep request on one array-carrier gates exactly that carrier's two PA paths and no others (this was the whole point of GRDEV-9323, and the thing that was broken before it). PA-mask examples: A0/A1 → 0x03, A2/A3 → 0x0C, both → 0x0F. Also cc_mode=BOTH does sleep in 1CC (the GRDEV-9285 worry that cc0-and-cc1 could never sleep single-carrier was not reproduced — all 4 PAs of the active column slept, the other 4 never did).
Measured savings
Up to 12.5 W (12.9%) on the 50 V rail at 59.3% blank DL symbols under real DU-generated traffic. Saving scales with blank-symbol density (correlation r = 0.944, ~0.202 W per 1% blank); a 0%-blank null control saves nothing. Validated on odin_lb, model Integrity-ME-0-B1B3B8B41-00-1, flavour b082028, Band 8.
uSleep vs Dynamic Vdd
Not the same feature. uSleep gates the PA enable on/off at symbol rate; Dynamic Vdd (GRDEV-8326, see PAE01) lowers the PA supply voltage at a much slower rate. They are independent and complementary — the savings are expected to compose (not yet co-measured).
Not operational in shipping builds yet — two gates
The feature cannot activate in any released build: the shipped FPGA has no pa_en field, and every personality ships usleep-supported: false. Both must change, in order: FPGA pin bump → personality flip → live. (The wiki tags every claim PROVEN / STRONG-INFERENCE / ASSUMPTION — a discipline worth copying in any validation report.)
Interview Q&A
Q: Why can't IQ playback be used to validate uSleep?
A: Because the uSleep detector taps the frequency-domain stream just after decompression (dl_chain_din), whereas IQ playback injects its samples five stages downstream at the WOLA output. The detector therefore never sees the played-back content, so a played waveform can never trigger (or fail to trigger) sleep — the validation must use real DU-generated downlink.
Q: uSleep vs Dynamic Vdd — how do they differ and combine?
A: uSleep switches the PA enable off during all-zero OFDM symbols (symbol-rate gating); Dynamic Vdd lowers the PA drain voltage as traffic falls (slow supply modulation). One saves on empty symbols, the other saves on low average load — they are orthogonal and their savings are expected to add.
RUPLAT01 RU Platform Software — the BSP/platform subsystems RU / Platform click to expand ▾
What it is
The RU's platform / BSP software layer that sits below the RF and PHY features — board bring-up, health, fault handling and the test scaffolding. The Confluence “RU Platform Software” area groups these High-Level Designs (HLDs).
The subsystems
SubsystemWhat it does
NGC BSP (3U VPX)board-support package for the 3U VPX board variant (GRDEV-7349)
PA Warmuptemperature-based mid-board attenuation — warm/stabilise the PA before use so gain/power are on-target from the first measurement
Reboot Cause Subsystemrecords why the RU rebooted (GRDEV-7271) — essential for reboot-stability RCA
Unit Test Frameworkon-target unit testing for platform code (GRDEV-6962)
Micro-Sleep (uSleep)symbol-rate PA gating for energy saving — see USLEEP01
Thermal Alarms v1/v2/v3temperature-triggered fault management (Metro AAU & Mini Metro); v2 is “current-state-first”
Why it matters for validation
These platform features underlie the things you test: reboot stability (Reboot Cause → RCA on 100+ reboot runs), thermal faults (Thermal Alarms → the RF/temperature LED states in LED01), PA readiness (PA Warmup → repeatable power/gain), and energy saving (uSleep). Knowing which subsystem owns a symptom speeds root-cause.
Interview Q&A
Q: What does the Reboot Cause subsystem give you as a validation engineer?
A: A recorded reason for every RU reboot (watchdog, crash, commanded, power, thermal, etc.). In a 100+ reboot stability run that turns "it rebooted" into a classified, countable signal, so you can separate expected restarts from real faults and hand developers a precise RCA instead of a log dump.
BKC01 BKC — Best Known Configuration (qualified images, CI/nightly map) RU / Platform click to expand ▾
What BKC is
The Best Known Configuration — the qualified, known-good software/firmware image set for each release, per RAT (2G / 4G / 5G-N78), that has passed RCT + E2E. It is the single source of truth for “which build to run,” with Release vs Develop tracks, per-band-combo test scenarios, and the current known issues. (Referenced by RCT03.)
What a BKC entry carries
Per RAT: the Access/EMS image paths, the CWS AAU firmware package, the data-model, and a test-scenarios / known-issues list per band combo (e.g. a B3B7 throughput-degradation item tracked under a GRDEV ticket). Two tracks: Release (stable) and Develop (latest).

Automation branches (what to run when)
Develop — updated several times a day; the main branch for all teams. RCT integ/CI — updated ~once a day/2 days; use for CI test suites. E2E integ/CICD — for end-to-end. Repo: git.parallelwireless.net/GR/ru-pytest (the ruauto RCT framework — see RCT01-03, CLI01, FWK1).
Interview Q&A
Q: What is the BKC and why does it exist?
A: The Best Known Configuration is the release's qualified, known-good image set (per RAT) that has passed RCT and E2E, published with its test scenarios and open issues. It exists so every team runs the same proven build — no "works on my image" — and so regressions are measured against a fixed baseline.
Q: Which automation branch do you point a CI run at?
A: The RCT integ/CI branch, which is stabilised roughly daily for CI suites; Develop moves too fast (several updates a day) for a repeatable CI baseline, and E2E integ/CICD is for the end-to-end suite.
DACG01 DAC Current & Carrier Digital Gain — the two TX power knobs Advanced click to expand ▾
The two knobs
Each band sets output amplitude with two controls: Carrier digital gain — per-carrier multiplier in the digital path before the DAC (fine); and DAC current — an analog setting shared by both carriers within a band (coarse). Lowering DAC current saves power and lowers the noise floor, but affects every carrier on that DAC. TX only — RX gain is independent.
The algorithm
Pick a (DAC current, per-carrier digital gain) tuple that: honours the ACS-requested per-carrier gain; preferentially lowers DAC current when no carrier needs the top 3 dB of headroom (saves power for the whole band); and falls back to per-carrier digital attenuation when at least one carrier does need the top 3 dB (keep the loud carrier loud, attenuate the others).
The numbers & independence
MAX_GAIN = 20 dB (from uplane-conf:max-gain); the 3 dB threshold (= MAX_GAIN−3 = 17 dB) is the inflection: below it DAC headroom is wasted, above it a carrier needs it. Runs per-band (separate DACs/RF chains — B1 and B3 don't constrain each other); within a band the two carriers share one DAC, which is why the algorithm exists. Ties to PAE01 (Dynamic Vdd) and GAIN01 (gain budget).
Interview Q&A
Q: Why not just use per-carrier digital gain and leave DAC current fixed?
A: Because a high fixed DAC current wastes power and raises the noise floor for every carrier on that DAC. When no carrier needs the top 3 dB of headroom you can lower the shared DAC current (coarse, efficient) and skip digital attenuation entirely; you only fall back to per-carrier digital gain when one carrier genuinely needs the headroom.
CAL01 Burning Dummy TX Calibration on a B41 FHGW Advanced click to expand ▾
What it does & when
burn_dummy_tx_calibration.sh writes a placeholder, B41-aligned TX calibration into the FHGW's I2C EEPROM so a fresh, uncalibrated board can come up and transmit. Use it to bring up a B41 FHGW that hasn't been factory-calibrated. The dummy values are not a real RF measurement — TX temperature compensation stays inaccurate until a real calibration is burned.
What gets written
I2C bus 1, addr 0x54, offset 2048, size 3072 bytes, generated by tx_calibration_eeprom.py encode_b41_defaults (aligned to B41 PA + C-reader limits). After reboot, start_transmission.sh re-decodes the EEPROM into tx_calibration_eeprom.json, which operations_manager reads for TX temp compensation.
Procedure & gates
Dry-run (no args) — checks the model gate + shows EEPROM state, no write. Burn (--yes) → reboot → verify the JSON exists. Model gate: the personality must advertise B41 in band-capabilities or the script refuses (exit 2). --force overwrites an existing valid cal (exit 3 without it). Exit 0 = ok.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why burn a dummy calibration instead of waiting for the real one?
A: A brand-new board has an empty cal EEPROM and won't transmit safely/correctly without one. The dummy, B41-aligned defaults let you power the unit up and run bring-up/integration immediately; you then schedule a real RF calibration run to replace them, because temperature compensation is only accurate with real measured values.
PAWARM01 PA Warmup — temperature-based midboard attenuation Advanced click to expand ▾
What it is
At low ambient temperature, extra midboard (MB) attenuation is applied on top of the production attenuation while the PAs warm the unit up; it is removed as temperature recovers. Steps and thresholds come from the thermal fault-management spec (§3, Table 3-1). GRDEV-9082.
Reuses existing building blocks
The MB PA-attenuation register (set_pa_atten/get_pa_atten) and the PM-manager temperature read (fetch_temperature, RFFE + MB column temps with min/max/avg outlier filtering). Warmup is added into the existing pa_protection state machine.
Gating & the fail-safe
Only on midboard v1.5 (MSPM0 MCU, HW Rev 01, personality midboard-version: v4); declared by two personality fields (warmup-supported + warmup-registers). The MB firmware applies the steps internally; ru-app polls an “attenuation applied” register and the PA-control path refuses PA-on until confirmed — fail-safe: no confirmation → PAs stay off.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why attenuate the PA more when the unit is cold?
A: Cold silicon has different gain/behaviour, so the design applies extra midboard attenuation while the PAs dissipate heat and bring the unit to its stable operating temperature, then removes it as temperature recovers — keeping output power and spectrum in spec throughout warmup rather than overdriving a cold PA.
THERM01 Thermal Alarms — temperature-triggered fault management Advanced click to expand ▾
What it is
Temperature-triggered fault management on the Metro AAU / Mini Metro. All temperature alarms funnel through system_monitor → fault_manager → the O-RAN alarm toward the SMO, and fold into the availability state.
Fault vocabulary & action
FaultSeverityAction
TEMP_HIGH (1)Minor+1 dB DAC attenuation (retry-latched)
TEMP_CRITICAL (2)CriticalUNIT_OUT_OF_ORDER + RESET_REQ → reboot
TEMP_LOW (4)—triggers PA warmup (see PAWARM01)
Three producer paths
(1) hwmon sensor path — per-sensor high/low/hyst limits from hwmon-aau-input.json; (2) MB alarm-register path — I2C bits, thresholds live in the MB firmware, every MB/RFFE over-temp bit maps to TEMP_CRITICAL → cascade → reboot; (3) BT-smallcell path — Mini Metro TMP1075 sensors (one per column/pol). Which paths are active is steered by the personality (Integrity-ME vs MM vs USG).
Link
This is what drives the RF/temperature LED states (LED01) and the thermal reboots you see in stability runs — classified by the Reboot-Cause subsystem (RBTCAUSE01).
Interview Q&A
Q: What is the difference in action between TEMP_HIGH and TEMP_CRITICAL?
A: TEMP_HIGH is a Minor alarm that backs the transmitter off by 1 dB (DAC attenuation) to shed heat while staying on air. TEMP_CRITICAL is a Critical alarm — the unit is dangerously overheating — so it is marked out of order and reboots to protect the hardware.
RBTCAUSE01 Reboot Cause Subsystem — attribute every reboot (GRDEV-7271) Advanced click to expand ▾
The problem
The old flow only recorded a reboot cause when userland explicitly called ruReset(reason) first. A bare system("reboot") bypassed logging; kernel panics, HW-watchdog trips, brown-outs, FSBL/PMUFW/ATF faults and U-Boot slot fallbacks all surfaced as POWER_ON; the record was a single overwriting struct (no history).
The fix
Attribute every reboot to a cause with provenance (process / file / function / line); read the Zynq PMU RESET_REASON register (0xFF5E0220) at boot to cover paths that bypass userspace; keep a rolling history on persistent storage; keep serving o-ran-operations:restart-cause; and raise a fault on a reboot-loop.
Design
Two-tier: reset-reason.h (low-level Zynq PMU bit enum + read/clear/visit) and reboot-event.h (high-level reboot_cause_t enum, the record, and the RU_RESET() macro — the single sanctioned reboot chokepoint that stamps file/line/func).
Why you care as a validation engineer
It turns “the RU rebooted” into a classified, counted cause with provenance across a 100+ reboot stability run — so you hand developers a precise RCA (which cause, how often, from where) instead of a log dump. Complements THERM01 (thermal reboots) and RUPLAT01.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why read the PMU RESET_REASON register at boot instead of trusting the software log?
A: Because many reboots never reach the software logger — kernel panics, hardware-watchdog trips, brown-outs and bootloader faults. The Zynq PMU latches the hardware reset reason in a register (0xFF5E0220) that survives the reboot, so reading it at boot recovers exactly the causes that would otherwise all masquerade as POWER_ON.
CA2CC01 2CC Multi-Carrier Conformance — the composite test (TS 36.141/104) Advanced click to expand ▾
What it is
The 2-component-carrier multi-carrier conformance test plan — single-RAT LTE, Wide-Area BS, e.g. Band 1 & Band 3. Methods per TS 36.141, limits per TS 36.104 (Rel-18). Complements PT09/CA01-04 and the RCT02 _2CC suite.
“Composite” = measured from the BS RF-BW edge
Every emission (DL) and interferer (UL) offset is measured from the Base Station RF Bandwidth edge (F_edge = Fc_outer ± BW/2), not from an individual carrier. The BS RF BW spans the lower edge of the lowest carrier to the upper edge of the highest. That single-window view is what makes it a composite measurement.
The two configs
ConfigLayoutCarrier-BW rule (36.141 §4.10)
ETC1contiguous — adjacent carriers, no gapnarrowest supported carrier at lower edge + 5 MHz at upper; fill with 5 MHz
ETC3non-contiguous — sub-block gapa 5 MHz carrier adjacent to each RF-BW edge, one per sub-block
Nominal spacing = (BW1+BW2)/2, multiple of 300 kHz, 100 kHz raster.
Sub-block gaps & band symmetry
As the gap widens the in-gap requirements switch on: CACLR at 5≤W_gap<15 MHz (in-gap offset 2.5 MHz, 44.2 dB), then in-gap blocking/IMD past 15/20 MHz. B1 & B3 are both Wide-Area FDD >1 GHz, so their RF limits are identical (EVM/ACLR/OBUE/sensitivity/blocking/PRACH); only the frequency ranges and reachable gap differ — B3's 75 MHz allows ≈35 MHz gaps vs B1's 60 MHz → ≈20 MHz.
Interview Q&A
Q: What makes a 2CC measurement "composite" rather than just two single-carrier tests?
A: All offsets (ACLR, SEM/OBUE, spurious) are referenced to the outer edge of the whole BS RF bandwidth, not each carrier — so the emission mask and adjacent-channel measurements treat both carriers as one aggregated signal. That catches inter-carrier effects (and, for non-contiguous configs, in-gap CACLR/blocking) that two independent single-carrier runs would miss.
FCREF Conformance Formulas & Limits — per-test quick reference (what · how · formula · limit) Reference click to expand ▾
For each RCT test: what's measured, how, the formula/definition, and the pass limit — with the 3GPP clause and the ruauto validator (function · utils.py line). Limits are the 3GPP defaults; live runs can override from kpi_thresholds / tc_cadence per band.

Total Power Dynamic Range — the detail (interview gold)
• The measured quantity is OSTP (OFDM Symbol Tx Power, TS 36.141 Annex F.3.3) — it accumulates all sub-carrier powers of OFDM symbol 4, chosen because it is pure PDSCH (no RS/PBCH/sync to contaminate the reading).
• It's a capability test (how far the BS can scale per-symbol power), not a power-accuracy test. The two ends are physical reference conditions, so you must subtract two captures: result = OSTP(E-TM3.1) − OSTP(E-TM2) — E-TM3.1 = upper (max power, all 64QAM PRBs, §6.1.1.4), E-TM2 = lower (1 allocated RB at min power, §6.1.1.3). Sheet columns: measured_pwr_ETM2, measured_pwr_ETM3.1, diff.
• Modulation-matched pairs: the a variants are 256QAM (E-TM2a→3.1a), b are 1024QAM (2b→3.1b). Difference within a pair — mixing 2a against 3.1 subtracts two different modulations and is meaningless.
• Report both limits: minimum requirement (36.104) vs test requirement = min − 0.4 dB Test Tolerance (36.141). e.g. 20 MHz = 20.0 (min) / 19.6 (test) — a value like 19.7 passes the test requirement but fails the strict minimum, so quoting one number alone can flip a verdict.
