Interview Q&A
Q: Where does the TX dynamic-range limit come from, and what's the number at 20 MHz?
A: It's 10·log₁₀(N_RB) — the RB count for the channel BW (TS 36.104 Table 6.3.2.1-1). At 20 MHz that's 100 RB → 10·log₁₀(100) = 20.0 dB; the framework hard-codes {5:13.9, 10:16.9, 15:18.7, 20:20.0}. PASS if the measured OSTP span ≥ that.
Q: For ACLR vs EVM, which way is "better" and how is the verdict computed?
A: ACLR higher is better, so the worst case is the min and you PASS if measured > (min_limit − tolerance) (default min 45 dB, tol 0.8). EVM lower is better, so the worst case is the max and you PASS if measured ≤ (min_limit + tolerance), with per-E-TM limits (e.g. 8% for QPSK ETM3.1). Get the direction backwards and every verdict inverts.
FCDSA DSA & dBFS Adjustment — RX calibration: why we shift them (and why sensitivity doesn't move) Advanced click to expand ▾
In plain English
Two knobs sit behind every RX/RSSI reading. DSA (Digital Step Attenuator) is a real attenuator in the receive path — it changes how much signal hits the ADC. adc_dbfs_adj (the dBFS→dBm adjustment) is a pure reporting offset — it never touches the signal, it just calibrates the number the radio prints. Knowing which is which is the whole game: one changes the radio, the other only changes the report.
Where DSA sits in the RX chain
DSA is in the path (before the ADC) → it moves real signal level. adc_dbfs_adj is applied only at reporting → it moves the printed number, not the signal.
Why shift the DSA
DSA sets the attenuation between the RF filter and the ADC, so it decides how much headroom the ADC has. Too little and the ADC over-ranges (clips) at only moderate input — you get "Rx out of order"-type faults and corrupted samples. Raising the DSA lifts that clipping ceiling — and here's the key: it raises the ceiling without moving the noise floor (the noise floor is set upstream by the LNA/NF, ahead of the DSA). So more DSA = more usable dynamic range at the top, same sensitivity at the bottom. That's why the DSA value is a real, version-controlled config setting per band/ADC.
Why shift the dBFS adjustment — and why it must track the DSA
The radio senses power in dBFS (relative to ADC full-scale) and converts to absolute dBm with a per-ADC offset:
RSSI(dBm) = 10·log₁₀(rssi_raw) − FS_const + adc_dbfs_adj[ADC]
Because DSA changes the signal level reaching the ADC, the dBFS reading shifts one-for-one with the DSA — change DSA by 3 dB and the reported RSSI moves by 3 dB. So adc_dbfs_adj must be characterised at the DSA the unit actually ships with. If it was calibrated at DSA 0 but the unit ships at DSA 10, every RSSI reading is ~10 dB out — huge against a typical ±2 dB readout limit. The fix is recalibrating the offset at the shipped DSA — not touching the radio.
The control experiment (how you PROVE it's a reporting bug, not a broken radio)
Change the DSA and watch two things: (1) reported RSSI moves by the full DSA (e.g. +3 dB DSA → +3 dB RSSI), but (2) sensitivity does NOT move (it stays within a few tenths of a dB). That split is the proof: if the receive path were genuinely broken, sensitivity would shift too. Since only the reported number moved, the radio is healthy — you fix the reporting offset, not the radio.
Calibrate on the linear plateau: sweep the generator up the power range and read PHY dBm / CLI dBm / raw dBFS together. The curve is straight in the middle but flattens below ~−100 dBm at the noise floor — so the dBFS→dBm offset can only be taken from the straight (plateau) section, never near the floor. The correction is EIRP − reported dBFS read on that plateau.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why raise the DSA, and does it hurt sensitivity?
A: You raise the DSA to give the ADC more headroom so it stops over-ranging/clipping at moderate input power (which otherwise throws Rx faults). It does NOT hurt sensitivity: the noise floor is set by the LNA/NF ahead of the DSA, so adding attenuation before the ADC lifts the clipping ceiling without raising the floor — more dynamic range at the top, same sensitivity at the bottom.
Q: RSSI reads ~10 dB off but sensitivity is fine — what happened and how do you fix it?
A: The dBFS→dBm reporting offset (adc_dbfs_adj) was characterised at a different DSA than the unit ships with. Since the dBFS reading tracks the DSA one-for-one, a wrong-DSA offset shifts every RSSI reading by the DSA delta — while sensitivity (a real receive-path property) is unaffected. Fix: recalibrate the offset at the shipped DSA, on the linear plateau of the power sweep. It's a reporting fix, not a radio fix.
Q: Why must the dBFS offset be calibrated on the plateau and not at low power?
A: Below ~−100 dBm the RSSI-vs-input curve flattens at the receiver noise floor, so the reading no longer tracks the injected power linearly. The dBFS→dBm offset is EIRP − reported dBFS, which is only valid where the response is linear — the plateau — so calibration points must come from the straight section, above the floor.
Q: The offset is per-ADC — what's a classic bug there?
A: Applying the offset by the wrong index — e.g. keying by the printed/logical ADC position instead of the physical hardware ADC slot — applies one band's offset to another band's channel, giving a fixed few-dB error on the affected antenna. Same class of bug as the antenna→ADC mapping error: always confirm the offset array is keyed by the physical ADC slot.
USLEEP02 uSleep Validation — end-to-end power test: allocation sweep, get-PSU + PM readings, on/off KPI (from the lab session) Advanced click to expand ▾
In plain English
The PA is the hungriest part of the radio, and it burns bias current even when it has nothing to send. uSleep (micro-sleep) switches the PA off during OFDM symbols that carry nothing, and wakes it just before the next symbol that does. USLEEP01 explains how the FPGA does it. This card is about how we prove it saves power: drive the radio at several traffic loads, measure power with uSleep off and then on, and turn the difference into a KPI. It is built from the walkthrough of the test design, the result archive (power-monitoring runs, dashboard, analysis scripts) and the E2E power-saving test plan.
Level 1 — the one idea you must get right: "load" in frequency vs in time
A traffic file of "10%", "25%", "busy hour" or "full load" changes how much data goes to the UE, while the control channels stay the same. The trap is where that data sits:
• Frequency-domain allocation: "10%" means 10% of the RBs in every symbol. Every symbol then carries some energy, so the PA can never sleep. uSleep saves ~0 W here, and that is correct behaviour, not a failure.
• Time-domain occupancy (duty): in real traffic the scheduler tends to fill a TTI completely or leave it empty. "10%" then means 10% of TTIs are busy and 90% are empty, and the empty ones give uSleep its opportunity.
So the saving depends on how many all-zero symbols there are, not on the "% RBs" label. At 0% load LTE still sends CRS and PDCCH. With 2 CRS ports and CFI=1, symbols 0, 4, 7 and 11 are occupied, leaving about 9–10 of 14 symbols empty. That is where the measured ~60% "blank symbol" ceiling comes from.
One LTE subframe at 0% load — which symbols can sleep
Subframes 0/5 also carry PSS/SSS/PBCH, so they have fewer empty symbols. More CRS ports (4-port) or a larger CFI also reduce the opportunity.
Level 2 — where power is measured on a 3-flavour AAU
The AAU is really three radios in one box, one FHGW per flavour: mid-band (B1/B3), low-band (B8/B20/B28) and B41. Each has its own PSU. Running get-PSU on one FHGW's CLI returns two lines for that flavour only (you cannot read the mid-band from the low-band CLI):
• the 12 V rail: FHGW + mid-board electronics (roughly constant);
• the PA rail (~40 V mid-band, ~45 V B41, ~48 V low-band on the units seen; nominal "50 V"): feeds all RFFEs/PAs of that flavour. This is the rail uSleep moves.
Power per line = V × I. Flavour power = P(PA rail) + P(12 V). AAU power = Σ over the three flavours. Example arithmetic from a live read: 40 V × 8.6 A ≈ 344 W on the PA rail and 12 V × 3.7 A ≈ 44 W on the 12 V rail. PAs that are enabled but not transmitting still draw that bias current, which is exactly the waste uSleep removes.

Three independent sources, so every number can be cross-checked:
SourceWhat it isCadenceUse
get-PSU (CLI)internal PSU telemetry per flavour, 2 railssampled every 1 s, 60 samples averaged → 1 value/minprimary live number; per-flavour split
PM / EPE (M-plane)on-board sensors on mid-board & each RFFE: TEMPERATURE, CURRENT, POWER, VOLTAGE (min/avg/max)60 s measurement interval; the RU writes a CSV every 5 min (5 one-minute blocks) → 12 CSVs per hourstandards-style (O-RAN PM) reporting; per-RFFE detail; temperature
Lab PSU / DC analyserbench supply on the common 48 V feedper-minute avg/min/maxindependent "truth" when available (not in every lab)
The get-PSU cadence (1 value/min) is chosen on purpose to match the PM 1-minute blocks, so the two can be overlaid minute by minute.
Measurement architecture
PM is enabled by pushing an XML over the M-plane that activates the EPE measurement objects (interval 60 s, file upload 300 s). Automation reads get-PSU on all three FHGWs at the same time.
Level 3 — the test procedure, step by step
1. Reboot all three FHGWs together, so no PA is left active from an earlier test and all start from a known state.
2. Push the PM XML (M-plane) to each FHGW. This starts the sensor readings and the 5-minute CSVs on the RU's data partition.
3. Start collection at the same moment: parse CSVs and poll get-PSU on all three flavours. Everything is time-aligned.
4. Activate all carriers on every band present and start IQ playback on all antennas of all three flavours at once, with the waveform for the allocation under test.
5. Run 1 hour with uSleep OFF, then let the unit cool down.
6. Run 1 hour with uSleep ON, same waveform. uSleep is enabled per PA through the RU CLI (set/get micro-sleep control). The wake-up advance delay is fixed and is not a test knob.
7. Repeat for each allocation, e.g. 0%, 10%, 25%, 50% (75% optional). A finer 10%-step sweep is possible but multiplies the data without improving the validation.
8. Build the KPI sheet: for each allocation, expected ΔP = Poff − Pon with a tolerance (e.g. ±10%). Report per flavour and for the whole AAU.
AllocationExpected uSleep savingWhy
0% (control only)largestmost symbols are all-zero (~60% ceiling)
10% / 25% (freq-domain RBs in every symbol)≈ 0every symbol has energy, so the PA never sleeps
same % as TTI duty (bursty)grows as duty fallsempty TTIs are all-zero symbols
full load≈ 0nothing to gate
Level 3b — the E2E version (DU-driven traffic, combined with Reduced Output Power)
In E2E the scheduler decides allocation, so load becomes a measured axis. The air interface is roughly bimodal (each TTI ≈100% or 0% RBs), so % allocation = busy-TTI duty cycle. iPerf -b steers it, and the MAC per-TTI log is the truth: bin results by measured duty.
• Variation matrix: RoP {off, 3 dB, 10 dB} × uSleep {off, on} = 6 variations (V0 baseline … V5 10 dB + uSleep).
• Load points: the ETSI ES 202 706-1 levels (idle, low, medium, busy-hour, full), mapped to duty through the unthrottled peak throughput. Repeat N=3.
• Per run: capture lab PSU + internal PSU + PM together; iPerf ≥ 15 min; parse the MAC log for measured duty and % empty TTIs; cross-check the EMS 15-min average; record throughput and BLER.
• Pass/fail: (1) gate: V0 must match the reference power-monitoring runs at every load, otherwise the pipeline is not validated; (2) RoP: P < V0, and 10 dB saves more than 3 dB; (3) uSleep: P < V0, saving grows as duty drops, ≈0 at full load; (4) combined saving ≈ RoP + uSleep (they should not interfere); (5) no throughput or BLER regression.
• Replicate on all bands and report per band group (B41 / B1·B3 / low band).
Level 4 — expert pitfalls (read before you trust a number)
Thermal drift is larger than the effect. In a whole-AAU run the lab PSU climbed from ~1266 W to ~1399 W over the first 30 minutes as the PAs heated. Compare on and off at thermal steady state (or trim the warm-up), cool down between runs, and ideally alternate the order (off→on→on→off) so the drift cancels.
Missing samples show up as zeros. The PM CSV series had isolated drops to ~0 W. Averaging them in drags the mean down and fakes a "saving". Filter zero or NaN samples before averaging.
Compare ΔP within one source. PM read ~16% below the lab PSU in a baseline (~710 W vs ~845 W for B1+B3), because the model excludes cable and common-board losses (CM14). Never subtract a PM "on" from a PSU "off".
Trim the start. Transmission begins after the test starts, and some bands (e.g. B8) come up later. Pick the analysis window after all carriers are on air.
The 12 V rail is your sanity check. uSleep should move the PA rail. If the 12 V rail moves as much, something else changed.
Telemetry resolution. A 0.1 A step on a 40 V rail is 4 W. That is why you average 60 × 1-s samples and use 1-hour windows.
Check RF quality, not just watts. Re-check EVM on the first symbol after each sleep and ACLR (PA switching can splatter), because a saving that breaks EVM is a fail.
IQ-playback caveat. USLEEP01 records that on the build studied, the uSleep detector taps the stream upstream of where IQ playback injects samples. If that is still true, playback content cannot trigger sleep. Run a null check first: 0%-allocation playback with uSleep off vs on. If ΔP ≈ 0 while DU-generated traffic at similar duty saves watts, the detector does not see playback and you must use DU traffic (the E2E plan).
Interview Q&A
Q: uSleep shows no saving at 10% allocation. Is the feature broken?
A: Not necessarily. If the 10% is a frequency-domain allocation (10% of RBs in every symbol), every OFDM symbol carries energy, so the PA can never be gated off. The saving is correctly ≈0. uSleep saves on all-zero symbols, which come from time-domain emptiness (idle TTIs, control-only symbols). Re-test with low TTI duty or 0% load before calling it a defect.
Q: How do you measure the power of a 3-flavour AAU?
A: Each flavour (mid-band, low-band, B41) has its own FHGW and PSU. get-PSU on each FHGW returns two rails: a 12 V rail (FHGW + mid-board) and the PA rail (~40–48 V, all RFFEs). Power per rail = V×I, flavour power = the sum of both rails, AAU power = the sum over the three flavours. It is read every second, averaged per minute, and cross-checked against the PM sensor CSVs (5-minute files) and a lab DC supply when available.
Q: Why is get-PSU averaged to one value per minute?
A: To line up with the PM (O-RAN performance measurement) cadence of 60-second measurement blocks, so CLI and PM data can be overlaid minute for minute. It also averages out telemetry quantisation (0.1 A ≈ 4 W on a 40 V rail) and the fast PA on/off swings.
Q: Your uSleep-on run shows a 12% saving, but the unit had just been rebooted before the off run. Do you trust it?
A: No. Warm-up drift alone can be ~10% (whole-AAU power rose ~130 W in 30 minutes in one run). Repeat with both runs at thermal steady state, cool down between them, or alternate the order, and compare ΔP within the same measurement source.
Q: What is the maximum saving you would expect at zero traffic in LTE, and why is it not 100%?
A: Roughly the fraction of all-zero symbols, about 60% of symbols at 0% load, since CRS (symbols 0/4/7/11 for 2 ports), PDCCH, and PSS/SSS/PBCH in subframes 0/5 must still be sent. The PA must be on for those, plus a short wake-up advance before each one, and the 12 V electronics are unaffected. So the power saving is well below 60% of total AAU power.
Q: How would you validate uSleep together with Reduced Output Power?
A: Run a 2-D matrix, RoP {off, 3 dB, 10 dB} × uSleep {off, on}, across ETSI load levels, with load defined by measured TTI duty from the MAC log. Gate on the baseline matching reference runs. Then expect RoP savings to scale with dB, uSleep savings to grow as duty falls, and combined ≈ the sum (non-interfering), all with no throughput or BLER regression.
From the recording — remaining details (what the walkthrough said that is not above)
These points come from re-reading the full 37-minute walkthrough of this test. Each one is either a practical detail you need at the bench or a place where the spoken explanation could mislead a newcomer.
TopicWhat was said, and what it means for you
The commandThe automation runs get-PSU on each FHGW CLI. In the recording the mentor twice says "get RSSI" by mistake and then corrects himself. RSSI is a separate task (the RSSI accuracy work, see RSSI04) and has nothing to do with power.
One CLI sees one flavourFrom the low-band FHGW you cannot read the mid-band PSU, and vice versa. The automation therefore got a new combined "setup" that holds all three FHGW setups, so one run can log in to all three CLIs and send get-PSU to each at the same moment.
What the "RFFE" line isThe PA-rail line from get-PSU is the total for every RFFE of that flavour. It is not one PA, and it is not limited to four RFFEs. If you need per-RFFE numbers, take them from the PM sensor CSV instead.
Rail voltageThe PA rail is described as "50 V", but the real value depends on the PSU. The live readings were 40 V mid-band (B1/B3), 45 V B41 and 48 V low band. During the demo the 40 V line was first called B41 and then corrected to B1/B3. Before you record a number, check which FHGW (model name) you are logged in to.
PM min / avg / maxEach one-minute PM block gives min, max and avg for every sensor, per RFFE and per band. The mentor was explicit: use the average value for the KPI, not min or max.
The earlier runsThe runs shown in the call (RUN1…RUN14, all PAs off, 0 %, 100 % and so on) were power-monitoring runs only, with no uSleep. They are the baseline, and they show which RFFE transmits and how much each one draws. See USLEEP03.
Pass/fail tolerancePass means the PM value and the CLI value agree. At the time of the call the tolerance had not been set: the developer of the PM feature has to fix it. Part of the first campaign is to find out how closely the two sources can agree.
DashboardYou can view the data in Kibana (Elasticsearch) or in the custom HTML "EPE dashboard" the team had built earlier. The custom dashboard was chosen. It plots power, current and temperature per RFFE and per band.
What the plots showedIn RUN14 the current stays low for the first minutes because transmission starts some time after the test starts. B1 and B3 come up first and B8 comes up later. RFFE temperature rises once TX starts. In the all-off run the temperature falls steadily over the hour. The lab PSU trace shows the same steps.
Why start logging before TXSomeone asked whether the first minutes, before carriers are active, spoil the result. The answer was no: you choose the analysis window afterwards in the dashboard. The idle segment before TX is also a useful built-in baseline.
Where the CSVs landThe PM feature writes one CSV every 5 minutes to the RU data partition 4 (/run/media/mmcblk0p4). A 1-hour run gives 12 files. The automation parses them while it is still polling get-PSU, so both series share one timeline.
Activate only what existsWhich carriers you activate depends on the bands fitted. The lab unit had B8 but no B28, so only B8 was activated on low band.
IQ playback is acceptableWhen asked whether IQ playback is good enough, the answer was yes: the bin files were made for this purpose. DU-generated traffic may be added later (that is the E2E plan). Playback on all antennas is iq_playback /srv/iq_samples/<file.bin> 255 0 0 (255 = all antennas, 0–3 = one antenna), and iq_stop stops it. Before trusting playback-driven savings, remember the null check in Level 4 above.
Run orderAt one point the mentor says "first on, then off". The step-by-step procedure he gives later is OFF first, cool down, then ON. Follow the procedure, and alternate the order when you repeat, so that thermal drift cancels.
Allocation listThe list moved during the call: first 0/10/25/50 %, later 0/20 (or 10)/25/50 % with 75 % as an option. A 10 %-step sweep from 0 to 100 % was proposed, like the 1 dB-step sweep used for Reduced Output Power. It was turned down as "too much data". The feature owners had already decided the coarse points were enough for validation, and E2E may sweep more finely later.
KPI sheetThe KPIs go into an Excel sheet: expected Poff − Pon per allocation, with a tolerance of "maybe 10 %". That 10 % is a starting guess, and the data comes first.
uSleep CLIThe RU CLI has set / get microsleep control commands, a lot of counters, and a per-PA enable status you can read back. The wake-up advance delay can be changed in the CLI, but it is fixed for this test: the automation only enables uSleep on all PAs.
TDD and FDDBoth duplex modes are tested. On TDD the PA is already gated in UL slots, so uSleep can only add savings in DL symbols. Expect a smaller relative gain on B41 than on FDD mid-band.
PriorityThe call ended with "finish the RSSI work first", because it had to be pushed that day. The uSleep automation came after it.
Reading tip about "10 %". Within a single minute the recording uses "10 %" in both senses. First it means 10 % of the time (bursts, with the PA toggling "like TDD"). Then it means 10 % of the RBs in every symbol (PA always on, so no saving). Level 1 above resolves this. When someone quotes a load percentage, ask whether they mean frequency-domain RBs or time-domain TTI duty.
VLOAD01 Variable Load — what "load" does to the TX chain, DPD, power and the RX front end (DSA/AGC & dBFS under changing input) Advanced click to expand ▾
In plain English
Conformance tests usually run the radio at full load (every RB filled, E-TM1.1). Real networks never sit there: traffic goes from idle at night to busy hour at lunch. Variable-load testing asks: does the radio stay compliant (ACLR, EVM, power) and efficient at every load, not only the one it was tuned at? On the receive side the equivalent question is: as the uplink input rises and falls (more UEs, interferers), does the RX chain keep enough headroom and still report RSSI correctly?
Level 1 — what changes when load changes (TX)
QuantityAt high loadAt low loadWhy it matters
Average output powernear rated (all REs on)lower (fewer REs), CRS always onPavg ∝ occupied REs at fixed per-RE power
Signal statistics / PAPRGaussian-like OFDM, CFR-limitedbursty; few RBs; CRS-dominatedDPD models are trained on the signal statistics
PA operating pointclose to compressiondeep back-off, lower efficiencythe AM-AM/AM-PM curve seen by DPD moves
PA temperaturehot (gain ↓ ~3 dB hot)coolergain, DPD coefficients and power trims drift with temperature
Power supply drawhighlow (opportunity for uSleep / Dynamic Vdd)energy KPIs are load-weighted
ETSI ES 202 706-1 defines the standard load levels (low, medium, busy-hour, plus full and idle) and a daily weighting, so a single "energy efficiency" number can be computed. Test the levels your plan names, and take the exact percentages from the spec version you test against.
Level 2 — variable load and DPD (the classic "variable-load DPD" test)
DPD learns an inverse of the PA from what it observes (DPD02). If it learns at one load and the load changes, it faces a different PA (other temperature, bias point and signal statistics). A healthy DPD re-adapts and holds ACLR/EVM, but a poorly-regularised one can:
• over-fit to the high-load statistics and mis-correct at low load (ACLR degrades as load drops);
• lag after a step change, so ACLR is bad for seconds after the change (this is why you wait for DPD to re-converge, ~60 s in lab practice, before measuring after any power or load change);
• lose lock at very low load, because the observation receiver sees too little signal to estimate coefficients. Good designs freeze or hold coefficients below a threshold.
How to test: set occupancy (e.g. 100% → 50% → 30% → 0%), wait for re-convergence at each step, and measure ACLR + EVM + channel power. Also step it down and back up to catch hysteresis or lag. Pair it with the PA-efficiency plan: at each load re-check the CFR working point and DAC current, because they interact.
In the regression suite this has no standalone test. It is covered indirectly because every TX run measures ACLR/EVM with DPD active, which is a gap worth knowing about.
Level 3 — the RX side: variable input, DSA/AGC and dBFS
On receive, the "load" is the total power arriving at the ADC: wanted UEs, other UEs and interferers. The ADC has a fixed full scale (0 dBFS ≈ +2 dBm at the ADC on this design), so the chain must be set so that:
• the weakest wanted signal is still above the noise (sensitivity is set by the LNA/NF, before any attenuator), and
• the strongest total input still leaves headroom. The design targets a maximum of about −15 dBFS at the ADC, leaving room for PAPR.
The design line-up shows the mechanism. In front of the gain stages there is a switched attenuator step (0 or 10 dB) with an "AGC / LNA mode change" level around −54 dBm input. Below it the step is out (best NF). Above it the 10 dB step switches in (more headroom, higher blocking tolerance). A DSA (digital step attenuator) placed before the ADC does the same job statically per band.
The consequence you must remember: any attenuation change (static DSA or AGC step) shifts the dBFS reading 1:1. So the dBFS→dBm reporting offset must track it, otherwise RSSI is wrong by exactly the step while sensitivity is unchanged. This is the FCDSA story (calibrate the offset at the shipped DSA, on the linear plateau) and the same physics as RX Dynamic Range (FC13) and blocking (FC14).
Level 4 — debugging variable-load failures
SymptomLikely causeCheck
ACLR passes at 100% but fails at 30%DPD over-fitted to high-load statistics / poor regularisationcoefficients vs load; does ACLR recover after a longer wait?
ACLR bad for ~seconds after a load step, then OKnormal DPD re-convergencemeasure after the settle time; report the transient separately
EVM worse at low loadCRS/control dominate, measurement window or allocation configEVM is computed on allocated RBs only, so check the analyser demod setup
Power not proportional to loadCRS/control floor, power-scaling configexpected P = Pfull + 10·log₁₀(occupied REs / total REs) + CRS floor
RSSI wrong by a fixed step at high UL inputAGC/DSA step switched but reporting offset not updatedread the attenuator state vs RSSI; FCDSA control test
Sensitivity OK, blocking failsnot enough attenuation/headroom at high inputblocking level vs the step threshold; ADC over-range counters
Interview Q&A
Q: Why run variable-load tests if the radio passes ACLR at full load?
A: Because DPD, PA bias, temperature and signal statistics all change with load. A DPD trained at full load can mis-correct at 30% load, or lag after a load step, so ACLR/EVM can fail at loads the full-load test never visits. Real networks spend most of their time at low or medium load, and energy KPIs are load-weighted too.
Q: After changing load or output power, why wait before measuring ACLR?
A: DPD needs time to re-estimate its coefficients for the new PA operating point and signal statistics. Measuring during the re-convergence transient reports a temporary ACLR degradation. In practice you wait ~60 s, or until the DPD reports convergence, then measure.
Q: On the RX side, what plays the role of "load", and how does the design cope?
A: The total power at the ADC. The chain keeps the maximum around −15 dBFS for PAPR headroom. An attenuator step (e.g. 10 dB) switches in above an AGC threshold (~−54 dBm input) to protect the ADC and improve blocking, and a per-band DSA sets static headroom. Sensitivity is unaffected because the noise figure is set by the LNA ahead of these attenuators.
Q: RSSI reads 10 dB high only when the uplink input is strong. What happened?
A: The 10 dB attenuator/AGC step switched in, but the dBFS→dBm reporting offset was not adjusted for the new state (or was calibrated in the other state). dBFS tracks attenuation 1:1, so the report is off by exactly the step. Fix the offset per attenuator state, calibrated on the linear plateau.
DPD02 DPD Deep Dive — from AM-AM/AM-PM to memory polynomials, the observation path, adaptation and how DPD fails Advanced click to expand ▾
In plain English
A GaN PA is efficient only when driven close to saturation, but near saturation it is non-linear. It squashes peaks and rotates their phase, which spreads energy into the neighbouring channels (bad ACLR) and blurs the constellation (bad EVM). DPD (Digital Pre-Distortion) deliberately pre-bends the digital signal in the opposite way, so after the PA bends it back, the result is straight. It is the reason a radio can be both efficient and clean.
Level 1 — the two non-linearities
AM-AM (amplitude → amplitude): gain compresses as input rises (P1dB, then saturation). AM-PM (amplitude → phase): output phase shifts with input amplitude. Both are strong in GaN near saturation.
Spectral view: a cubic term (x·|x|²) creates 3rd-order intermodulation (IM3) occupying ~3× the signal bandwidth, and 5th-order occupies ~5×. That skirt is what ACLR measures. IM3 rises 3 dB per 1 dB of output, so ACLR (dBc) worsens by ~2 dB per dB of extra power. That is why 1 dB of back-off buys ~2 dB of ACLR without DPD.
DPD typically improves ACLR by ~15–20 dB, which lets the PA run a few dB closer to saturation. At rated power that means many watts saved.
DPD loop (indirect-learning style)
In the AAU design the observation path taps ~20 dB after the final PA and returns through switches and the FPCB to the FHGW ADC. Total path loss from PA output to ORX input is ~65–70 dB.
Level 2 — models: why "memory" matters
Memoryless DPD (a LUT of gain/phase vs |x|) corrects static AM-AM/AM-PM. But a real PA also has memory: its output depends on past samples (bias-network time constants, thermal effects, matching networks across wide bandwidth). Memory effects make ACLR asymmetric (lower and upper adjacent channels differ) and limit what a LUT can fix.
Memory polynomial (the workhorse): z(n) = Σk Σm akm · x(n−m) · |x(n−m)|k−1, with odd orders k = 1,3,5,7 and memory depth m = 0…M (a few taps). GMP (generalised MP) adds cross terms between lagging and leading envelopes, and Volterra series are the most general but too heavy. The coefficients akm are found by least squares.
Indirect learning (ILA): train a post-distorter that maps the (gain-normalised) PA output back to its input, then copy it in front of the PA. Direct learning (DLA): iteratively adjust the pre-distorter to minimise the error between x and y/g. DLA is more robust to noise and ORX imperfections, while ILA is simpler.
Level 3 — the observation receiver (ORX) is half the DPD
DPD can only correct what it sees, so the ORX must be clean, wide and well aligned:
• Bandwidth: must capture the distortion (≈3–5× the signal BW) or the model cannot see what to cancel.
• Alignment: time delay (to a fraction of a sample), gain and phase between x and y must be estimated every update. A delay error looks exactly like memory and ruins convergence.
• Level: the coupled signal must sit in the ORX ADC's sweet spot, neither clipping (which corrupts peaks, where the distortion lives) nor buried in noise.
• Isolation: other transmitters must not leak into the ORX tap (the design spec is > 60 dB TX-to-OB isolation), or DPD "corrects" someone else's signal.
CFR comes before DPD: CFR clips the peaks to a target PAPR (e.g. ~8 dB). This costs a little EVM but lets the PA run hotter. DPD then only has to linearise up to that clipped peak. If CFR is too loose, the peaks push the PA into hard saturation, and no DPD can undo a hard clip.
Level 4 — how DPD fails, and how it looks on the analyser
SymptomProbable causeHow to confirm
ACLR ~10–20 dB worse than normal, both sidesDPD off / not converged / bypassedread DPD state/convergence; compare ACLR with DPD forced off
ACLR asymmetric (one side much worse)uncorrected memory effects, ORX delay error, IQ imbalancetry more memory taps; re-run delay alignment; LO/IQ cal
ACLR good right after start, degrades over minutesthermal drift outpaces adaptation, or adaptation frozenlog temperature vs ACLR; adaptation update rate
ACLR degrades at low load onlyORX SNR too low to adapt, over-fit to high-load statisticsVLOAD01 sweep; coefficient freeze threshold
EVM bad but ACLR finein-band problem: CFR too aggressive, phase noise, IQ, quantisationEVM vs CFR target; EVM per symbol; constellation shape
DPD diverges / oscillatesORX clipping, wrong gain normalisation, coupler path mis-calibratedORX power level; coupler cal; LS regularisation
Fails only at max powerPA past saturation (hard clip): DPD cannot add power that does not existback off 1 dB: if ACLR jumps a lot, you were at the wall
Lab rules: after any change of power, carrier, bandwidth or load, wait for re-convergence (~60 s) before measuring. Record DPD state with every ACLR result. When debugging, always compare with DPD forced off. The delta tells you whether the problem is the PA/linearisation or something else.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why does ACLR get worse by about 2 dB for every 1 dB increase in output power?
A: The main adjacent-channel leakage is 3rd-order intermodulation, which grows at 3 dB per dB of input (cubic). The carrier grows at 1 dB per dB, so the ratio between them (ACLR in dBc) shrinks by 3 − 1 = 2 dB per dB.
Q: What is a memory polynomial and why is a LUT not enough?
A: z(n) = Σ_k Σ_m a_km · x(n−m)·|x(n−m)|^(k−1): odd non-linear orders applied to the current and a few past samples. A LUT is memoryless and only fixes static AM-AM/AM-PM. Wideband GaN PAs have memory (bias networks, thermal, matching), which shows as asymmetric ACLR a LUT cannot correct. The memory terms model that dependence on past samples.
Q: What must the DPD observation receiver get right?
A: Enough bandwidth to see the distortion (3–5× the signal BW), precise time/gain/phase alignment to the reference, a level that neither clips nor sinks into noise, and isolation from other transmitters. A delay-alignment error masquerades as memory and prevents convergence. In the AAU the ORX taps ~20 dB after the PA and loses ~65–70 dB in total back to the FHGW.
Q: ACLR is fine at 40 W but 1 dB higher it collapses by 8 dB. Why?
A: You have reached the PA's saturation wall. DPD can pre-expand the signal only up to the maximum the PA can physically deliver, and beyond that the peaks are hard-clipped and no pre-distortion can restore them. Either back off, tighten CFR, or accept that the extra dB is beyond the PA's linearisable range.
Q: How do you prove a bad ACLR is a DPD problem and not the PA or a filter?
A: Measure with DPD forced off and on. A healthy DPD gives a large improvement (~15–20 dB). No improvement means DPD is not running, not converged, or its ORX is broken. If DPD-off ACLR is already far worse than the PA's known performance, suspect the PA, bias or drive level. If only one side or far-out emissions fail, look at memory effects, filters or spurious sources.
ADC02 ADC & DAC Deep Dive — sampling, full scale, dBFS↔dBm, quantisation & ENOB, NSD/ADC noise figure, jitter, DAC images & sinc (with the AAU design numbers) Advanced click to expand ▾
In plain English
The DAC is the door from numbers to RF on transmit, and the ADC is the door from RF to numbers on receive. Everything digital (DPD, CFR, RSSI, the PHY) lives on one side, and everything analog (PA, LNA, filters) on the other. Their limits (full scale at the top, noise at the bottom, and sampling in frequency) decide the dynamic range of the whole radio. The AAU uses RF-sampling converters: the ADC samples the RF band directly (≈3 GS/s class) and the DAC synthesises RF directly, so there is no analog mixer in the chain.
Level 1 — full scale, dBFS and the conversion to dBm
dBFS = power relative to the converter's full scale: 0 dBFS is the largest sine that fits, and everything real is negative. In the PHY with 16-bit samples: dBFS = 20·log₁₀(RMS / 215).
On this ADC, 0 dBFS ≈ +2 dBm at the ADC input (full scale ≈ 1.1 Vppd). So:
dBm@ADC = dBFS + ~2 and dBm@antenna = dBm@ADC − RX gain
Worked example from the design sheet: a −100 dBm carrier plus the noise floor in its bandwidth (−104.5 dBm for 5 MHz at 2.5 dB NF) gives a total RSSI of −98.7 dBm. RSSI measures everything in the band, including noise. With 37 dB RX gain that is −61.7 dBm at the ADC, which is −63.6 dBFS (the sheet: dBFS = RSSI + RX gain − 1.95). That is the whole RSSI calibration idea (EXP6, RSSI02): the reporting offset is this gain + full-scale constant.
Why back off from full scale? OFDM has a high peak-to-average ratio (PAPR ~8–12 dB), so the average must sit well below 0 dBFS or the peaks clip. The RX line-up targets ≤ −15 dBFS at max input, and the TX DAC runs about 8.6 dB below its max output (≈ −2 dBm average vs 6.5 dBm max) for the same reason.
Level 2 — the noise floor: quantisation, ENOB, NSD and "ADC noise figure"
Ideal quantisation SNR (full-scale sine): SNR = 6.02·N + 1.76 dB, so 12 bits ≈ 74 dB and 14 bits ≈ 86 dB. Real ADCs are worse, which is described by ENOB = (SINAD − 1.76)/6.02.
That noise is spread over the Nyquist band (Fs/2). A 20 MHz carrier sees only its slice, so there is processing gain of 10·log₁₀(Fs/2 / BW). At ~3 GS/s that is ~19 dB. Oversampling is why a "12-bit" RF ADC is good enough.
RF engineers usually quote the ADC as NSD (noise spectral density, dBFS/Hz). The design sheet gives ≈ −151 dBFS/Hz at −35 dBFS input. Converting to an equivalent noise figure:
NFADC = NSD(dBFS/Hz) + FS(dBm) − (−174 dBm/Hz) ≈ −151 + 2 + 174 ≈ 25–27 dB (per band, 25.6–27.3 dB in the sheet).
A 27 dB NF sounds terrible, but in the RX line-up there is ~33 dB of gain in front of the ADC, so by Friis it adds only ~0.7 dB: the cascade goes from 1.72 dB to 2.44 dB total NF. This is the gain-vs-headroom trade-off in one line. More gain before the ADC hides its noise, but leaves less headroom for strong signals.
Clock jitter sets another ceiling that gets worse with input frequency: SNRjitter = −20·log₁₀(2π·fin·tj). At 2.1 GHz, 100 fs rms jitter limits SNR to ≈ 58 dB (full-scale). That is why RF sampling needs a very clean clock (the clock chip is on the POST list for a reason).
Level 3 — sampling in frequency: Nyquist zones, DDC/DUC, DAC images and sinc
ADC: an RF-sampling ADC deliberately places the band in a higher Nyquist zone (e.g. 1.9 GHz sampled at ~3 GS/s is in zone 2). Anything else that lands in the same zones aliases on top of the band, so the RF filters in front are the anti-alias filters. The DDC (digital down-converter: NCO mixer + decimating filters) then shifts the carrier to 0 Hz and decimates to the carrier rate (30.72 MS/s for 20 MHz LTE) toward the PHY.
DAC: the DUC (interpolating filters + NCO) moves each carrier to its frequency. A DAC output holds each sample for one period, which gives:
• images at k·Fs ± f (must be filtered),
• a sinc roll-off of the wanted band: 20·log₁₀|sin(πf/Fs)/(πf/Fs)|. It is ~−3.9 dB at Fs/2 and tilts wide carriers, so there is usually a digital inverse-sinc filter.
DAC output level: a current-steering DAC's full-scale current sets the analog output level. This is the "DAC current" knob (DACG01, PAE01): it scales output power without changing the digital signal, which is why it is used with digital gain to trim power.
Level 4 — converter problems you will actually see
SymptomConverter causeWhere to look
"Rx out of order" / corrupted samples at moderate inputADC over-range (clipping), not enough headroomDSA/attenuator setting, over-range counters (FCDSA)
Sensitivity a few dB worse than the line-uptoo little gain before the ADC, so ADC NF dominatescascade NF with the actual gain; DSA too high
A spur in-band that moves when you change Fs or the carrieraliased interferer or ADC interleaving spurchange NCO/carrier: an alias moves differently from a real signal
Spurs at k·Fs ± f on TXDAC images not filteredspurious sweep (FC19) around the image frequencies
Tilt across a wide carrier / flatness failDAC sinc roll-off not compensatedinverse-sinc enable; flatness vs frequency
EVM floor that does not improve with powerconverter SNR, jitter or quantisation floorEVM vs level curve: it flattens at the converter floor
RSSI off by a fixed dB after a config changefull-scale/offset constant or attenuation state changeddBFS→dBm offset vs DSA (FCDSA, RSSI03)
Interview Q&A
Q: Convert −40 dBFS at the ADC to dBm at the antenna for a chain with 33 dB gain, given 0 dBFS = +2 dBm.
A: dBm at the ADC = −40 + 2 = −38 dBm. dBm at the antenna = −38 − 33 = −71 dBm. The RSSI reporting offset is exactly this full-scale constant plus the chain gain.
Q: The RF ADC has a 27 dB noise figure. Why doesn't that ruin sensitivity?
A: Friis: its noise is divided by the gain in front of it. With ~33 dB of LNA and gain stages ahead, it raises the cascade NF only from ~1.7 dB to ~2.4 dB. The trade-off is headroom: that gain also lifts strong signals toward full scale, which is why an attenuator/DSA exists for high inputs.
Q: What is ENOB and how do you get ADC SNR from bits?
A: Ideal SNR = 6.02·N + 1.76 dB for a full-scale sine. ENOB = (measured SINAD − 1.76)/6.02 is the "real" number of bits after noise and distortion. For a narrow carrier inside a wide Nyquist band you also gain 10·log₁₀((Fs/2)/BW) of processing gain.
Q: Why does an RF-sampling ADC need such a clean clock?
A: Jitter-limited SNR = −20·log₁₀(2π·f_in·t_j), which gets worse with input frequency. At 2 GHz, even ~100 fs rms jitter caps SNR near 58 dB. At RF the clock is effectively part of the signal path.
Q: What are DAC images and sinc roll-off, and what do you do about them?
A: A DAC holds each sample for a clock period, so its spectrum repeats at k·Fs ± f (images) and is shaped by sinc(f/Fs), drooping ~3.9 dB at Fs/2. Images are removed by filtering (and checked in spurious tests). Sinc droop is corrected with a digital inverse-sinc filter so wide carriers stay flat.
TXRX02 TX & RX Path — follow one signal stage by stage with real levels: DAC → PA → antenna and antenna → LNA → ADC (AAU B1 line-up) Advanced click to expand ▾
In plain English
Every RF test on this site measures something that happens at one stage of these two chains. If you can say, at each stage, what the level is and what can go wrong, you can place any failure on the map. The tables follow a single B1 path through the design line-up. Values are rounded, part numbers are omitted, and the gain budget (GAIN01) has the per-band targets.
Level 1 — TX path, one PA path of a 40 W B1 configuration (dBm)
StageGain / loss (dB)Level after (dBm)What this stage is for

feeder + FPCB (FHGW → mid-board)−16.1−21.3flex-PCB cable is lossy (rises with f and temperature)

Read it like an engineer: the chain loses ~50 dB in cables, splitters and pads and regains it with three gain stages, then the PA adds 40 dB. The V-ATT is the only adjustable element, and its range is the temperature/flatness margin. Four such paths (4 PAs × ~10 W) make the "40 W" configuration. The ~1.7 dB after the PA (coupler, circulator, filter) comes straight off the rated power, which is why it is budgeted to the tenth of a dB.
Level 2 — RX path, from the antenna to the ADC (dBm)
StageGain / loss (dB)Level after (dBm)What this stage is for

That gap is the room for strong signals. At the top, the design targets ≤ −15 dBFS, and above ~−54 dBm input the 10 dB step switches in to keep it there (VLOAD01).

Level 4 — isolating a fault to a stage (method)
1. Work in levels, not verdicts. Convert every reading to dBm at a known point (port, coupler, ADC) using the line-up, and compare with the expected level. A 6 dB shortfall at the port with a normal ORX level points after the coupler (filter/connector). A shortfall at both points points upstream of the PA.
2. Use the built-in probes: the DPD ORX (after the PA), RSSI (at the ADC), per-RFFE IQ playback (FC20, isolates one RFFE and polarisation), and temperature sensors.
3. Split TX/RX and per path. The four PA paths are identical, so compare them. One path 3 dB low means a local fault (connector, phase-shifter state, PA). All four low means a shared stage (mid-board, FPCB, DAC).
4. Temperature first. The RFFE loses ~3 dB of gain hot. Always record temperature with power and RSSI results before blaming hardware.
Interview Q&A
Q: Where is the noise figure of the receiver decided, and what is it in this design?
A: At the very front: every dB of loss before the LNA adds about 1 dB of NF, and the LNA's own NF (~0.55 dB) plus ~0.9 dB of filter loss gives ~1.5 dB after the LNA. The rest of the chain, including the ~27 dB-NF ADC behind ~33 dB of gain, adds under 1 dB by Friis, for ~2.4 dB total.
Q: The TX chain loses about 50 dB before the PA. Why design it that way?
A: The FHGW, mid-board and RFFEs are separate boards joined by flexible-PCB cables. Each run costs ~13–16 dB, and a 4-way divider splits one signal to four PA paths. Gain stages are placed to make up the loss while keeping each stage in its linear range, and a variable attenuator gives ≥ 6 dB of trim for temperature and flatness.
Q: Output power is 3 dB low on one of four PA paths only. Where do you look?
A: Something local to that path: its RFFE gain stage, phase-shifter or V-ATT state, PA, coupler/circulator or the connector to its filter. Shared stages (DAC, first FPCB, mid-board) would affect all four. Compare the DPD ORX level on that path to see whether the loss is before or after the coupler.
Q: Why does the ADC sit ~60 dB below full scale at sensitivity?
A: That gap is the headroom for everything stronger than the weakest wanted signal: other UEs, interferers and blockers, plus the signal's own PAPR. The design keeps the maximum near −15 dBFS and switches in a 10 dB step at high input so the ADC never clips.
ACLREVM01 ACLR & EVM Together — the physics link, the real requirement (45 dBc or the absolute floor), EVM budgets and a joint debug matrix Advanced click to expand ▾
In plain English
ACLR asks: how much of my power spills outside my channel into my neighbour's? EVM asks: how accurately did I draw the constellation points inside my channel? They are the outside and inside view of the same transmitter imperfections. Looking at both together tells you which imperfection you have. FC01/FC02 cover each test and its automation, and this card connects them.
Level 1 — definitions you can derive on a whiteboard
ACLR = Passigned channel / Padjacent channel, in dBc, measured in each adjacent channel (E-UTRA with a square filter over the occupied BW; UTRA with an RRC filter). LTE BS requirement: 45 dBc for the first and second adjacent channels.
EVM = √(mean |error vector|² / mean |ideal|²) × 100%, measured after the analyser removes frequency, timing, phase and gain offsets, on allocated REs. Limits: QPSK 17.5%, 16QAM 12.5%, 64QAM 8%, 256QAM 3.5% (TS 36.141 §6.5.2).
EVM ↔ SNR: if the error is noise-like, EVMrms ≈ 1/√SNR, so 8% ≈ 22 dB, 3.5% ≈ 29 dB and 1% = 40 dB. That is why 256QAM needs such a clean transmitter.
Level 2 — the requirement is not always 45 dBc
The ACLR limit is "45 dBc or an absolute limit (−13 dBm/MHz for Category A), whichever is less stringent". The absolute limit wins when the carrier's own power spectral density is low. The design workbook works this out per band and bandwidth: with ~39.6 dBm per path over 18 MHz, PSD ≈ 27 dBm/MHz, so the absolute floor allows 27 + 13 = ~40 dBc, which is less stringent than 45. At 5 MHz the PSD is higher and 45 dBc binds.
Carrier BW (B1 path ~39.6 dBm)PSD (dBm/MHz)−13 dBm/MHz ⇒ dBcBinding ACLR requirement
5 MHz~33~4645 dBc
10 MHz~30~43~42–43 dBc
20 MHz~27~40~39–40 dBc
The workbook then adds a 2 dB design margin and checks OBUE the same way. Know this nuance: an automation limit fixed at 45 dBc can be stricter than the spec at 20 MHz. That is fine as an internal target, but say so when you report a "fail".
Level 3 — one impairment, two symptoms: the joint matrix
ImpairmentACLREVMTell-tale
PA compression / DPD offbad (both sides, ~2 dB/dB)bad (outer points pulled in)constellation corners compressed; ACLR jumps with 1 dB back-off
PA memory effectsasymmetricmoderatelower ≠ upper adjacent channel
CFR too aggressiveOK / goodbadEVM worsens as PAPR target tightens; ACLR unchanged
Phase noise (LO/PLL)close-in skirt ↑bad, rotationalpoints smeared along arcs; worse at higher SCS/frequency
IQ imbalance / LO leakageimage / centre spurbadmirror-image error, DC spot in the centre
DAC/ADC noise floor, quantisationfar-out floor ↑bad floorEVM flat vs power (does not improve at lower power)
Filter group delay / flatnessOKbad at band edgesEVM worse on edge subcarriers; the equaliser helps
Wrong analyser setupoddoddwrong BW/E-TM/cable loss/trigger: fix the measurement first
Level 4 — lab discipline for trustworthy numbers
• Test model matters: ACLR uses E-TM1.1 (full power); EVM uses E-TM3.1/3.1a (64QAM/256QAM) and E-TM2 (low power) because EVM must hold at low power too.
• Averaging: ACLR on a bursty/TDD signal needs gating and averaging, otherwise it is noisy. Per-RFFE ACLR was flaky until ACP averaging was added (it already existed for EVM).
• Analyser dynamic range: an EXA/EXM has its own ACLR floor (~−70 dBc class with noise correction). Near that floor you are measuring the instrument. Optimise the attenuation (mixer level) and use noise correction.
• Wait for DPD after any change (~60 s) and record temperature, DPD state and output power with every result.
• Report the margin, not just PASS: 46 dBc vs a 45 limit is a warning, and 55 dBc is healthy.
Interview Q&A
Q: ACLR passes but EVM fails. What does that tell you?
A: The problem is in-band only, not a spreading non-linearity. Suspects: CFR clipping too hard, phase noise (points smeared along arcs), IQ imbalance or LO leakage, a converter noise floor (EVM flat vs power), or edge-subcarrier distortion from filter group delay. PA compression would normally hurt ACLR too.
Q: Is the LTE ACLR requirement always 45 dBc?
A: No. It is 45 dBc or an absolute limit (−13 dBm/MHz for Category A), whichever is less stringent. For a wide carrier at modest per-port power the PSD is low (e.g. ~27 dBm/MHz at 20 MHz), so the absolute limit corresponds to ~40 dBc and that becomes the binding requirement.
Q: Convert 8% EVM to an SNR.
A: EVM ≈ 1/√SNR for noise-like error: SNR = 1/0.08² ≈ 156 ≈ 22 dB. 3.5% (the 256QAM limit) ≈ 29 dB.
Q: Why is EVM also tested with a low-power test model?
A: At low power the converter noise floor, quantisation and fixed spurs are a larger fraction of the signal, so EVM can degrade even though the PA is very linear. The E-TM2 low-power test catches a transmitter that is only clean at full power.
Q: Your ACLR reads 68 dBc on one bench and 58 dBc on another for the same RU. Which is right?
A: Possibly neither is the RU. 68 dBc may be near the analyser's own floor, and 58 may have a wrong attenuation/RBW or no noise correction. Check the instrument ACLR floor with a clean source, optimise mixer level, enable noise correction and use the same averaging and gating. Then compare.
PRA02 PRACH Frequency Placement — prach-FrequencyOffset, where the 6 RBs sit, and the FHGW register offset formula (single cell / shifted centre) Advanced click to expand ▾
In plain English
The LTE PRACH is a 6-RB-wide block (1.08 MHz) in the uplink, where UEs send their random-access preamble. The eNB tells UEs where it is with prach-FrequencyOffset (the first PRB). On a split radio the front end must look in the same place: the FHGW's PRACH extraction is programmed with a register offset from the carrier centre. If the stack and the FHGW disagree, preambles are sent into a place nobody is listening, and PRACH detection or attach fails even though RF is perfect.
Level 1 — the numbers
• 1 RB = 12 subcarriers × 15 kHz = 180 kHz. PRACH = 6 RBs = 1.08 MHz, with 839 subcarriers of 1.25 kHz (format 0–3).
• The FHGW register counts in 625 Hz units (half a PRACH subcarrier), so 1 RB = 180 000 / 625 = 288 units.
• PRACH usually sits just inside the band edge, above the PUCCH RBs (NRB_CQI etc.), and Msg3 is typically scheduled right after it (start PRB = PRACH start + 6).
Level 2 — the register formula (derived from the calculation sheet, checked on every row)
Register = (prach_RB_offset − NRB/2) × 288 + 852
(prach_RB_offset − NRB/2) is the PRACH start relative to the carrier centre in RBs, ×288 converts to 625 Hz units, and +852 (= 532.5 kHz) moves the reference from the PRACH's lower edge to its centre: half of 6 RBs (540 kHz) minus a 7.5 kHz half-subcarrier shift.
BWNRBprach_RB_offsetRegisterCheck
5 MHz25141284(14−12.5)·288+852 = 1284 ✓
10 MHz50353732(35−25)·288+852 = 3732 ✓
15 MHz75597044(59−37.5)·288+852 = 7044 ✓
20 MHz1008310356(83−50)·288+852 = 10356 ✓
Level 3 — moving the PRACH (the "offset configuration" in the sheet)
The register is linear: every RB the PRACH moves changes it by 288. To place the PRACH 1.8 MHz lower (−10 RBs) on the same carrier (centre still 1950 MHz, e.g. to test a non-default prach-FrequencyOffset), the 5 MHz RB offset goes 14 → 4 and the register becomes 1284 − 10×288 = (4 − 12.5)·288 + 852 = −1596. The sheet labels this shifted reference 1950 → 1948.2 MHz. The other bandwidths follow: 35→25 (852), 59→49 (4164), 83→74 (7764). A register value that goes negative is normal, because it is a signed offset from the carrier centre. The reverse also holds: if the carrier centre is retuned and the PRACH keeps the same RB offset, the register does not change, because it is relative to the centre.
The second table in the sheet lists, per bandwidth, the PRACH start PRB and Msg3 start PRB for delta-shift 1–3 (PUCCH shift), NRB_CQI 2 vs 4, and single cell vs a multi-cell (BCS) configuration. More PUCCH resources push PRACH one RB inwards, which is why it depends on the PUCCH config.
Level 4 — debugging "no PRACH detected"
1. Compare the eNB SIB2 prach-FrequencyOffset with the RB offset implied by the FHGW register (use the formula backwards).
2. If they differ by the PUCCH shift (1 RB), check NRB_CQI/delta-shift assumptions. A difference of a whole planned number of RBs means the PRACH was moved in one place (SIB2 or FHGW) but the other was not recomputed.
3. Check the root sequence index and Ncs (PRA01): the right place but the wrong sequence also gives no detections.
4. Confirm on a spectrum analyser in the UL band that the preamble energy (1.08 MHz block) sits where the register says.
5. Timing: a TA or timing offset error shows as detections with a wrong TA rather than none (EXP5).
Interview Q&A
Q: How many 625 Hz units are in one LTE RB, and why 625 Hz?
A: 180 kHz / 625 Hz = 288. 625 Hz is half of the 1.25 kHz PRACH subcarrier spacing, so the register can place the PRACH on the half-subcarrier grid used by the preamble mapping.
Q: Derive the FHGW PRACH register for 20 MHz with prach offset 83.
A: (83 − 100/2) × 288 + 852 = 33 × 288 + 852 = 9504 + 852 = 10356. The 852 (532.5 kHz) is half the 6-RB PRACH width minus a 7.5 kHz half-subcarrier shift.
Q: You need the PRACH 1.8 MHz lower on the same 5 MHz carrier. What are the new RB offset and register?
A: 1.8 MHz = 10 RBs, so the RB offset goes 14 → 4. The register is linear at 288 per RB: 1284 − 2880 = −1596, which matches (4 − 12.5)·288 + 852. Negative is fine because it is a signed offset from the carrier centre. Update SIB2 prach-FrequencyOffset to match.
Q: SIB2 prach-FrequencyOffset and the FHGW register disagree by one RB. Likely cause?
A: A PUCCH configuration difference: NRB_CQI or delta-shift changed the number of edge RBs reserved for PUCCH, and the PRACH/Msg3 start moves by one RB. Recompute the register from the actual SIB2 value.
Power & energy saving — uSleep reference runs
USLEEP03 Power-Monitoring Reference Runs — what a 5-band AAU actually draws (RUN1–RUN14) RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
Before you can say uSleep "saves 50 W", you need to know what the radio draws without it, band by band and load by load. This card is the reference: 14 one-hour power-monitoring runs (all with uSleep off) on a multi-flavour AAU. They cover all PAs off, then one band, two bands and all flavours at 0 %, 50 % and 100 % allocation. Each run was measured three ways: the lab DC supply, the internal PSU telemetry (get-PSU) and the O-RAN PM sensor CSVs. Think of it as reading the electricity meter with every appliance off, then switching them on one at a time. The single most useful lesson is that a transmitter with 0 % traffic still burns roughly half of its full-load PA power. That idle burn is exactly what uSleep attacks. USLEEP02 describes the test method. This card gives the numbers and shows how to read them critically.
What the AAU draws from the lab supply, by state
Numbers re-computed from the archived DATA.txt files. RUN9 used a DC analyser log instead of DATA.txt.
Level 1 — the unit, the rails and the baseline
Unit under test: AAU model family Integrity-ME-0-B1B3B8B41-00-x, with three flavours, each having its own FHGW and PSU:

B8B20B28 (low band)B8unused≈47.5–48.1 V
Baseline with all PAs off (RUN1), internal PSU:

The lab supply for the same "nothing on air" state (RUN11, where B41 never actually radiated, see Level 3) read 206 W. So the lab supply sees about 45 W more than the internal telemetry: cable, PSU conversion and common-board losses (CM14).
The 12 V rail barely moves in any run: 46–51 W (B1B3), 38–43 W (B41), 32–35 W (low band). It is your sanity reference. If it moves a lot, something other than the PAs changed.
Level 2 — the reference numbers
Mid-band series (lab supply, second-half mean):
RunStateLab WPM current per active RFFE
RUN4B1 on, B3 off, 0 %337≈0.93 A
RUN5B1 off, B3 on, 0 %343≈0.95 A
RUN6B1 + B3, 0 %507≈0.97 A (all 8)
