Read it as increments. Going from 0 % to 100 % adds ≈174 W for B1 and ≈183 W for B3, and ≈358 W for both, so the bands add up. On the PA rail, a mid-band RFFE draws about 0.93 A × 40 V ≈ 37 W at 0 % and about 1.95 A × 40 V ≈ 78 W at 100 %. At zero traffic each PA already draws ~45–50 % of its full-load power. CRS and PDCCH keep it biased and radiating in every subframe.

Low band and B41:
RunStateLab WInternal PA rail WΔ vs idle
RUN11B41 "0 %" (did not radiate)206B41 2–3idle reference
RUN12B8 0 %250LB 72 (off: 28)lab +44 · internal +44
RUN10B8 100 % (first ~30 min)297LB ≈119lab +91 · internal +91
RUN9B41 100 %346 (DC analyser)B41 138 (off: 3)lab +140 · internal +135
The key quality check is that the increments agree between sources to within a few watts (44/44, 91/91, 140/135). The absolute levels do not agree, because of the ~45 W offset. That is why ΔP (on − off) must be taken within one source.

All flavours together: at 50 % (RUN8) the internal PA rails were B1B3 ≈430 W, B41 ≈145 W (first 40 min only) and low band ≈205 W. At 100 % (RUN14) the lab supply climbed from 1266 W to 1439 W over the hour (≈170 W of thermal drift), with PM showing all 8 mid-band RFFEs at ≈2.2–2.5 A. A second full-load run logged on a DC analyser read only ≈1013–1039 W, but its low-band PM file is empty and its B41 currents are lower. It was not the same operating state, so the two cannot be compared directly.
Level 3 — read the archive critically (what the summary tables hide)
Re-computing the runs from the raw files shows that several are not the state their folder name claims. This is the most transferable lesson on this card.
• RUN13 "B41 + B1B3 + LB 0 %": the PM currents show only RFFE0-3 (B1) active on the mid-band flavour. B3 (RFFE4-7) stayed at the 0.032 A idle leakage. B41 radiated (≈100 W PA rail) for only the first ~16 minutes, then fell to ≈3 W. The lab supply dropped 503 → 404 W at that moment, and the 99 W step matches the B41 drop. A second-half average quoted as "B41 0 % = 2 W" is therefore wrong.
• RUN8 (50 %): B41 stopped transmitting after ~40 minutes, so its "38 W" second-half figure is an artefact of the averaging window.
• RUN10 (B8 100 %): the low-band PA rail sat at ≈119 W for ~30 minutes, then fell to ≈28 W (the off level). The lab supply stepped 297 → 206 W at the same moment. Both sources agree, so this is transmission stopping mid-run, not a logging dropout.
• RUN11 (B41 0 %): the B41 RFFE currents never rose above ≈0.01 A, so nothing was radiated. Treat it as an idle run, not as "B41 at 0 % load".
• RUN9: the low-band PA-rail voltage read ≈35 V instead of the normal ≈48 V. That is unexplained, so flag it rather than use it.
• The internal PSU CSV min columns contain 0.0000 samples, and the PM CSVs have isolated 0 W blocks. Filter them before averaging, because zeros fake a saving.

Rules the analysis script applies (power_plots.py): time axes are clamped to 0–60 min. Folder names are mapped to band groups (b1b3 → B1B3, b8b20b28 → B08, b7b41 → B41). RFFE4-7 of the B08 and B41 groups are ignored, because that silicon is unused and only reports idle leakage. Streams are aligned on a common grid without zero-filling, since zero-fill would fake savings. The 12 V consumer is labelled "FHGW+MidBRD".

File formats you will meet: lab DATA.txt lines look like Minute N: Average Power = … W, Max Power = …, Min Power = …. The internal PSU CSV has window_start, window_end, n_samples, v50_*, i50_*, v12_*, i12_*, temp_*, p50_*, p12_* (min/max/avg, ~16 samples per one-minute window). PM CSVs are named C<start>+0000_<end>+0000_<serial>.csv, with one row per object (TEMPERATURE, CURRENT, POWER, VOLTAGE) per minute and per RFFE min/max/avg.

Checklist before quoting any run: (1) check that per-RFFE currents show the intended bands radiating for the whole window; (2) check that the 12 V rail is flat; (3) choose the window after all carriers are up and before any stop; (4) take the lab-vs-internal increments, not the absolute levels; (5) note the thermal state (full load drifts ~170 W in an hour).
Interview Q&A
Q: A multi-band AAU at 0 % allocation draws almost as much as at 50 %. Why, and why does it matter for uSleep?
A: At 0 % allocation LTE still sends CRS in several symbols of every subframe, plus PDCCH and the sync and broadcast channels. The PA stays biased and switched on all the time. In the reference runs a mid-band PA drew ~37 W at 0 % against ~78 W at 100 %. That idle burn is the headroom uSleep targets: gate the PA during the all-zero symbols.
Q: Your lab supply reads 206 W with nothing on air, but the internal PSU telemetry sums to 161 W. Which is right?
A: Both are right. They measure at different points. The lab supply includes cabling, PSU conversion and common-board losses (about 45 W here), while the internal rails do not. Compare increments within one source: adding B8 at 0 % added +44 W on both, and B8 at 100 % added +91 W on both. Never subtract a PM or internal "on" value from a lab "off" value.
Q: A summary sheet says "B41 at 0 % load = 2 W PA rail". What would you check?
A: Whether B41 actually radiated during the averaging window. Look at the per-RFFE PM currents and the lab-supply trace for a step. In the archive, B41 radiated for only the first ~16 minutes of that run (≈100 W) and then stopped. The lab supply fell by the same ~99 W. The 2 W figure is a second-half average taken after TX stopped.
Q: Why does the analysis script refuse to zero-fill missing samples?
A: A missing sample filled with 0 W pulls the mean down. In an on-versus-off comparison that looks like a power saving that never happened. The script aligns streams on a common grid and leaves gaps as gaps. It also drops the unused RFFE4-7 on single-band flavours, whose leakage readings would otherwise add noise.
Q: How big is thermal drift compared with a plausible uSleep saving?
A: At full load on all flavours the lab supply rose ~170 W (1266 → 1439 W) in one hour as the PAs heated. On mid-band alone it was ~46 W in 20 minutes. That is as large as, or larger than, the saving you are trying to measure. So compare on and off at thermal steady state, cool down between runs, and alternate the order.
Conformance campaigns & results
FCAAU01 Full-AAU RF Conformance Campaign — 248 points, how to read the result, and the B28 receive finding RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
A single RCT test tells you whether one measurement on one antenna passes. A conformance campaign is the full picture for a customer configuration: every TX and RX test, on every antenna, on every band and carrier the customer will run, on the full AAU (FHGW + RFFEs + antennas) as shipped. It is the last gate before the unit is cleared for customer E2E. Think of a vehicle inspection that checks all four wheels, not just one. This card walks through a real campaign of 248 conformance points on two customer configurations. It covers how the count is built, how to read "pass / fail / not tested", and the one hardware finding it produced: B28 receive sensitivity 3.4–4.8 dB short, with Band 3 on the same unit used as the control.
The B28 finding at a glance
B3 is the control: if the bench, cabling, DU or reference plane were wrong, both bands would move.
Level 1 — what was measured and the result
Suite on every antenna (TS 36.141): TX covers output power, ACLR, EVM, frequency error, occupied bandwidth, SEM, spurious emissions and output-power dynamics. RX covers reference sensitivity (§7.2), dynamic range (§7.3) and PRACH detection (§8.4).
ConfigurationBands / carriersPointsResult
Customer A: 4-band AAU (Type 1b), 15 MHz FDDB3 DL 1812.5 / UL 1717.5 MHz · B28 DL 795.5 / UL 740.5 MHz10492 pass (88 %), 2 fail, 10 not tested
  ↳ B34 antennas52 (40 TX + 12 RX)all pass
  ↳ B28 TX4 antennas40all pass
  ↳ B28 RXANT A/B measured12ref-sens fail ×2; the rest not run (unit returned for investigation)
Customer B: 5-band AAU (Type 2)B1 10 MHz FDD on two carriers (2159/1969 and 2164/1974 MHz) · B41 20 MHz TDD at 2545 MHz144all pass
  ↳ B12 carriers × 4 antennas104 (80 TX + 24 RX)all pass
  ↳ B414 antennas (the only TDD config)40 (28 TX + 12 RX)all pass
  ↳ B28 10 MHz (793/738)unit not available—not executed, and excluded from the 248
Total248236 pass · 2 fail · 10 not tested. Every fail and every untested point is B28.
Scale behind it: 276 test campaigns, 284 result workbooks, 1,478 instrument screenshots, 3 benches calibrated, and 41 pull requests across the framework, the radio application and the instrument controller.
Sanity-check the arithmetic yourself. One page of the source deck says "232 pass", but 92 + 144 = 236 and 236 + 2 + 10 = 248. Summary slides get retyped, so recompute the totals from the workbook.
Level 2 — how to read a campaign result
• The customer workbooks are the record of truth. The automation sheets are intermediate and may be graded against a different limit (see the ACLR 55-vs-44.2 trap in KPI01).
• "Fail", "not tested" and "not executed" are three different things. Not tested = in scope but not run (here, because the unit was returned). Not executed = a whole configuration that never started, with empty workbook sheets, so it is left out of the count rather than counted as a pass.
• Look for the pattern, not the count. 236/248 sounds like "95 % good". The real statement is that every problem is on one band, which points to hardware on that band's path and not to the test system.
• A systematic miss across all bands points at the measurement. Total-power dynamic range read short of the TS 36.104 §6.3.2 minimum on every configuration: B3 17.68–18.05 against 18.7 dB, B28 18.15–18.40 against 18.7, B1 15.66–16.24 against 16.9, and B41 16.5–16.9 against 20.0. The shortfall was traced to the 1-RB minimum-power reading sitting ~1 dB high, and re-measurement was left open (see FC06). One radio failing is a finding. All radios failing the same way usually means the method is wrong.
• The reference plane decides everything. Cable calibration was done per unit, per band and per frequency (antenna port → instrument connector) and kept in version-controlled config, so a re-run reproduces the same plane. The cabling was verified so that a named antenna in a sheet is a known physical port. As the source put it, mis-mapped cabling is "the most expensive test error because every result looks plausible".
• FHGW rig vs full AAU. The FHGW-in-a-box rig has no PA and no antenna. A pass there proves the fronthaul and PHY chain, not the shipped product. The rig stays as the fast-feedback loop, and conformance sign-off happens on the full AAU.
• Framework defects surface only against the instrument. Real runs exposed seven framework bugs that no dry run caught: the SEM per-segment index read the wrong segment, the dynamic-range results column was shifted, the SG trigger delay was gated on vendor instead of duplex mode, the PRACH re-offset was never written or verified, the PRACH stats console was not enabled, an EIRP→TRP correction was not band-aware, and the carrier cycle around a gain write was not atomic. Each was found by comparing framework output with what the analyser screen showed (see FWK3).
Level 3 — the B28 receive finding as a case study
Measured: B28 UL reference sensitivity at 740.5 MHz, 15 MHz, on the full-RCT unit: ANT A −104.6 dBm, ANT B −103.2 dBm against the programme's −108 dBm requirement, so 3.4 and 4.8 dB short.
The control: B3 on the same unit, DU, PHY build, instrument and calibration plane passed on all four antennas at −111.5 / −111.8 / −113.3 / −110.4 dBm. A test-setup fault would have moved both bands.
Ruled out before escalation: the instrument, RF ports and cabling, the DU/PHY build, the calibration reference plane, the RX gain configuration and synchronisation.
Independent corroboration from PRACH: B3 had 0 % missed detection at −87 dBm, while B28 had 9.16 % missed detection at −84.3 dBm. B28 did worse at a stronger input, which a second, unrelated RX test would not show if the sensitivity test were at fault.
Not a dead path: manual injection gave 2164 kbps, 0 BLER and +14.5 dB SNR. The uplink works, so this is a sensitivity deficit, not a broken chain.
E2E cross-check: a RACH coverage sweep found the B28 coverage limit at about −85 dBm against −110 dBm for B3, a 25 dB gap. The same unit also stalled B28 TCP throughput through UL ACK loss. RF conformance and live-network symptoms pointed to the same place.
From one unit to a build-lot question: a second unit had been returned with a low-band RX LNA fault, and B8 and B28 share the low-band receive chain. One bad unit is an RMA. Two out of three on the same chain is a population question, so the escalation asked for a check across the build lot. The third unit had never been characterised on low band, so it is unknown, not good.
Expert note on the limit: −108 dBm is stricter than the 3GPP single-port figure for these bandwidths (−100.8 dBm, FRC A1-3, TS 36.141). Before calling a sensitivity "short", confirm whether requirement and measurement are both single-port or both combined (FC09D). Here B3 easily met the same −108 target on the same bench, so the comparison is like-for-like whichever convention applies. FC09D gives the step-by-step isolation playbook for exactly this kind of shortfall.
Interview Q&A
Q: A campaign reports 236 of 248 points passing. Is the product 95 % good?
A: That is the wrong way to read it. Look at where the 12 non-passes sit. Here all 2 fails and all 10 untested points were on B28 RX, while B3, B1 and B41 were fully clean on the same kind of hardware. The real statement is that one band's receive path has a hardware problem and everything else conforms.
Q: B28 sensitivity is 4 dB short. How do you prove it is the radio and not your bench?
A: Use a control on the same setup: B3 on the same unit, DU, PHY build, instrument and calibrated reference plane passed by 2–5 dB. Rule out the instrument, cabling, build, RX gain config and sync one by one. Then corroborate with an independent test: PRACH missed detection was worse on B28 at a stronger input. Finally check with manual injection that the path is alive, which shows it is a deficit and not a dead path.
Q: Why is a pass on the FHGW-in-a-box rig not enough for customer sign-off?
A: The rig has no PA and no antenna. It proves the fronthaul, PHY and digital chain, but not the RF front end the customer receives. The same test list has to run on the full AAU, on every antenna, per customer configuration. The rig remains the fast regression loop.
Q: Every configuration fails dynamic range by a similar amount. What do you suspect first?
A: The measurement. A uniform miss across different bands, bandwidths and units suggests a common cause. Here the single-RB minimum-power reading sat about 1 dB high, which shrinks the computed range on every run. Re-measure the low-power point (analyser noise floor, attenuation, averaging) before blaming the hardware.
Q: What is the difference between "not tested" and "not executed" in a campaign report?
A: "Not tested" points are in the counted scope but were not run. Here the unit was returned mid-campaign, so they appear in the denominator. "Not executed" means a whole configuration never started. Its workbook sheets are empty templates, so it is excluded from the count and carried forward. Mixing the two either inflates the pass rate or hides open work.
RCOP01 Reduced Carrier Output Power — 0 / −3 / −10 dB (GRDEV-7438) and why ACLR gets worse at lower drive RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
Reduced Carrier Output Power means asking the radio to transmit a carrier a set number of dB below its rated power. Operators use it for smaller cells, for interference control and for energy saving (the RoP axis in the USLEEP02 E2E matrix). The test is simple: command 0, −3 and −10 dB, measure what actually comes out, and check that the transmitter is still clean. The surprise, and the reason this card exists, is that turning the power down made ACLR worse, not better. Most people expect the opposite, because "less drive means more linear". The reason is that DPD, the digital pre-distortion that linearises the PA, was trained at full power. Think of glasses made for reading at arm's length: hold the page closer and it gets blurrier, even though you are "doing less".
Operating points and the measured trend
Illustrative AM-AM sketch. The measured values in the panel are from the epic workbook (one antenna, Pol A).
Level 1 — the test and the result
Set-up: nominal TX gain is 20 dB. The test commands a reduction of 0, −3 and −10 dB. The automation actually steps 0 → −10 dB in 1 dB increments, and the workbook records the three specification points. At each level it measures carrier power, ACLR, EVM, PAPR and SEM.
Verdict rule: the achieved reduction must match the commanded one within ±1.5 dB.
CommandedAchievedErrorVerdict
0 dBreference——
−3 dB−2.76 dB+0.24 dBpass
−10 dB−9.17 dB+0.83 dBpass
Per band: B3 and B41 were inside ±1.5 dB at both steps. The B1 −10 dB step read +1.74 and +1.57 dB, just outside the tolerance. B28 was not run (its workbook sheets are empty).
Pattern: the error grows with the size of the step, and it is always on the positive side (the radio reduces a little less than commanded). That points to a gain-law or calibration slope that is not exactly 1 dB per dB, which is worth characterising per band rather than dismissing as noise.
Level 2 — how it is automated and measured
• Test: test_Tx_Reduced_Carrier_Power in reduced_carrier_power.py (ruauto PR #683, story GRDEV-7438).
• Atomic gain change: the gain write sits inside a carrier cycle (deactivate → write → reactivate). That cycle was made atomic (PR #692), so it cannot be left half-done with the carrier in an undefined state.
• Wait for DPD after each gain change before measuring. A reading taken while DPD is still adapting mixes two effects.
• Measure the same things at every level (channel power, ACLR at all four offsets, EVM, PAPR/CCDF, SEM) so the trend is visible, not just the pass/fail at the spec points.
• ACLR is still graded against the 3GPP requirement, 44.2 dB in TS 36.141 (see KPI01 for the 55 dBc automation-limit trap). A worsening trend inside the limit is recorded as a characteristic.
• Relation to other power-reduction features: PA Protection (FC11) is a fixed 3 dB back-off on carrier activation. DAC current and digital gain (DACG01) are the two knobs underneath. The O-RAN M-plane equivalent is max-power control (array-max-power-reduction).
Level 3 — why ACLR degrades at lower drive, and the PAPR gotcha
The finding: ACLR degraded monotonically as drive was reduced, across all four offsets (±first and ±second adjacent) and at both steps, by up to 6.2 dB at the +30 MHz offset. It stayed at least 6.2 dB inside the 44.2 dB requirement, so it is a characteristic, not a failure.
Why: DPD builds an inverse model of the PA's AM-AM and AM-PM behaviour (and its memory) from observation-path captures at the operating point where it was trained, normally rated power. When the gain drops by 3 or 10 dB, the PA sits at a different point on its curve, with a different bias current, a different thermal state and different memory effects. The coefficients no longer match, so the "correction" partly becomes a distortion of its own. On top of that, at low output the fixed noise and spur floor of the DAC, the observation receiver and the analyser is a larger fraction of the adjacent-channel power, so the ratio in dBc shrinks. A PA that is simply "more linear at back-off" would show better ACLR. A DPD-linearised PA shows worse ACLR unless DPD is retrained or the PA is re-biased for the new level. (DPD02 covers the DPD model and ADC02 covers converter floors.)
Why it matters: RoP is sold as an energy-saving and coverage knob. If the design intent is to run for long periods at −10 dB, the DPD training and bias strategy have to cover that point, or the operator can see ACLR margin eroding in the field.
Correct the common belief: an older overview (M13) says reducing carrier power improves ACLR and EVM. That is true for an un-linearised PA near compression. It is not what was measured on this DPD-linearised AAU.

The PAPR gotcha: at −3 and −10 dB, PAPR agreed within 0.055 dB (11.375 against 11.430 dB). The 0 dB reference read 8.99 dB and looked like a failure. It had been captured on a 0.0001 % CCDF tail statistic. Re-measured at full count, it came to ≈11.4 dB and both rows passed. Lesson: a PAPR number means nothing without its CCDF probability (0.01 % vs 0.0001 %) and sample count. Rare-tail statistics need millions of samples before they settle.
Interview Q&A
Q: You reduce carrier power by 10 dB and ACLR gets worse. Is the radio broken?
A: Not necessarily. On a DPD-linearised PA this is expected unless DPD is retrained. The coefficients were learned at rated power, so at back-off the PA's AM-AM/AM-PM and memory behaviour no longer match the model. Fixed noise floors also matter more at low output. Here ACLR fell by up to 6.2 dB but stayed 6.2 dB or more inside 44.2 dB, so it was recorded as a characteristic.
Q: Commanded −10 dB, achieved −9.17 dB. How do you grade it, and what would you look at next?
A: Grade the achieved step against the commanded one: the error is +0.83 dB, inside ±1.5 dB, so it passes. Next, note that the error grows with step size and is always positive, and that B1 read +1.74/+1.57 at −10 dB. That suggests a per-band gain-law slope below 1 dB per dB. Characterise it in 1 dB steps per band, because an operator configuring −10 dB expects −10 dB.
Q: Your PAPR at 0 dB reads 8.99 dB, but 11.4 dB at −3 and −10 dB. Explain it.
A: Check the CCDF settings. The 0 dB value came from the 0.0001 % tail statistic rather than a full-count capture. At full count it read about 11.4 dB, like the others. Always report PAPR with its probability level and sample count.
Q: Why must the gain change be done inside an atomic carrier cycle?
A: The gain write needs the carrier deactivated, then written, then reactivated. If the automation is interrupted between those steps (timeout, exception or a parallel step), the carrier can be left down or at an unknown gain. The next measurement then grades the wrong state. Making the cycle atomic, so it always completes or rolls back, removes that failure mode.
RSSI04 RSSI Readout Calibration Campaign — plateau method, one value per band, the B8 frequency-response problem, framework defects RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
The radio reports how strong the uplink signal is (RSSI). It measures the signal in ADC units (dBFS) and converts to dBm with one stored correction per band, adc_dbfs_adj. If that correction is wrong, the radio receives perfectly well but reports the wrong number. That misleads SON, uplink power control and every engineer who looks at a counter. This card follows a real calibration campaign on a 5-band AAU. It covers how the right correction was measured (only on the straight part of the power sweep), how one number was chosen for a whole band (put it in the middle of the spread), and why for one band (B8) no single number can work. An analogy: one pair of glasses per person. If your two eyes differ by less than the lens tolerance, one prescription works. If they differ by more, no single lens can fix both eyes. FCDSA explains the DSA and offset concepts, and RSSI02/RSSI03 cover the gain-budget method.
Level 1 — the formula, the limit and the results
RSSI(dBm) = 10·log10(rssi_raw) − 84 + adc_dbfs_adj[ADC]
The adjustment is stored per ADC in the RU hw.json, as one value per band. It is written live, with no reboot, because get-rssi re-reads the file on every call (this was confirmed on the bench). The conformance limit on reported RSSI is ±2 dB.
Why it was wrong: the control experiment changed the DSA from 0 to 10 dB. Reported RSSI moved by the full DSA amount (B3 +3.08 dB for a 3 dB DSA change), but sensitivity stayed at −105.9 to −106.3 dBm EIRP, a 0.4 dB spread. So the radio was fine and only the readout was off. B8's stored −36.61 had been characterised at DSA 0, but the unit ships at DSA 10, which put B8 RSSI about 11 dB out.
Band (flavour)Frequencies sweptBWsConfigured adjWorst point errorVerdict
B1 (b0103)1922.5–1977.5 MHz5/10/15/20−34.41+1.09 dB (spread 2.10 dB)Pass
B3 (b0103)1712.5–1782.5 MHz5/10/15/20−35.02−0.18 dB (spread 0.16 dB)Pass
B8 (b082028)882.5–912.5 MHz5/10−25.70+3.19 dB at 897.5 MHz (spread ≈4.4–4.5 dB)Fail
B28 / B41——in progress / per-antenna values, re-run due—open
11 of 13 calibrated points are inside ±2 dB. Both failures are B8 at 897.5 MHz, one at 10 MHz (+2.97) and one at 5 MHz (+3.19). Seeing the same frequency fail at two bandwidths shows it is a property of the band, not of one bad run.
Campaign scale: 447 workbooks, 216 instrumented runs, 2,520 graphs and captures, and 1,792 calibration rows on the plateau.
Level 2 — the plateau method
The correction is EIRP − reported dBFS. The hard part is choosing where on the power range to read it.
• Sweep: the generator walks from about −110/−113 dBm up to −40 dBm, reading PHY dBm, CLI dBm and raw dBFS together at each step. That gives ~700 points per antenna, per frequency and per bandwidth.
• Below about −100 dBm the curve flattens at the receiver noise floor, so the readout no longer tracks the input.
• Near the top (about −46…−40 dBm) it bends into the knee.
• Only the −80…−50 dBm plateau is used, averaging every row on it: 120–480 rows per point instead of the old 4–16.
• The old method sampled −46…−40 dBm, inside the bend. It read high by +0.01 to +0.58 dB, and because that bias is not constant it could not simply be subtracted. Moving to the plateau is what recovered B1's margin.
• Spread on the plateau: the tightest point was B1 1950 MHz, with 0.15 dB across 240 rows. The widest was 1.03 dB across 480 rows, still half the error budget. Shipped values are medians.
• BLER is recorded alongside every sweep, so each RSSI row is known to come from a healthy link.

The six-step apply loop (nothing is accepted on a single reading):
#StepGuard
1Characterise: full sweep, plateau rows only, averaged120–480 rows per point
2Confirm the DSA by reading it back from the radioabort on mismatch (exactly what B8 got wrong before)
3Choose one value per band by minimaxbest worst case = half the measured spread
4Apply to hw.json by scripthard DSA gate + stale-premise guard (refuses unless the current array is a known starting state)
5Verify the live value via get-rssino reboot, re-read on every call
6Re-sweep and compare with the predictionaccepted only if they agree (here within 0.10 dB at all 7 B1/B3 points)
Choosing one value per band (minimax)
Computed from the per-frequency measured adj values in the report.
Level 3 — minimax, the B8 problem, and the framework defects
The rule: each frequency wants its own correction, but the radio stores one per band. Whatever you store, each frequency is wrong by the difference, so pick the value that makes the worst error smallest: the middle of the measured spread. The best achievable worst case is half the spread.
Worked example, B1: the four frequencies want −35.50 / −34.45 / −34.05 / −33.39 dB (spread 2.10 dB). Storing the lowest value gives a worst error of 2.11 (fails at the top of the band). Storing the highest also gives 2.11 (fails at the bottom). Storing the middle, −34.41, gives 1.09 and passes everywhere. Note that a mean of the four is not the rule: minimax uses only the extremes.
Why B8 cannot be solved this way: its per-frequency values span about 4.4–4.5 dB, because 897.5 MHz sits in a dip about 3.5 dB away from the rest. Half the spread (≈2.2 dB) already exceeds ±2 dB. Even the best value, −26.64, leaves a worst case of ±2.25 dB. The option table:
OptionWorst errorCost
1. Re-centre to −26.64±2.25 dB (still fails, by 0.25 instead of 3.19)config change only
2. Exclude the 897.5 MHz dip from the supported range< 1 dBproduct-scope decision
3. Per-channel correction (index by frequency as well as ADC)< 0.5 dBfirmware change
The right choice depends on the customer's actual B8 channels. If they never deploy near 897.5 MHz, option 2 is free. A frequency-response ripple across a band is a front-end filter or duplexer property, and a single-coefficient calibration model simply cannot represent it.
Two ways to quote the error: the report headline gives B1 ±1.50 and B3 ±0.92. Those are the worst individual rows. The per-point mean errors are +1.09 and −0.18. State which one you mean.

Defects the campaign exposed (each produced plausible but wrong numbers):
• get-rssi applied adc_dbfs_adj by the printed ADC position, while the array is keyed by hardware ADC slot. On b0103 it applied B3's offset to a B1 channel, a 4.39 dB error (ruauto-qa PR #166, GRDEV-10138).
• The DSA read-back parser linearised the address as tile×4+block, mislabelling 6 of 8 RX ADCs, so the tool could "confirm" the wrong attenuation (ruauto PR #782).
• Results were keyed without rb_offset, so the 20 MHz sweeps collapsed into one and 3 were silently dropped. Recovering them took the row count from 650 to 755, and the calibration moved by only 0.076 dB.
• A tuple-unpack mismatch inside a broad except meant the RSSI graph was never written in all 12 runs, and nothing reported it.
• There was no bounds check on the ADC index, so a short reply from the radio gave a wrong-but-plausible value. It now raises a ValueError naming the flavour and band.
• A rejected hypothesis (an interleaved ADC map) looked right on paper, but on the bench it read the noise floor while the test still passed. It was withdrawn before merge. A test that passes for the wrong reason is worse than one that fails.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why calibrate RSSI only on the −80…−50 dBm plateau?
A: Below about −100 dBm the reading flattens at the noise floor, and near −46…−40 dBm it bends into the knee. In both regions the readout does not track the input one-for-one. The old method sampled the knee and read high by up to 0.58 dB, with a non-constant bias. Averaging 120–480 plateau rows gives a stable, linear offset.
Q: The radio stores one RSSI correction per band, but each frequency wants a different one. Which value do you store?
A: The minimax value, the middle of the measured spread, so the worst error anywhere in the band is half the spread. For B1 the spread was 2.10 dB, so storing −34.41 gives a worst case of 1.09 dB, inside ±2 dB. Storing either extreme gives 2.11 dB and fails.
Q: B8 fails ±2 dB whatever value you store. What are your options?
A: Half of B8's ≈4.5 dB spread already exceeds 2 dB, so one coefficient cannot work. Option 1: re-centre to −26.64, which still fails by 0.25 dB. Option 2: exclude the 897.5 MHz dip from the supported range, a product decision. Option 3: add a per-channel correction indexed by frequency, a firmware change good to under 0.5 dB. Pick based on the customer's real B8 channels.
Q: RSSI moved by exactly the DSA change, but sensitivity did not move at all. What does that tell you?
A: The receive path is healthy and only the reporting offset is wrong. adc_dbfs_adj tracks the DSA one-for-one and never touches the signal. B8's offset had been characterised at DSA 0 but shipped at DSA 10, which gave an ~11 dB readout error. The fix is to recalibrate at the shipped DSA and to gate every apply on a DSA read-back.
Q: How do you know a calibration is understood and not just tuned until it passed?
A: Predict the post-change error from the plateau model, apply the value, re-run the full sweep and compare. Here prediction and hardware agreed within 0.10 dB at all seven B1/B3 points. Guard the apply step too: a DSA gate, a stale-premise check, and a live read-back.
SMOKE01 5-Band AAU (MidBoard 1.5) RCT Smoke Test — ACLR + EVM go / no-go per unit, flavour and antenna RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
When a new hardware build arrives, here a 5-band AAU with the new MidBoard 1.5, you do not start with the 248-point campaign (FCAAU01). You first run a smoke test: a fast go / no-go that every unit, in every flavour, on every antenna, actually transmits a clean signal. It measures only two things, ACLR (is energy leaking next door?) and EVM (is the constellation accurate?), but it measures them everywhere. Like switching on every light in a new house before you check the wiring in detail, a smoke test is about breadth, not depth. Its job is to make sure nothing is silently dead or missing before anyone spends days on full RCT or E2E.
The smoke-test matrix
Level 1 — scope, units and model names
• What: a basic RCT smoke test (ACLR + EVM) on the new 5-band AAU units built with MidBoard 1.5.
• Units: the two E2E units (bottom and top of the lab stack), with one sub-task per unit (GRDEV-8498, GRDEV-8499). The middle unit is the full-RCT unit and is out of scope here, because it is tracked by the full conformance campaign.
• Extra case (GRDEV-8507): 5 MHz channel bandwidth on B3 and B28, on all E2E units and all antennas.
• Executed by the ECS team (RAT). Parent epic: GRDEV-7254.
FlavourBandsModel name
0B1B3Integrity-ME-0-B1B3B8B28n41-01-0
1B8B28Integrity-ME-0-B1B3B8B28n41-01-1
2n41Integrity-ME-0-B1B3B8B28n41-01-2
Reading a model name: the band list names the bands the AAU hardware carries, and the last digit is the flavour, meaning which FHGW and personality you are talking to. The older 4-band unit used in the power runs (USLEEP03) is Integrity-ME-0-B1B3B8B41-00-x. The two-digit field differs (00 vs 01), so check the internal model-name structuring page for its exact meaning before relying on it. Each flavour is a different radio personality, so a pass on one flavour says nothing about another.
Level 2 — how to run it, and the pass rule
Per unit, per flavour: bring the FHGW up with the right model name/personality → activate the carrier(s) for that flavour → play the test model on each antenna in turn (per-RFFE IQ playback, FC20 / RFFE01) → measure ACLR (both sides, first and second adjacent) and EVM → record per antenna.
Test models: E-TM1.1 at full power for ACLR, and E-TM3.1 (64QAM) for EVM, as in the full suite (FC01, FC02).
Limits (TS 36.141): ACLR per §6.6.2, which is 44.2 dB for paired spectrum (see the KPI01 note on the 55 dBc automation limit). EVM per §6.5.2: QPSK 17.5 %, 16QAM 12.5 %, 64QAM 8 %, 256QAM 3.5 %.
Pass / fail, as written in the story:
1. ACLR and EVM within spec on every antenna, every flavour, both E2E units.
2. No antenna or flavour silently broken or missing.
Rule 2 is the important one. A report showing 11 green cells out of an expected 12 is a fail. Build the expected matrix first (units × flavours × bands × antennas), then check the results against it, so a path that never ran cannot drop out quietly.
Dependencies: blocked until PWK support for ACLR+EVM on the 5-band MidBoard 1.5 (GRDEV-8121) and the firmware-upgrade design changes for MidBoard 1.5 (GRDEV-7154) landed. On new hardware the test tooling and firmware often trail the boards, so plan the smoke test after those enablers, not in parallel with them.
Level 3 — why smoke tests earn their keep on a new build
What breadth catches that depth misses. Most new-build failures are not "ACLR is 1 dB marginal". They are "this flavour does not come up", "this antenna is dead" or "this band uses the wrong calibration". The MidBoard 1.5 units showed exactly that class of problem:
• False RFFE over-current on every boot (MidBoard V1.5 firmware v2.6, GRDEV-8838): CRITICAL faults 15 "Unit out of order" and 26 "Power Supply Faulty" on all four RFFEs. It was fixed in a later release.
• Missing calibration file on one flavour (fault 12, tx_calibration_eeprom.json not found on B41 carriers, GRDEV-9046). A start-up script matched hard-coded model strings, missed a sub-variant and skipped generating the file. That flavour then transmits several dB low while the other flavours look fine.
• A low-band RX LNA fault on the top unit, which was returned. A smoke test is TX-only, so it cannot catch an RX fault. This is why smoke never replaces full RCT.

Why add 5 MHz on B3 and B28? A narrower channel uses a different channel-filter and DPD configuration, and a customer may deploy it. A clean 10/15 MHz result does not prove 5 MHz. Bandwidth changes on this platform have their own history of defects (CM17: a runtime BW change left the DFE filter at the old width).

What to keep from each smoke run: the unit serial, flavour and model name, FW/BKC version (BKC01), and per-antenna ACLR (both sides) and EVM with margin, not just PASS. Also keep the analyser screenshot. Smoke results become the baseline you compare against when a later build regresses.
Interview Q&A
Q: What is the difference between a smoke test and full RCT conformance?
A: A smoke test is breadth-first and fast: two TX measurements (ACLR, EVM) on every unit, flavour and antenna, to prove nothing is dead or grossly wrong. Full RCT is depth-first: the whole TS 36.141 TX and RX suite per customer configuration. Smoke gates the start of deeper testing. It cannot replace it, because for example it has no RX coverage.
Q: Your smoke report is all green, but it has 22 rows where you expected 24. Pass or fail?
A: Fail, or at best incomplete. The pass rule explicitly requires that no antenna or flavour is silently missing. Build the expected matrix up front and reconcile against it. A missing row can mean a flavour that did not boot, an antenna whose playback never started, or a script that skipped a band.
Q: Why is a pass on flavour 0 (B1B3) no evidence for flavour 2 (n41) on the same unit?
A: Each flavour is a separate FHGW personality with its own model name, start-up path, calibration data and RF chain. Real defects have hit one flavour only, for example a missing TX calibration file on B41 carriers because a start-up script did not recognise that model sub-variant. Test every flavour.
Q: Why test 5 MHz separately on B3 and B28?
A: The narrower bandwidth uses a different filter and DPD setup, and customers may run it. Results at 10 or 15 MHz do not carry over. Bandwidth-dependent configuration has caused real defects on this platform, such as a DFE filter not following a runtime bandwidth change.

G2TX01 2G GSM TX Conformance — TS 51.021 §6.2–§6.6: modulation accuracy, mean power, PvT mask (+ the CUSTom trap), ORFS, spurious & the Band-8 antenna RCA RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
A GSM carrier does not transmit continuously. It sends bursts, one per timeslot (8 slots of about 577 µs make a 4.615 ms TDMA frame). Think of a tap dancer on a shared stage. Each step must be the right loudness (mean power, §6.3). It must be clean (phase error or EVM, §6.2). It must start and stop on the beat inside a timing mask (power vs time, §6.4). It must not stamp on the neighbours (ORFS, §6.5, and spurious, §6.6). TS 51.021 chapter 6 is the rule book for all of this. This card explains each test, how ruauto measures it on the Keysight EXM, and the traps found while bringing up Band 8. The RX side (§7.3 static sensitivity) is covered in G2SENS01.
One GSM burst and its power-vs-time mask (schematic, not to scale)
BTS mask shapes: TS 45.005 §4.5.1 + Annex B (Fig B.1 GMSK, Fig B.2 8-PSK), 300 kHz measurement bandwidth. §4.5.2 is the MS mask, which is a common citation mistake.
Level 1 — the six TX tests and their limits
Band 8 (GSM 900) numbers used throughout: DL 925–960 MHz, UL 880–915 MHz. E-GSM ARFCN 975 = 925.2 MHz. P-GSM ARFCN n (1–124) gives FDL = 935 + 0.2·n MHz. E-GSM n (975–1023) gives FDL = 935 + 0.2·(n − 1024) MHz. The bench carriers were 925.2 (BCCH), 925.8, 926.4 and 927.0 MHz, 0.6 MHz apart.
§TestWhat it provesEXM appCore limit (normal conditions)
6.2Modulation accuracythe burst is modulated cleanly and on frequencyPFError (GMSK) / EEVM (8-PSK)GMSK: phase error ≤5° RMS, ≤20° peak. Frequency error ≤0.05 ppm (≈±46 Hz at 925 MHz). 8-PSK: EVM ≤7 % RMS, ≤22 % peak, 95th percentile ≤11 %
6.3Mean transmitted RF carrier powerpower at each TX antenna connector matches the declared value; static power steps workTXPower±2 dB of declared max (±2.5 dB extreme). Static power control in 2 dB steps, at least 6 steps (Nmax)
6.4Transmitted RF carrier power vs timeburst shape fits the mask; power is stable over the useful part; idle slots are quietEPVTime (not PVTime)Annex B mask, averaged over 100 bursts. Residual on an unactivated timeslot ≤−30 dBc. Tested at Pmax and Pmin
6.5Adjacent channel power (ORFS)spectrum due to modulation and due to switching transients stays inside the offset tableEORFspectrrelative limits per offset, with an absolute floor of −65 dBm (§6.5.1.4.1)
6.6.1Spurious, in the TX bandno discrete spurs near the carrierswept SA + peak marker−36 dBm. RBW 30 kHz for 1.8–6 MHz offsets, 100 kHz for ≥6 MHz, clipped to the band edges
6.6.2Spurious, outside the TX bandno leakage into the own RX band or co-sited systemsswept SA, absolute windowsown RX 880–915: −98 dBm. DCS1800 TX 1805–1880: −47 dBm. DCS1800 RX (co-site) 1710–1785: −98 dBm. UTRA bands: −62 dBm (100 kHz RBW)
Terms: TRX is one transceiver (carrier). The bench had 4: 1 BCCH + 3 TCH. BCCH is configured but is not one of the measured TRX in §6.4. Pmax/Pmin are the highest and lowest static power levels from §6.3.
Level 2 — how ruauto runs it on the EXM
Road-trip order. test_2g_tx_road_trip nests the loops as band → carrier frequency (bottom/middle/top) → modulation (GMSK, 8-PSK) → topology variant (single_trx_4ant, multi_trx_4ant) → test. §6.3 runs before §6.2/6.4/6.5 because it caches Pmax. The cache key is (band, freq, mod, trx_mode, ant, trx) and the TTL is 1800 s, which is long enough to survive the ~15 min §6.2 run in between. Every sub-test is wrapped in its own try/except, and the traceback goes to pw_log. Without that, one exception silently ended the whole matrix and the run looked as if it had "just stopped early".

Trigger = IMMediate everywhere. RFBurst triggering was removed (GRDEV-6844). The EXM finds T0 by correlating on the midamble training sequence (TSC) inside the captured buffer, so the trigger choice does not move T0.

Five XMLs drive one 2G carrier setup:
XMLLayerResponsibility
oammgrconfig.xmlHW / M-planeRRH type (rrhType)
vran2gconfig.xmlL1trx2AntMap (which TRX goes to which antenna)
CH_FREQ_B<n>_CC0_4ANT.xml + ACTIVE_B<nn>C00*.xmlRU M-planecarrier frequencies and which array-carriers are active
rctCfg.xmlL2TRX table: trxId, dlFrequencyHz, antennaPort, carrIdx
rctCmdList.xmlL2command order: cellSetup + paired tchSetup / tchDlFpConfig
§6.4 slot activation is special. The other tests use a live run_sequence. For PvT that raced the XML-driven activation. Instead the harness rewrites rctCmdList.xml with one adjacent tchSetup + tchDlFpConfig pair per (TRX, TS). The UE slot index is ueIndex = TRX×8 + TS, so TRX1–3 on TS4 give 12/20/28. It then restarts phystart and waits about 15 s. Grouping all tchSetups first and all tchDlFpConfigs second caused an earlier "only the last TRX radiates" bug. The original file is backed up and restored per variant. A dirty flag lives on the test instance so that teardown restores it even after an exception.

The PvT SCPI recipe that gives a real verdict (condensed):
INST:SEL GSM
:CONFigure:EPVTime
:SENSe:EPVTime:MASK:LIST:UPPer:TIME ... / :RELative ... / :ABSolute ...
:SENSe:EPVTime:MASK:LIST:LOWer:TIME ... / :RELative ... / :ABSolute ...
:SENSe:EPVTime:MASK:SELect CUSTom      <- use OUR list, not the built-in preset
:CALCulate:EPVTime:LIMit:TEST ON       <- enable limit evaluation
:SENSe:EPVTime:AVERage:STATe ON
:SENSe:EPVTime:AVERage:COUNt 100       <- N bursts = N acquisitions
:INITiate:CONTinuous OFF               <- single sweep, so *OPC? waits for all 100
:INITiate:REST
*OPC?
:FETCh:EPVTime10?                      <- 19 scalars: power averaged, mask result, stability...
:FETCh:EPVTime2?                       <- trace
:CALCulate:CLIMits:FAIL?               <- 0 = pass against the SELECTED mask
Pmin is calculated, not measured: Pmin = Pmax − Nmax·2 dB, with Nmax = 6 by default. The xlsx column says "Pmin dBm (calculated)" on purpose. §6.4 really wants a measured lowest static step, so do not quote this value as a conformance result. §6.5 uses switching-transient averaging type MAXimum. ORFS is skipped in multi_trx, because multi-carrier ORFS is a separate case (§6.12); leaving it on produced 28 false fails. §6.6.2 covers only the ≤6 GHz subset that the EXM can reach. The full 100 kHz–12.75 GHz sweep is out of scope. The −98 dBm windows sit below a single-sweep noise floor, so the harness turns on the preamp and uses RMS averaging. That lowered the floor from about −85/−94 to −102/−107 dBm. A noise-floor guard reports Info (TE noise-limited) instead of a false FAIL when the limit is below what the instrument can see.
Level 3 — traps and a real RCA
1. The CUSTom-mask trap. The harness loaded a deliberately "wide-open" custom mask, yet perfect bursts still came back Fail. The cause: loading MASK:LIST only fills the custom slot. The EXM default is MASK:SELect STANdard, so CLIMits:FAIL? kept judging against the built-in Annex B mask, with its ±1 dB inner tolerance, and the ~1.9 dB-unstable burst failed. Fix: send SELect CUSTom + LIMit:TEST ON, and read back MASK:SELect? (expect CUST) and LIMit:TEST? (expect 1) as a diagnostic.

2. Phantom rows and hollow passes. One run had a TRX whose TXPower probe read −92 dBm (silent), yet EPVTime reported −14.5 dBm with plausible stability. That was a measurement of nothing. The fix is a per-(ant, TRX) gate: probe power just before acquisition and skip if ≤−50 dBm. Similarly, §6.2 once reported "Pass" while every EVM and IQ-offset field was nan, so only frequency error had been checked. And §7.3 once passed at ~100 % CRC error. Rule: a verdict must depend on every measured sub-metric being numeric and in limits. It must never depend on the commanded power alone.

3. The Band-8 "two dead antennas" RCA, a lesson in hypotheses. On a 4-antenna multi-band RU (Integrity-ME B1B3B8B41), §6.3 failed all 28 rows. Two antennas read about −69 dBm (noise) and two read about −14.5 dBm, which is +3.5 dB over the −18 dBm nominal. The investigation went through three rounds:
HypothesisWhy it looked rightWhy it was rejected
A docker product class overrode the XML update and skipped forcing trx2AntMap to 1:1 (a combiner map folds 4 TRX onto 2 antennas)the override really did omit the call (a real latent code bug, fixed with a shared helper)a forced 1:1 map gave the same 2-live / 2-dead pattern, and so did single_trx, where all TRX share one frequency
cable_loss.json has no Band-8 entriesthe top-level keys looked like frequenciesthe keys (5025/5125/5225/5325) are EXM port IDs. Under each port there are ~2200 frequency points from 500 kHz to 6 GHz, including ~925 MHz. A real ~−4.2 dB B8 correction was applied
RU personality: the CFR/DPD pulse-configs give band 8 antenna-bitmask 3 (A0+A1) and the B20/B28 group ("band 9999") bitmask 12 (A2+A3)OAM showed both pair-carriers READY/ACTIVE and ModifyPA on all 4 antennas, so the limit lives below OAM. Proposed fix: a 2-antenna B8 topologylater PvT logs showed ant3/trx3 at −14.6 dBm "TX OK", then −92 dBm about 6 s later. Carriers flapped on every TRX, so the PvT master doc marks "B8 = A0/A1 only" as superseded. Other status docs still treat A2/A3 as not meaningful. Treat it as open
What to take away: (a) check the RU personality and antenna bitmask before blaming automation. (b) Decode what config keys mean before calling them "missing". (c) Write each hypothesis down with its disproof, so it is not re-adopted later. (d) When OAM says READY but the analyzer says noise, the fault is in the FPGA/PHY/activation layer, and you need PHY/L2 logs. Two real product findings came out of the same campaign: the live B8 carriers run about 2–3.5 dB hot against the declared nominal (still open), and TX-to-own-RX leakage of −91.4 dBm in 880–915 MHz against the −98 dBm §6.6.2 limit. The preamp-lowered floor showed that one as a genuine emission 11–16 dB above the floor.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why does ruauto run §6.3 before §6.4 and §6.5?
A: §6.3 measures Pmax per (band, freq, mod, trx_mode, ant, trx) and caches it for 1800 s. PvT needs Pmax (and a Pmin derived from it), and ORFS needs the carrier power reference. If §6.4 runs on its own, it measures Pmax inline.
Q: Your PvT mask verdict is Fail on bursts that look perfect, even with a very loose custom mask. What do you check?
A: Whether the custom mask is actually selected. The EXM defaults to EPVTime:MASK:SELect STANdard, so CLIMits:FAIL? evaluates the built-in Annex B mask. Send SELect CUSTom and CALC:EPVT:LIM:TEST ON, then read them back.
Q: What is the "useful part" of a GSM burst, and where is T0?
A: The 147 bits centred on T0, the transition between bits 13 and 14 of the 26-bit training sequence (midamble). Mean power and stability are computed over it. The analyzer finds T0 by TSC correlation, so an IMMediate trigger is fine.
Q: Two of four antennas read noise floor on Band 8 while OAM shows every carrier READY. How do you proceed?
A: Confirm the pattern follows the TRX/antenna and not the analyzer port. Check whether it also happens in single_trx. Then read the RU personality (per-band antenna bitmask in the CFR/DPD pulse config) and the RU operations-manager log for ModifyPA. If OAM is correct, collect PHY/L2 logs around activation. Rule out config-key misreads such as cable-loss port IDs before blaming calibration.
Q: Why can an out-of-band spurious test report "Info (TE noise-limited)" instead of Fail?
A: Limits like −98 dBm in the own RX band can sit below the analyzer floor for a single sweep. The harness adds the preamp and RMS averaging. If a reading is still at the instrument floor and the limit is below that floor, the result cannot be judged, so it is flagged Info rather than a false Fail. A reading clearly above the floor, like the −91.4 dBm RX-band leak, still fails.
BLK01 In-band Blocking — where the interferer may sit: Group A/B/C windows, the 7.5 MHz guard & worked examples (extends FC14) RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
FC14 introduced the blocking family. This card answers the practical question: at which frequencies may the lab put the interferer? Picture your base station listening to a quiet phone (the wanted signal), while a strong 5 MHz LTE signal from someone else transmits nearby. The standard says: do not put that interferer right on top of the phone (that would be co-channel, a different test). Keep it at least 7.5 MHz from the edge of the wanted channel, and anywhere inside a window around the uplink band. The window is usually 20 MHz beyond each band edge. It is shorter on the side where the operator's own downlink band starts, because that region is protected by the duplexer and by other requirements. The receiver passes if it still decodes at least 95 % of the throughput.
Where the interferer centre may sit: Band 8, 10 MHz channel at Fc = 897.5 MHz (Group B)
The allowed zones are the green boxes. The upper zone ends at 925 MHz, exactly where the B8 downlink begins, so it is only 15 MHz wide against 25 MHz below.
Level 1 — the rule and the band groups
TS 36.141 §7.6 / TS 36.104 §7.6: in-band blocking (LTE BS).
ParameterValue
Wanted signalFRC at PREFSENS + 6 dB (e.g. −101.5 + 6 = −95.5 dBm for a 10 MHz Wide Area BS)
Interferer5 MHz E-UTRA signal. −43 dBm (Wide Area), −38 dBm (Medium Range), −35 dBm (Local Area)
Minimum offsetinterferer centre ≥ 7.5 MHz from the wanted channel edge, so the interferer's own edge is 5 MHz away. With a 10 MHz wanted channel that protects a 25 MHz zone. (For 1.4 / 3 MHz channels the interferer matches the channel BW, with 2.1 / 4.5 MHz offsets.)
Passthroughput ≥ 95 % of maximum (BLER ≤ 5 %) at every interferer position
Out-of-band blocking (same clause)CW at −15 dBm from 1 MHz to 12.75 GHz, outside the in-band window
The three band groups (window for the interferer centre frequency):
GroupBandsWindowWhy
A1–7, 9–11, 13, 14, 18, 19, 21–24, 27, 30, 33–45, 48, 50, 52, 65, 66, 68, 70 (and others)ULlow − 20 … ULhigh + 20 MHzenough spectrum on both sides
B8, 26, 28ULlow − 20 … ULhigh + 10 MHzsmall duplex gap: the own DL band starts 10 MHz above UL (B8: 915 → 925; B28: 748 → 758)
C20, 71 (as grouped in ruauto)ULlow − 11 … ULhigh + 20 MHzreversed duplex: DL sits below UL (B20: DL top 821 = 832 − 11; B71: DL top 652 = 663 − 11)
A handy memory trick: the window always stops where the operator's own downlink starts. For a new band, check the current 36.104 table rather than guessing its group.
Level 2 — worked windows and how the harness steps them
Worked examples (10 MHz wanted channel at the band middle; the interferer centre is stepped through both ranges):
BandUL (MHz)FcWindowLower rangeUpper rangeNote
B1 (A)1920–198019501900–20001900–1937.51962.5–2000symmetric, 37.5 MHz each side
B3 (A)1710–17851747.51690–18051690–17351760–180545 MHz each side
B8 (B)880–915897.5860–925860–885910–925upper side only 15 MHz
B28 (B)703–748725.5683–758683–713738–758upper 20 vs lower 30 MHz
B20 (C)832–862847821–882821–834.5859.5–882lower side only 13.5 MHz
B71 (C)663–698680.5652–718652–668693–718lower 16 vs upper 25 MHz
How ruauto builds the list. The unified LTE RX test uses cf_range_ib when the range is "in band":
cf_range_ib = LteUtils.build_interferer_cf_range(
    Ful_low - 20,            <- window low   (Group C: -11)
    freq - bw/2 - 7.5,       <- lower range stops at the guard
    freq + bw/2 + 7.5,       <- upper range starts at the guard
    Ful_high + 20,           <- window high  (Group B: +10)
    number_of_points, step_of_1MHz=True)
With step_of_1MHz=True the generator starts at the guard edges and walks outward in exact 1 MHz steps, alternating lower and upper. So the hardest positions (closest to the wanted channel) are tested first, and the interferer never enters the guard. For B1 that is about 38 + 38 points per frequency (B/M/T) per antenna. Point count is the main driver of blocking test time, which is why blocking sits in the long P2 cadence (FC16). Each point then runs the receive check with the interferer on (search algorithm and BLER settings in FC14).
Level 3 — bugs, pitfalls and how to read a failure
1. A real window bug. For Band 8 the helper once returned a window top of 935 MHz (the Group A +20 rule) instead of 925. The interferer was then stepped 10 MHz into the B8 downlink band, a region the in-band requirement does not cover. That can create false failures, or spend time testing something the standard never asks for. After the fix, the verification table checks all four boundaries for every group: window low/high, lower-range end and upper-range start. It also checks that the guard is 25 MHz wide. Always verify the four numbers per band when adding a new band.

2. Your own signal generator can fail the test for you. The interferer is 52 dB stronger than the wanted signal (−43 vs −95.5 dBm). If the interferer generator's adjacent-channel leakage or broadband noise is poor, some of it lands inside the wanted channel. Example: with 65 dB of SG ACLR, the leaked power in the wanted channel is about −108 dBm. The receiver's own noise in 10 MHz is kTB (−104 dBm) + NF (~5 dB) ≈ −99 dBm. So the leak adds about 0.5 dB of desense before the DUT has done anything wrong. Check the SG spec (or add a band-pass filter) when blocking fails only close to the guard.

3. Reading a failure pattern. Failures only at the closest offsets point to LNA/ADC compression, SG leakage, or reciprocal mixing (LO phase noise mixing the strong interferer onto the wanted channel). Failures only near the band edge, on the side toward the other band, point to duplexer or RX filter roll-off. Failures at every offset at a fixed level suggest the AGC/DSA setting or the wanted level itself is wrong (compare with the sensitivity baseline, FC09/DSA3). The in-band interferer sits inside the duplexer passband, so the RX filter gives no help there. Linearity and gain distribution do all the work.

4. Do not confuse the tests. Adjacent channel selectivity (§7.5, interferer at −52 dBm right next to the channel) and narrow-band blocking (§7.5, 1 RB interferer at −49 dBm) cover the region inside the 7.5 MHz guard. In-band blocking covers from the guard out to the window edge. Out-of-band blocking (CW −15 dBm) covers everything beyond the window. Together they tile the whole spectrum.
Interview Q&A
Q: Where is the interferer placed in LTE in-band blocking for a 10 MHz channel?
A: Its centre frequency is stepped from the window edge (ULlow − 20 MHz for most bands) up to 7.5 MHz below the wanted channel's lower edge. On the other side it runs from 7.5 MHz above the upper edge to ULhigh + 20 MHz. The 25 MHz zone around the wanted channel is excluded. The receiver must keep ≥95 % throughput with a −43 dBm 5 MHz interferer (Wide Area).
Q: Why is the Band 8 upper window only +10 MHz?
A: Because the B8 downlink starts at 925 MHz, 10 MHz above the 915 MHz UL edge. The in-band window stops where the operator's own DL begins. Bands 26 and 28 are the same (Group B). Bands 20 and 71 have reversed duplex, so their lower side is shortened to −11 MHz instead.
Q: B1 at 1950 MHz, 10 MHz BW: give the two interferer ranges.
A: Lower: 1900 to 1937.5 MHz. Upper: 1962.5 to 2000 MHz. Wanted channel 1945–1955, guard 1937.5–1962.5.
Q: Blocking fails only at the offsets closest to the guard. What do you suspect first?
A: Check the test setup before the DUT: interferer generator ACLR/noise leaking into the wanted channel. Then check DUT linearity (LNA/ADC compression, IMD) and reciprocal mixing from LO phase noise. Compare against a run with a filtered interferer, and against the plain sensitivity result.
NRTX01 5G NR TX Conformance in ruauto — n78/n78L/n101: ON/OFF power, TAE 65 ns, SEM reference level, TDD gate delays & PA-protection polling RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
A 5G TDD radio switches from talking (downlink) to listening (uplink) many times per frame, on the same frequency. Conformance checks four things. When it talks, it must be loud enough and clean (power, EVM, ACLR, emissions). When it stops, it must be really quiet (OFF power). The switch must be quick (transient period). And all four antennas must speak in step (TAE). The analyzer has to be told when to listen. Otherwise it averages talking and silence together and every number is wrong. This card collects the implementation notes for the NR TX suite in ruauto (TS 38.104 ch.6, GRDEV-2020) on n78, n78L and n101. It also covers the PA-protection timing detail that FC11 leaves out, and corrects a few numbers in the internal doc.
TDD gating: why every NR TX measurement needs a trigger, a delay and a gate
The slot pattern is illustrative. The delay from the frame trigger to the first DL slot depends on the trigger source and the TDD pattern, so it is calibrated per bench (compare B41T for the LTE B41 case).
Level 1 — what is implemented and the limits
Test (ruauto name)38.104 clauseLimit / KPI usedNote
test_Tx_BS_Output_Power6.2diff = configured − measured, ±2.5 dB3GPP core ±2 dB, widened by the test tolerance in 38.141-1
TransmitOnOffPower_6_4 (GRDEV-6229)6.4.1 / 6.4.2OFF power < −85 dBm/MHz, averaged over 70/N µs (N = SCS/15). Transient < 10 µs both waysLTE for contrast: transient 17 µs (FC08). The conformance test limit is slightly relaxed by test tolerance
test_Tx_TimeAlignment (GRDEV-6230)6.5.3 (38.141-1 §6.6.4)KPI 65 ns + 25 ns tolerancethe internal doc labels it 6.5.4; the spec numbering is 6.5.3
test_Tx_modulation_analysis6.5.1 / 6.5.2EVM per modulation, frequency error3-sample averaging, auto-preset on error value
test_Tx_ACLR6.6.3BS requirement 45 dB (or an absolute limit, whichever is less stringent)see Level 3: the doc's −30/−33 dBc are UE-type numbers
OBUnwantedEmissions_6_6_4 / test_Tx_SEM6.6.4OBUE mask (general + narrowband)reference level rule below
SpuriousEmissions_6_6_56.6.5Cat B: −36 dBm (9 kHz–1 GHz, RBW 1/10/100 kHz), −30 dBm/1 MHz above 1 GHzneeds an analyzer with a spurious licence (PXA/UXA class)
Per-band parameters (PW_RU_5G, selected by fhgw_band):
n78n78Ln101

Level 2 — gating, read-outs and the PA-protection poll
TDD gating. Channel power uses gate view ON, a 1 ms gate (one DL slot) and 10 averages. The gate delay comes from a map keyed by the TDD configuration: config 2 → 18.46 ms (calibrated on one vendor's RU), config 3 → 21 ms, anything else → 15.3 ms. A wrong delay puts the gate on UL or guard symbols, so power reads low and ACLR/EVM look terrible. The n78 SmokeTest group uses ext_trig_delay = 0.00998675 s (about 9.99 ms, close to one 10 ms frame minus a small offset, the same idea as the B41 9.9765 ms in B41T).
sa_set_gate_view_state('ON')
sa_set_trigger_gate_length(0.001)                           <- :SENSe:PVTime:GATE:LENGth
sa_set_trigger_gate_delay(tdd_gate_delay_map.get(cfg, '15.3 ms'))  <- :GATE:DELay
ON/OFF:  :CONF:PVT  ->  :INIT:PVT   with   :TRIG:PVT:SOUR EXT2
TAE:     :DISPlay:EVM:VIEW MIMO ; :SENSe:RADio:MIMO:STATe 1 ; :FETCH:EVM000030?
TAE read-out. The MIMO summary table is one comma-separated list. The TAE values sit at indices [6, 28, 50, 72, 94]. The harness takes abs(), drops values ≥1e30 (the analyzer's "invalid" marker) and reports the max. If nothing is valid it returns −999, which fails the test. The validator gives three states: ≤65 ns Pass, 65–90 ns Marginal, above 90 ns Fail. The usual −999 fixes: MIMO state not enabled, signal below about −30 dBm at the analyzer, or a misaligned TDD trigger. Then preset, wait ~3 s and read again.

SEM reference level. This is the analyzer reference level (headroom above the average power), not a limit. OFDM test models peak several dB above average. Too low a reference level clips the analyzer's front end/ADC, and the clipping splatter looks like DUT emissions. Too high a level buries the mask in analyzer noise. The harness uses +7 dB for the wideband n78 carriers and +6 dB for the 10 MHz n101 carrier.

PA protection (test_Tx_Pa_Protection, GRDEV-6801). The method: read the FHGW DAC current at nominal (carrier inactive) with rfdc-app --debug, activate the carrier, then poll for 25 s. That window covers the ~10 s gain_delay_time PA-warm-up plateau plus ~15 s of carrier-ready latency. The harness latches the deepest dip per DAC block and passes if the reduction is 3.0 ± 0.2 dB. Polling replaced a single timed read that failed whenever the carrier came up late. A result near 0 dB is logged with both possible causes: the PA really is off, or the carrier took longer than the window to reach READY. In 5G it runs once at the top of test_main_procedure, before the per-group loop, and a FAIL does not abort the suite. DAC_MAP maps (fhgw_band, band) to tiles/blocks, and a missing row raises a clear RuntimeError.

SmokeTest path (GRDEV-6620). A group whose Tests list contains test_PreChecks starts TX (M-plane update → TM → PHY), runs the n78 pre-checks (FC12), writes the PreChecks sheet, calls pytest.fail() if the overall result is FAIL, and then breaks the group loop. A smoke run never continues into conformance.
Level 3 — corrections and pitfalls
1. ACLR numbers in the internal doc. The doc says "offset A < −30 dBc, offset B < −33 dBc". Those match the UE ACLR requirements (NR 30 dB, UTRA 33 dB). The NR BS requirement in 38.104 §6.6.3 is 45 dB for the first and second adjacent channels, with an absolute alternative, so the less stringent of the two applies. PW KPI tables also gate at about 45 dB (KPI01, ACLREVM01). If a report passes at 31 dB against the doc limit, the conformance claim is wrong.

2. The spurious sweep must go higher than you think. For NR the upper end of the spurious range is 12.75 GHz or the 5th harmonic of the upper DL band edge, whichever is greater. For n78 (3.8 GHz) that is 19 GHz. An EXM-class analyzer tops out near 6 GHz, which is why the doc insists on a PXA/UXA-class analyzer for 6.6.5. Also plan a high-pass or notch filter so the carrier does not overload the analyzer while it looks for −30 dBm harmonics.

3. OFF power is a noise-floor measurement. −85 dBm/MHz sits just above an unpreamped analyzer's floor. Add a 30 dB coupler/attenuator and it may not be measurable at all. The 70/N µs window is short: at 30 kHz SCS, N = 2, so about 35 µs. The trigger must place that window inside the UL period and away from the ramps. Check the analyzer floor with the DUT off before trusting an OFF-power pass.

4. Pattern labels in comments are not the pattern. The gate-delay map comments describe config 2 and 3 with slot strings that do not match the usual LTE UL/DL configuration table. Derive the gate from the actual configured slot pattern and trigger offset, and re-calibrate the delay on each bench and RU vendor. "Calibrated on one vendor's RU" is the honest label.

5. TAE is a relative number. A 20 cm cable-length mismatch is about 1 ns, so cables rarely explain a 100 ns TAE. Look at per-chain digital delay, JESD lane alignment or a mis-set per-antenna delay compensation (FC05). And remember that TAE compares antenna connectors. Measuring through unequal splitter paths adds error of your own.
Interview Q&A
Q: What does the TX ON/OFF power test check on an NR TDD BS, and what are the limits?
A: In UL periods the transmitter OFF power must be below −85 dBm/MHz, averaged over 70/N µs with N = SCS/15. The OFF→ON and ON→OFF transient periods must each be under 10 µs (LTE allows 17 µs). It protects the BS's own and neighbouring receivers in the UL slots.
Q: Your NR ACLR test passes at 32 dB. Is the radio conformant?
A: No. 32 dB passes the UE-style −30 dBc limit printed in the internal doc, but the BS requirement in 38.104 is 45 dB (or the absolute limit, if that is less stringent). Check which limit the KPI file actually applies.
Q: TAE comes back as −999. What happened?
A: −999 is the harness sentinel for "no valid TAE value in the MIMO table". Enable :SENS:RAD:MIMO:STAT 1, make sure every chain is above about −30 dBm at the analyzer, and check the TDD trigger/gate. Then preset and re-read.
Q: Why does the PA-protection test poll for 25 s instead of reading once?
A: The 3 dB reduction appears after carrier activation. It lasts through a ~10 s gain-delay plateau, and the carrier itself can take up to ~15 s to become READY. A single timed read missed the dip whenever activation was slow. Polling and latching the deepest dip removes that race.
Q: How high must a conducted spurious sweep go for n78?
A: To the greater of 12.75 GHz and the 5th harmonic of the upper DL band edge. For n78 (3.8 GHz) that is 19 GHz, so a PXA/UXA-class analyzer is needed, not an EXM.
UPERF01 Conformance Clause 8 — UL performance tests: PUSCH / PUCCH / PRACH under fading (EPA/EVA/ETU, IRC, HARQ) RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
Clause 7 asks whether the receiver hears a clean signal (sensitivity, blocking). Clause 8 asks whether it still understands a real, messy uplink. The phone is moving, the signal bounces off buildings, and it fades up and down many times a second. So the lab sends standard uplink channels (PUSCH data, PUCCH control, PRACH access) through a fading simulator and adds noise to a set SNR. It then checks that the base station still decodes enough data, detects enough ACKs, or finds enough preambles. Think of a driving test on a wet, bumpy road instead of an empty car park. PRACH (§8.4) already has its own cards (FC10, PRA01, PRACHDM01). This card covers the PUSCH and PUCCH part.
A clause-8 test chain
The TX of the BS can be off. Single carrier only. Tested at the middle frequency, and at the lowest and highest supported channel bandwidths.
Level 1 — channel models and the test list
Propagation models (LTE, TS 36.141 Annex B):
ModelMeaningTaps / max excess delayDoppler used
EPAExtended Pedestrian A: short delay spread7 taps / 410 ns5 Hz
EVAExtended Vehicular A: medium9 taps / 2510 ns5 Hz, 70 Hz
ETUExtended Typical Urban: long delay spread9 taps / 5000 ns70 Hz, 300 Hz
Names read as model + Doppler, e.g. EVA70 = EVA at 70 Hz maximum Doppler. NR (38.141-1 clause 8) uses TDL models the same way: TDLA30-10, TDLB100-400, TDLC300-100 (delay spread in ns, then Doppler in Hz).

LTE clause 8 test list (TS 36.141):
ClauseTestPass metric
