Level 2 — how the tests are run
A PUSCH example. 5 MHz, 2 RX antennas, normal CP, EPA5, FRC A3-4. The requirement is 30 % of maximum throughput at −4.1 dB SNR. The procedure: set AWGN to the level in the configuration table, set the FRC, channel model and SNR from the requirement table, run with HARQ retransmissions, and count correctly decoded transport blocks. Throughput = decoded bits / time, compared with the FRC maximum.

PUCCH detection tests alternate "PUCCH sent" and "nothing sent" (noise only, or noise + interferers in the multi-user case). ACK/NACK repetition is disabled. Missed ACKs are counted in the sent periods, and false ACKs in the idle periods. Format 1a carries 1 bit. Format 1b with channel selection carries 4 encoded bits for up to 2 CCs. Format 3 carries up to 10 ACK bits + SR in FDD (20 in TDD), for up to 5 CCs. LTE has formats 1/1a/1b/2/2a/2b/3/4/5 in total.

TTI bundling (8.2.5). Normally a NACK costs an 8 ms round trip before the retransmission. With bundling the UE sends the same PUSCH in 4 consecutive subframes. In the test a new transport block starts every 20 ms, and the residual BLER after HARQ must be < 2 %: A/B, where A = blocks still wrong after retransmissions and B = blocks sent, not counting repeats.

IRC tests (8.2.6/8.2.6A) add dominant interferers on the same RBs, modelling a nearby UE in the next cell: 1 interferer for 2 RX, 2 for 4–8 RX, 16QAM. The asynchronous version offsets the interferers by 0.33 ms, so they do not line up with the wanted subframes. The receiver must use interference rejection combining: it estimates the interference's spatial covariance across the RX branches and steers a null at it. MRC only maximises the wanted SNR and would fail.

Equipment. You need a UE emulator or signal generator with FRC waveforms, a multi-channel fading emulator (one independently faded path per BS RX port, with the defined antenna correlation), and calibrated AWGN. The BS side supplies CRC/ACK/CQI statistics from L1. An internal 2021 overview notes these tests were not part of band qualification. They sit with PHY/receiver validation (compare the third-party PHY matrix, PHYT01), while the lab inventory lists channel emulators among the extra equipment (FWK6).
Level 3 — what makes clause-8 results trustworthy
1. Is HARQ really closed-loop? Throughput requirements assume the UE retransmits after the BS sends NACK. A plain signal generator that plays a fixed waveform cannot react. What you measure then is first-transmission BLER, not HARQ throughput. That is a useful engineering number, but it is not the clause-8 result, so label it. Conformance-grade setups use an emulator that decodes the BS's HARQ feedback (or a defined fixed-retransmission pattern the standard allows).

2. SNR is per receive antenna and the curves are steep. Near the 70 % point a 0.5 dB SNR error can move throughput by 10–20 points. Calibrate the fader's insertion loss per path. Check that the AWGN covers the whole signal bandwidth. Leave crest-factor headroom, because fading adds deep peaks and a clipped generator output adds hidden distortion. Verify the noise level on each RX branch separately. An unbalanced branch looks like a bad receiver.

3. Correlation and timing matter. Fading paths that are more correlated than specified remove diversity gain, and the DUT fails through no fault of its own. The UL timing adjustment test uses a moving propagation condition, where the path delay slides back and forth. It exercises the BS timing-advance loop, so it fails for a slow or wrong TA estimator, not for poor sensitivity.

4. Watch for errors in slides and summaries. One internal slide says the moving UE's throughput "shall be ≤ 70 %". The requirement is ≥ 70 %. Detection probabilities are floors (≥ 0.99). False-alarm and NACK→ACK rates are ceilings. When in doubt, reason about which direction is "good" for the operator.
Interview Q&A
Q: How do clause 7 and clause 8 of TS 36.141 differ?
A: Clause 7 covers RF receiver characteristics with static, clean signals: sensitivity, dynamic range, selectivity, blocking, IMD. Clause 8 covers performance: demodulation of PUSCH/PUCCH/PRACH under multipath fading and noise at a defined SNR, with throughput or detection-probability metrics.
Q: What do EPA5, EVA70 and ETU300 mean?
A: Channel model plus maximum Doppler. EPA is short delay spread (410 ns), EVA medium (2.5 µs), ETU long (5 µs). 5/70/300 Hz is the Doppler, i.e. how fast the fading varies. That relates to UE speed and carrier frequency.
Q: What is the pass criterion for PUCCH format 1a ACK detection?
A: At the specified SNR, the ACK detection probability must be at least 0.99 when ACK is sent, and the false-detection probability at most 0.01 when only noise is present.
Q: Why do the Type-A interference tests require an IRC receiver?
A: A dominant co-channel interferer on the same RBs cannot be removed by MRC, which only maximises the wanted SNR. IRC uses the interference covariance across the RX antennas to null it. With N RX antennas it can suppress up to N−1 strong interferers, hence 1 interferer for 2 RX and 2 for 4 or more RX.
Q: Your PUSCH fading result is 8 points below the requirement. What do you check before blaming the PHY?
A: SNR calibration per RX branch (fader loss, AWGN level and bandwidth), fading correlation settings, generator headroom/clipping, and whether HARQ is really closed-loop. Then check the FRC and the channel-model configuration against the requirement table.
OTA01 OTA Conformance Method — EIS, EIRP/TRP, chamber path loss & SG = EIS_target + PathLoss RCT click to expand ▾
In plain English
An AAU or active antenna has no cable connector to clip the analyzer onto. The radio and the antenna are one box. So the lab tests it the way a phone would see it: over the air, inside a shielded, echo-free room (an anechoic chamber). Because the air, the cables and the probe antenna all lose signal, the lab first measures that loss, the path loss, at every frequency and angle. It then adds it back to every reading. For receive tests, the question becomes "how weak can a signal arriving from this direction be and still be decoded?" That is EIS. For transmit tests, it is "how much power comes out in this direction" (EIRP) and "how much in total over the whole sphere" (TRP). SPEC03 lists the NR OTA clauses. This card explains the method and the arithmetic.
The OTA measurement chain and the two formulas that matter
The path-loss table is indexed by (port/polarisation, frequency, azimuth, elevation). It replaces the per-port cable-loss calibration used for conducted tests.
Level 1 — the vocabulary
TermMeaningUsed for
EIRPeffective isotropic radiated power: the power an ideal isotropic antenna would need to give the same field in that direction (P + antenna gain)radiated transmit power per declared beam/direction (NR 38.104 §9 / 38.141-2 §6.2)
TRPtotal radiated power: EIRP integrated over the whole sphere, /4π, both polarisations summedOTA BS output power, and OTA ACLR / unwanted emissions / spurious (TRP-based)
EISequivalent isotropic sensitivity: the power arriving at an ideal isotropic antenna position, from a given direction, that still gives the reference throughput (≥95 %)OTA sensitivity (over the declared direction range) and OTA REFSENS
Path losseverything between the instrument port and the DUT reference point: cable + free-space loss − probe gaincorrecting every SG/SA level
Far fielddistance where the wave front is flat enough: R > 2D²/λ (D = largest DUT dimension)deciding whether a chamber is big enough
Which spec? NR: BS type 1-C is conducted only (38.141-1). 1-H is hybrid, with conducted tests at the transceiver-array connectors plus some OTA. 1-O (FR1) and 2-O (FR2) are fully OTA (38.141-2). For LTE/multi-RAT active antenna systems the equivalent split is TS 37.105 (requirements) with TS 37.145-1 (conducted) and TS 37.145-2 (OTA). The OTA-only requirements are directional: radiated transmit power (EIRP), OTA sensitivity (EIS), spatial emissions.
Level 2 — the arithmetic, step by step
RX worked example (illustrative numbers from an internal draft plan). B3, middle frequency 1747.5 MHz. The target EIS is taken equal to the conducted REFSENS, −101.5 dBm, for illustration. The chamber boresight path loss is 75 dB (feed cable + horn + free space).
SG_amplitude = EIS_target + PathLoss(f, az, el)
             = -101.5 dBm + 75 dB = -26.5 dBm     (gate window e.g. -28.5 ... -24.5 dBm)

Search down until BLER > 5 %, keep the lowest passing SG level:
EIS_measured = SG_min - PathLoss = -27.0 - 75 = -102.0 dBm   -> 0.5 dB better than target
Pass: BLER ≤ 5 % at every (frequency, az, el) point, with at least boresight (az 0°, el 0°), using the A3-x FRC family (A3-4 to A3-7 by bandwidth). For TDD (B41) the SG must burst in step with the UL subframes: :RAD:LTE:UL:TDD:CONF 3, :SSFR 8, TRIG:SOUR FRAME, BURS:STAT ON. A continuous SG would also put energy into DL periods.

TX worked example. B3, 1842.5 MHz, path loss for that TX port at boresight 42.1 dB. It is entered on the SA as an external-gain correction of :CORR:BTS:GAIN -42.1 (loss = negative gain), so the SA reads the value referred to the DUT. Prated = −15.7 dBm. A reading of −15.3 dBm is 0.4 dB off, which passes a ±1.5 dB gate. A reading of −17.6 dBm is 1.9 dB off and fails. Re-run the SA auto-level after each correction, because every (port, freq, angle) has a different path loss.

Sanity-check the path loss with Friis. Free-space loss = 20·log10(4πR/λ). At 1842.5 MHz (λ = 0.163 m) and R = 3 m that gives about 47.3 dB. Subtract a probe horn gain of about 8 dBi and add a few dB of cable, and you land near the 42 dB above. If a table value is 10 dB away from that estimate, suspect the table before the DUT.

Far field check. A 0.3 m radiating aperture at 1.84 GHz needs R > 2·0.3²/0.163 ≈ 1.1 m, which is easy. A 1.6 m multi-band AAU at 700 MHz (λ = 0.43 m) needs about 12 m. That is why large arrays are measured in compact antenna test ranges (a reflector makes a plane wave at short range) or by near-field scanning with a transform.
Level 3 — calibration, polarisation and draft-plan pitfalls
1. How the path-loss table is made. Put a reference antenna of known gain (a standard-gain horn) at the DUT position. Measure the transfer from the instrument port at every frequency, polarisation and (if the probe moves) angle. The table then holds "instrument port to isotropic point at the DUT". Any change of cable, probe, connector torque or chamber layout invalidates it. The draft plan also asks for a 15-minute settle after positioner moves (thermal drift) and a check that the positioner is in hold.

2. Polarisation. AAUs usually use ±45° dual-polarised elements. EIRP and EIS are defined for the total over two orthogonal polarisations. For power you measure both and power-sum them. For sensitivity you either drive a known polarisation and account for it, or use a dual-pol probe. Measuring only one linear polarisation against a slant element under-reads by up to about 3 dB.

3. TRP is not EIRP at boresight. TRP needs a sphere (or a standard-accepted reduced grid, or a beam-based approximation). One boresight point measures EIRP. The per-port "OTA output power" in the draft plan is really a path-loss-corrected power referred to the antenna port. That is useful for bring-up, but it is not a TRP or EIRP conformance number.

4. Ratios survive, sign conventions do not. ACLR measured OTA keeps its value, because path loss is flat to about 0.1 dB across ±2 BW and cancels in the ratio. But the draft plan's worked example concludes that −47.0 dBc fails a −45 dBc gate, calling more negative "worse". That is backwards. 47 dB of adjacent-channel suppression is better than 45 dB and passes. Always write ACLR as a positive ratio and compare magnitudes.

5. Treat the internal OTA plan as a draft. It still has TBDs: the OTA pass gates, positioner control commands and the per-antenna boresight table. In the middle of its RX example it even corrects itself after first computing an impossible +48.5 dBm SG level. The solid parts are the method, the formulas and the TDD SG gating. OTA uncertainty is larger than conducted, so the standards allow larger test tolerances (roughly 1–2 dB against ~0.7 dB conducted), and internal gates should not simply copy conducted ones.
Interview Q&A
Q: What is EIS and how do you measure it?
A: Equivalent isotropic sensitivity: the lowest power, referred to an ideal isotropic antenna at the DUT position, arriving from a given direction, at which the receiver still meets the reference throughput (BLER ≤ 5 %). You search the SG level down and subtract the calibrated path loss: EIS = SGmin − PathLoss(f, az, el).
Q: Your chamber path loss is 75 dB and the EIS target is −101.5 dBm. What SG level do you set?
A: SG = EIS_target + PathLoss = −101.5 + 75 = −26.5 dBm, re-evaluated for each frequency and angle because the path loss changes.
Q: EIRP vs TRP: when is each used?
A: EIRP is directional (per beam or direction) and is used for radiated transmit power declarations. TRP is the sphere-integrated total and is used for OTA output power and for unwanted emissions (ACLR, OBUE, spurious), where interference to others does not depend on one direction.
Q: Why does a 1.6 m AAU need a compact range or near-field system?
A: The far-field distance 2D²/λ is about 12 m at 700 MHz for D = 1.6 m. That is far beyond a normal anechoic chamber. A compact antenna test range makes a plane wave with a reflector at short distance. Near-field scanning measures close in and transforms the result to far field.
Q: An OTA report shows ACLR = −47 dBc marked FAIL against a −45 dBc limit. Comment.
A: The verdict logic is inverted. −47 dBc means the adjacent channel is 47 dB below the carrier, which is better than the 45 dB requirement, so it passes. Compare magnitudes of the ratio, and fix the comparison in the harness.
